posts.title: Build the (a + b)³ proof in 3D
Animate a finished character
posts.text:
Animate a finished character
All tutorials
One character, two baked clips and a timeline. Read what the file carries, start the body on cue, keep a camera on a character who walks, and check every claim by sampling the pose at a time and reading the numbers. It also says plainly where this scene stopped working.
Where the character comes from, and the credit. The character is made outside Strata, with three browser tools from the Web-CLI family, all of which run on your device (their pages say nothing leaves it). Character creation: portrait.webcli.app (portrait-webCLI: a photo in, a VRM out whose face blendshapes are driven from the face it read; the shape and colour matching is described on its page as a rough nudge, not a likeness) and look.webcli.app (look-webCLI: a VRM in, an edited VRM out, with its textures, colours, materials, outfits and accessories changed). Animation rigging: rig.webcli.app (bodyrig-webCLI: retargets BVH, FBX or GLB motion, and ARKit-52 face records, onto a skinned character and exports one GLB with every animation as its own named track). This page starts where they stop: with the finished file open in Strata.
What you'll need. The scene, facebind.json in tejaswigowda/test1, pinned to a commit (it opens without a token; it is a 21 MB scene with its geometry and textures beside it, so give it half a minute). Open the Shell tab and paste each block in order. Each Shell line is its own scope: a const on one line is gone on the next, so the blocks below repeat the selector instead of naming it.
The scene as it opens, held at 6 s with holdTimelineAt(6): the body clip is playing, and the character is in the middle of the frame.
1 Give the character a name you can type
The importer names the character's group after the file and derives a class from it, .vroidv110femalev1132-tracksglb. Add a short class and use that from now on:
tagClass(scene.children[0], 'actor'); $S('.actor').count()
1
(End the line with the count: tagClass on its own returns the whole object, and the Shell prints all of it.)
2 Read what the file carries
The scene has 198 objects, 22,021 vertices and 32,914 triangles. Most of that is 73 skinned meshes (56 of them pieces of hair) sharing one skeleton of 118 bones, and three animations:
editor.scene.animations.map(a => a.name + ': ' + a.duration.toFixed(1) + ' s, ' + a.tracks.length + ' tracks')
[ "Timeline: 35.1 s, 0 tracks", "test: 33.1 s, 119 tracks", "testface: 11.5 s, 9 tracks" ]
Animation What it is Timeline The scene's own clock (35.1 s), with no tracks of its own: the timeline in step 3 drives the other two. test The body: 994 keys at 30 frames a second over 33.1 s, on 118 rotation tracks (one per bone) and one position track (the hips, J_Bip_C_Hips). The hips position is the character's root motion: she does not dance on the spot. testface The face: 346 keys over 11.5 s, as one morph-weight track on each of the nine face meshes. Each mesh has 124 morph targets, the VRoid expressions (Fcl_MTH_A, Fcl_EYE_Close, …) and the 52 ARKit names (jawOpen, mouthSmileLeft, eyeBlinkLeft, …). The clip moves 44 of the 124 by more than 0.05.
The file is named …_2-tracks.glb: two tracks, the body and the face. They are baked data, and Strata does not edit their keys. What you author is control: which clip, when, how fast, and what lies over it.
3 The timeline is two events
The scene's clock, editor.timeline, holds one play event per clip:
JSON.stringify(editor.timeline.toJSON().tracks.map(t => [t.target, t.events.map(e => [e.at, e.op, +e.dur.toFixed(1)])]))
[["#test",[[2,"play",33.1]]],["#testface",[[0,"play",11.5]]]]
The body starts at 2 s and the face at 0. To see what that does, holdTimelineAt(t) jumps the whole scene to t seconds, and then the bones and the morph weights can be read like any other property. Run it at a few times and read the hips, one upper-arm bone and the total morph weight on the face:
holdTimelineAt(6); JSON.stringify([scene.getObjectByName('J_Bip_C_Hips').position, scene.getObjectByName('J_Bip_R_UpperArm').quaternion].map(v => v.toArray().map(x => +x.toFixed(3))))
[[-0.766,0.82,-1.069],[-0.167,0.511,-0.363,0.761]]
The same reading at eight times (measured on this scene; the face column is the sum of the absolute morph weights on the first face mesh, Facebaked_custom):
t (s) hips (x, y, z) arm quaternion face 0 −0.397, 0.848, −0.577 0.027, 0.149, −0.306, 0.940 9.573 1.9 −0.397, 0.848, −0.577 0.027, 0.149, −0.306, 0.940 4.751 2 −0.397, 0.848, −0.577 0.027, 0.149, −0.306, 0.940 9.358 6 −0.766, 0.820, −1.069 −0.167, 0.511, −0.363, 0.761 12.896 11.4 −0.794, 0.795, −1.123 −0.074, 0.627, −0.463, 0.622 4.483 11.6 −0.827, 0.828, −1.128 −0.083, 0.622, −0.488, 0.607 5.493 20 −0.031, 0.824, 0.046 −0.156, 0.600, −0.459, 0.636 5.493 35.1 −1.316, 0.809, −0.023 −0.162, 0.595, −0.496, 0.611 5.493
Two things in the table are the point of this page:
The body holds its first pose for two seconds. The hips and the arm are identical at 0, 1.9 and 2, then move. Before a clip's first play it holds its first frame, so a character that should be moving from the first frame of the render is standing still for 2 s. The face stops at 11.5 s. The face column changes up to 11.4 s and is then 5.493 at 11.6, 20 and 35.1: the clip has ended and holds its last frame, while the body carries on for another 23.6 s with a frozen face.
4 Start the body at zero
The obvious fix is wrong, and it is worth seeing why:
$S('#test').at(0).play('test')
This does not move the clip's event: it adds a second one. The timeline now has play events for test at 2 s and at 0 s, and the two fight. Sampling the arm shows it: at 1 s it moves, and at 2 s it is back at the first pose (0.027, 0.149, −0.306, 0.940), because the event at 2 s restarted the clip. Undo it (Undo, or undo()), then move the event that is already there, by its id:
editor.timeline.moveEvent(editor.timeline.tracks[0].events[0].id, 0)
true
(tracks[0] is the #test track here; the event is the purple block on that row of the Animations tab, which you can drag instead.) This edit is not on the Undo stack (checked: the undo count did not change, and Undo afterwards took back the tagClass of step 1 and left the event at 0), so reload the scene to get the original timing back. Sampling again, the arm is at its first pose at 0 s and has moved by 1 s and by 2 s, with no reset:
Before After moveEvent(…, 0): both clips start at 0 and the readout is 00:33.099.
The panel does not redraw by itself. A screenshot taken right after moveEvent still showed the block at 2 s and the old duration; zooming or pressing Fit redrew it. The move had happened (the arm samples in the table above are from after it), so redraw before you trust what you see. The duration is not a separate step: it fell from 35.099 s to 33.099 s because the timeline's length follows its last event.
t (s) arm quaternion, body event at 0 0 0.027, 0.149, −0.306, 0.940 1 −0.258, 0.428, −0.421, 0.757 2 −0.141, 0.605, −0.533, 0.575
.play() takes the other controls too, and each adds its own event: { speed: 0.5 } makes the event 66.2 s long (the clip at half speed), and { loop: true } keeps the 33.1 s. Use them on a clip you have removed or not yet placed, not on top of the one already there.
5 The face: what the clip leaves, and a warning
Step 3 showed the face clip ending at 11.5 s and the body carrying on. Everything the clip drives is frozen at its last value from then on, including the eyelids: sampled at 11.6, 20 and 35.1 s the face is identical (5.493), so for the last 23.6 s of the take she does not blink. The way to fix it in Strata is an authored face (Authoring a face): keys that name the shapes you want, which win over the clip's frozen value for those shapes only, plus a seeded idle layer for the blink. In the one run of this scene where such a key finished, a smile key at 14 s (face.keyAt(14, { shapes: { mouthSmileLeft: 0.8, mouthSmileRight: 0.8 }, duration: 600, easing: 'ease-out' })) read back like this:
t (s) mouthSmileLeft eyeBlinkLeft 10 0.509 0.688 13.9 0.764 0.431 14.7 0.800 0.431 20 0.800 0.431
The key took the smile from the clip's last value to 0.8; eyeBlinkLeft, which the key did not name, stayed at the clip's last value, 0.431, to the end of the take.
Do not paste face edits into this scene yet. They are not offered here as a recipe because they hung the browser tab on this character: of five attempts (face.keyAt twice on the long class and once on a short class, face.idle({ seed: 7 }) twice), four froze the tab until the browser killed its renderer, and only the smile above finished. Camera and clip edits (steps 4 and 6) did not do this. The cause is not known; it may be specific to a character whose face morphs are driven by a baked clip. If you try it, save first and expect to lose the tab.
6 Keep her in frame
The scene's camera, cam-render, sits at (−1.97, 0.80, 2.51) and has no keys of its own, but the hips travel about 1.3 m in x and 1.2 m in z in the sampled frames in step 3, so a camera that never turns lets her drift to the edge of the frame (the first screenshot below). A camera key arrives at a time with an aim point (lookAt). The first key of a camera needs a position (keyAt: the first key of a camera needs a pos is the error otherwise); later keys that name only lookAt turn the camera without moving it. Rather than type aim points, sample the hips with holdTimelineAt every 2.5 s and aim at them, at about chest height:
for (let t = 0; t <= 35; t += 2.5) { holdTimelineAt(t); const p = scene.getObjectByName('J_Bip_C_Hips').getWorldPosition(new THREE.Vector3()); const aim = [+p.x.toFixed(2), 1.0, +p.z.toFixed(2)]; $S('#cam-render').keyAt(t, t === 0 ? { pos: [-1.97, 0.8, 2.51], lookAt: aim } : { lookAt: aim }) }
… a promise: its result is shown when it settles ✨ Scene updated — 15 commands executed
Fifteen keys (the first lands at 0.001 s), one undo step each, and the camera never leaves its position. Check the aim the same way as the body: sample the scene, and measure the angle between the camera's forward direction and the direction from the camera to the hips at chest height:
17.5 s, before the loop: the camera has not moved, and she is at the right edge. 17.5 s, after the fifteen keys: the same moment, with her in the middle.
t (s) 0.5 1.25 2 3.75 6 8.75 13 16.25 20 26.25 28 33 35 off aim (°) 0.6 1.5 2.3 2.1 1.8 1.2 0.4 12.5 0 1.2 1.5 1.3 0
The camera is within 2.3° of her at twelve of the thirteen times, and 12.5° off at 16.25 s, between the keys at 15 and 17.5 s: the hips move faster there than a straight turn between two keys follows. Add a key ($S('#cam-render').keyAt(16.25, { lookAt: [x, 1.0, z] }) with the hips at that time) or sample every second in the loop. $S('#cam-render').keys() lists the keys and .smooth(true) plays them as one curve; Editing camera moves by hand has the one-click moves.
7 Render it
Open the Render tab. The scene's one shot (cam-render from 0 s) is in the Camera Sequence; pick the size and frame rate, and render. The length of the take is the timeline's duration, which the saved scene has as 35.1 s because the body starts at 2 s. After step 4 the readout in the Animations tab fell to 33.1 s (checked, once the panel was redrawn), so the take ends when the body clip does; look at it before you render.
What was checked, and what was not. Checked in the editor, on the pinned scene, with the Shell blocks as written: steps 1 to 3 (their outputs are copied from the editor); the second event and the arm resetting at 2 s in step 4; moveEvent, the arm samples after it, and that it is not an undo step; the camera loop in step 6 and the thirteen aim measurements. The smile table in step 5 is from the single run that finished, with the long class .vroidv110femalev1132-tracksglb in place of a short one. The screenshots and the thumbnail are of this scene in headless Chrome with software rendering, taken by the blocks above in that order (one run, the editor at its default size), so the look of the shading is not what a graphics card gives. Not checked: dragging the event in the Animations tab instead of calling moveEvent; the Render tab in step 7 (no render was made); any face edit after the first (they hung the tab); and the "Open example" player for this page. Which of the three tools made which part of the file is as credited at the top; this page did not run those tools.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script, scene) Assets facebind.json (the character scene): Tejaswi Gowda, test1 repository; the character was made with portrait.webcli.app, look.webcli.app and rig.webcli.app Licence: not stated. posts.title: Why cells are small: surface area to volume
Authoring a face: gaze and idle
posts.text:
Authoring a face: gaze and idle
All tutorials
Two characters watch each other for 53 seconds. Most of the acting is where they look and not looking dead — both are timeline data you can edit.
The idea. A face is two keyed channels on the same track as the body clip: expression (continuous morph weights with easing and duration per key) and gaze (where the eyes and head aim), with a seeded idle layer underneath. They are versioned, diffable and agent-drivable like everything else. This is the animator's face — hand-keyed, on a stylized character — not a face-capture substitute.
What you'll need. A scene with two rigged characters that carry face morph targets (ARKit-style blendshapes, as on VRoid / VRM models) and eye and head bones, each with a body clip on the timeline — for example a cut made in Editing captured motion as data. Everything is pasted into the Shell tab; nothing needs the viewport.
1 Make them look at each other
A gaze key whose target is a selector follows that character as it moves; a point holds. Start both fighters on each other:
const A = $S('#a'), B = $S('#b'); A.gaze(0, '#b', { duration: 0 }); B.gaze(0, '#a', { duration: 0 });
Eyes and head are separate. The head weight (default 0.35) is the share of the aim the head takes — 0 is a glance, higher is a turn. When the target changes, the eyes lead and the head lags: it starts 0.1 s later and takes 40% longer to arrive. Past about ±30° the eyes stop at their anatomical limit and the head takes the rest, so a target behind a character becomes a head turn, never doll eyes.
2 Look away between exchanges
A glance away and back is two keys. 'away' is a fixed averted look (35° to the character's left, 10° down):
for (const t of [6.4, 14.2, 28, 34.4, 40.2, 44.1]) A.gaze(t, 'away', { duration: 250, head: 0.2 }).gaze(t + 0.9, '#b', { duration: 300 }); for (const t of [6.9, 14.7, 28.6, 34.9, 40.6, 44.6]) B.gaze(t, 'away', { duration: 250, head: 0.2 }).gaze(t + 0.9, '#a', { duration: 300 }); A.gazeKeys(); // [{ index, time, target, head, duration, easing, label }]
Measured on a real 52.9 s cut: wherever the other fighter is inside the eyes' range, the eyes sit within about 1° of that fighter's head, and sampling the whole face costs about 0.6 ms per frame.
3 Don't look dead: the idle layer
Fully keyed faces read as corpses; real faces are never still. The idle layer adds a blink, a faint breath and a little gaze micro-noise:
A.face.idle({ seed: 11 }); B.face.idle({ seed: 12 });
Seeded. The same scene renders the same blinks on every run and every machine. An underlayer. It is never baked into the keys; A.face.idle(false) removes it and every authored key is untouched. It never fights an authored beat. An authored value owns a shape it drives; a held beat (hold: true) keeps blinks and noise out of it.
4 Add an expression, with timing
Keys are continuous values with easing and duration — a slow fall and a hard snap are the same two keys with different timing:
A.face.keyAt(20, { shapes: { browInnerUp: 1, eyeWideLeft: 1, eyeWideRight: 1 }, duration: 0 }); // snap to alarm A.face.keyAt(24, { shapes: { browInnerUp: 0, eyeWideLeft: 0, eyeWideRight: 0 }, duration: 2000, easing: 'ease-in-out' }); // slow fall B.face.applyPreset('focus', 30, { duration: 500, hold: true }); // a held beat A.face.keys(); // the explicit per-shape keys — a preset is never stored, only its values
A preset expands to explicit keys you can then edit, move or delete (moveKey(i, …), deleteKey(i)).
5 The same keys in the GUI
Open the Customize tab. Under Expression, tick Key at playhead (set a duration and an easing): the preset Apply button and the sliders now write keys that arrive at the playhead. Under Face performance, pick a target and Key at playhead to key a gaze; tick Idle layer and set a seed. The key list (with ×) and the command text update live, whichever surface made the change. Open the Animations tab: face and gaze keys are blocks on the character's row (a key arrives at the block's right edge) and the code panel shows them — edit the text and save to change the same keys. Undo is one stack for all of it.
6 Reproduce it exactly
console.log(A.face.asCommand()); // the commands that rebuild this face byte for byte console.log(B.face.asCommand());
Same keys, same face, every run — no viewport needed, so an agent can author a performance deterministically. Morph weights, and the eye and head rotations, are baked into a glTF export by running the real sampler, so the file matches what you saw.
Honest scope. This is for stylized targets and for the face you want to author. Speech (audio-derived mouth shapes) is not built. And if a character's face was reshaped to a photo by Face bind, its morph targets are carried through that reshape untouched, so authored expressions on a strongly reshaped face are approximate — see the authored-face guide for the measured numbers.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets None used. Tools None used.

posts.title: Build a bubble shooter scene
posts.text:
Build a bubble shooter scene
All tutorials
This scene deliberately stops short of gameplay: it builds a lane, a background, a sign — and exactly one bubble. Real bubble-shooter logic clones and recolors bubbles at runtime, so the scene's job is to hand that logic one well-formed, easy-to-find template rather than a whole pre-built grid. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
The whole scene: a lane, one clonable Bubble, a wooden score sign, and a rainforest backdrop.
Build the data the logic needs, not the logic itself. "The game logic (wired later) will clone and color the bubbles" is a spec for the scene, not an invitation to also stub out shooting/matching/popping. One named, class-tagged template object is a complete, correct deliverable — it's exactly what findObject('Bubble') or $S('.bubble') needs to locate and .clone() later. Building a pre-filled grid of 40 bubbles would be guessing at a layout the actual game logic hasn't specified yet.
1 Build the lane
A flat lane bounded by two rails reuses the exact structure from the paddle game table tutorial — a real receding surface, not a flat arcade screen, so the camera can stand at one end and look down its length:
const group = new Group(); group.name = 'Bubble Shooter'; const tableMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x1c5c3a, roughness: 0.7 }); const railMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff, roughness: 0.5 }); const table = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(12, 0.4, 24), tableMat); table.name = 'Table'; table.position.set(0, -0.2, 0); group.add(table); const railL = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.3, 0.5, 24.4), railMat); railL.name = 'Rail Left'; railL.position.set(-6.15, 0.25, 0); group.add(railL); const railR = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.3, 0.5, 24.4), railMat); railR.name = 'Rail Right'; railR.position.set(6.15, 0.25, 0); group.add(railR); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, group));
2 Add exactly one clonable Bubble
A glossy, slightly translucent white sphere — pure template, no gameplay color yet. Tag it with a class as well as a name: a class survives being cloned N times without every clone colliding on one #id, so later code can do $S('.bubble') across every clone and findObject('Bubble') to find this original:
const bubbleMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff, roughness: 0.2, metalness: 0.05, transparent: true, opacity: 0.88 }); const bubble = new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.45, 24, 24), bubbleMat); bubble.name = 'Bubble'; bubble.position.set(0, 0.45, 9.5); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, bubble)); tagClass(bubble, 'bubble');
Cloning a template later, from game logic: const shot = findObject('Bubble').clone(); shot.material = shot.material.clone(); shot.material.color.set('#e0455a'); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, shot)); — cloning the material too (not just the mesh) is the part that's easy to skip, and skipping it means recoloring one bubble silently recolors every clone that still shares the original material instance.
3 Frame it with a rainforest
Same flat-clearing ground technique as the desert version in the paddle game tutorial — measure distance from the lane's true world center, not the ground mesh's own locally-offset origin, so undergrowth never rises above the lane's own surface. Trees are a trunk cylinder plus a few stacked icosahedra for foliage:
const jungle = new Group(); jungle.name = 'Rainforest Scenery'; const groundMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2f4f2a, roughness: 0.95 }); const groundGeo = new PlaneGeometry(90, 90, 64, 64); const gp = groundGeo.attributes.position; const CLEAR = 15, FADE = 12; for (let i = 0; i < gp.count; i++) { const x = gp.getX(i), y = gp.getY(i); const wz = -5 - y; // this ground mesh sits at position.z = -5 — see the note below const d = Math.sqrt(x * x + wz * wz); const t = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (d - CLEAR) / FADE)); gp.setZ(i, Math.sin(x * 0.1 + 2.1) * Math.cos(wz * 0.11) * 0.35 * t); } groundGeo.computeVertexNormals(); const ground = new Mesh(groundGeo, groundMat); ground.name = 'Moss Ground'; ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; ground.position.set(0, -0.46, -5); jungle.add(ground); const trunkMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4a3524, roughness: 0.9 }); const foliageColors = [0x2f6b32, 0x3a7d3e, 0x275c2b, 0x437f3f]; function makeTree(x, z, scale) { const t = new Group(); t.name = 'Tree'; const trunk = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.22 * scale, 0.3 * scale, 3.2 * scale, 8), trunkMat); trunk.position.set(0, 1.6 * scale, 0); t.add(trunk); for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // (i - x) can go negative — see the note below on JS's % operator. const idx = ((i + Math.round(x)) % foliageColors.length + foliageColors.length) % foliageColors.length; const foliage = new Mesh(new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry((1.1 - i * 0.18) * scale, 0), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: foliageColors[idx], roughness: 0.85 })); foliage.position.set((i - 1) * 0.35 * scale, (3.1 + i * 0.75) * scale, (i - 1) * 0.2 * scale); t.add(foliage); } t.position.set(x, -0.15, z); return t; } [[-11, 5, 1.1], [11.5, 8, 0.9], [-13, -8, 1.2], [13, -6, 1.0]].forEach(s => jungle.add(makeTree(s[0], s[1], s[2]))); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, jungle)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, new AmbientLight(0xbfe0a8, 0.5))); const canopyLight = new DirectionalLight(0xdfead0, 1.0); canopyLight.position.set(-10, 26, 12); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, canopyLight)); setFog('FogExp2', '#4d6b52', 0, 0, 0.018); setBackground('#5f7a63');
Two real bugs from building this scene, both worth checking for. (1) gp.getY(i) on a ground plane gives coordinates in the plane's own local space, which is offset by wherever you positioned the mesh (position.set(0, -0.46, -5) here) — computing "distance from the lane's center" from raw local coordinates measures from the wrong point unless you correct for that offset first (wz = -5 - y above, derived from the plane's rotation.x = -Math.PI/2). Skipping this correction was exactly how an earlier version of this lane ended up with a sand dune poking up through the table. (2) JavaScript's % can return a negative result for a negative left-hand operand (-9 % 4 === -1, not 3) — indexing an array with that silently reads undefined instead of throwing, which surfaces later as a vague THREE.Material: parameter 'color' has value of undefined console warning and unexpectedly white geometry. The ((n % m) + m) % m pattern above always lands in range.
4 Add a wooden, single-score sign
Two posts, a plank frame, and a canvas-textured panel — painted, not glowing, and one score, not two (a bubble shooter is one player against the board, not two paddles):
const bezelY = 8.8, bezelH = 2.6; const postH = (bezelY - bezelH / 2) - (-0.46); const woodMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6b4a2f, roughness: 0.85 }); const sign = new Group(); sign.name = 'Wooden Scoreboard'; [-3.1, 3.1].forEach((x, i) => { const post = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.2, 0.24, postH, 8), woodMat); post.name = i === 0 ? 'Post Left' : 'Post Right'; post.position.set(x, -0.46 + postH / 2, -14); sign.add(post); }); const frame = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(7.8, bezelH, 0.4), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x7a5636, roughness: 0.8 })); frame.name = 'Sign Frame'; frame.position.set(0, bezelY, -14); sign.add(frame); const c = document.createElement('canvas'); c.width = 512; c.height = 176; const ctx = c.getContext('2d'); const grad = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, 176); grad.addColorStop(0, '#a9814f'); grad.addColorStop(1, '#8a6539'); ctx.fillStyle = grad; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 512, 176); ctx.textAlign = 'center'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle'; ctx.fillStyle = '#2b1c10'; ctx.font = 'bold 34px Georgia'; ctx.fillText('SCORE', 256, 38); ctx.font = 'bold 92px Georgia'; ctx.fillText('000', 256, 122); const panel = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(7.2, 2.15), new MeshStandardMaterial({ map: new THREE.CanvasTexture(c), roughness: 0.7 })); panel.name = 'Sign Panel'; panel.position.set(0, bezelY, -13.79); sign.add(panel); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sign));
5 Stand the camera at the shooter's end
Same technique as the paddle game tutorial — position behind the Bubble, elevate for a 3/4 view, and verify with NDC projection before trusting a screenshot:
const cam = editor.camera; cam.position.set(0, 4.5, 23); cam.fov = 60; cam.lookAt(0, 0.5, -10); cam.updateProjectionMatrix(); editor.controls.center.set(0, 0.5, -10); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(cam); editor.signals.objectChanged.dispatch(cam);
6 Sanity-check before handing off
Confirm the one thing later game logic actually depends on — that exactly one addressable, clonable template exists — rather than eyeballing the viewport:
$S('.bubble').count(); // 1 findObject('Bubble').material.transparent; // true — confirms it's the template, not a stray clone editor.scene.children.length; // top-level group count, compare to what you expect editor.history.undos.length; // commands issued this session

posts.title: Build a night scene from scratch
posts.text:
Build a night scene from scratch
All tutorials
Open embed
No importing assets, no AI — just the JS Shell, a handful of reusable helper functions, and the Universal Timeline. This walks through the same workflow used to build "Last Stop," a procedural night bus-stop scene: helpers → environment → a structure → night lighting → a moving object → a static hero camera → render. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
Where this tutorial ends up (minus the full detail — see the note at the bottom for the complete scene).
Why the Shell, not clicking. Every edit below is a real, undoable, git-diffable command (editor.execute(...) under the hood). Procedural scenes especially benefit from this — a road, a fence, a field of rocks are all "the same shape N times with varied params," which is a loop, not N clicks.
1 Write reusable helpers first
Almost everything you build is one of a few shapes: a box, a rounded box, a rod between two points. Write these once at the top of your session and every later step gets shorter:
function mat(color, opts = {}) { return new MeshStandardMaterial({ color, roughness: 0.7, ...opts }); } function mesh(geometry, material, x = 0, y = 0, z = 0, parent = null) { const m = new Mesh(geometry, material); m.position.set(x, y, z); m.castShadow = m.receiveShadow = true; if (parent) parent.add(m); else editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, m)); return m; } function box(w, h, d, material, x, y, z, parent) { return mesh(new BoxGeometry(w, h, d), material, x, y, z, parent); } function rod(a, b, radius, material, parent) { const dir = new Vector3().subVectors(b, a); const seg = mesh(new CylinderGeometry(radius, radius, 1, 8), material, 0, 0, 0, parent); seg.position.copy(a).add(b).multiplyScalar(0.5); seg.scale.y = dir.length(); seg.quaternion.setFromUnitVectors(new Vector3(0, 1, 0), dir.clone().normalize()); return seg; }
Every later helper (rounded boxes, canvas textures for signs, procedural rock fields) is the same idea: a small function you write once, then call in a loop.
2 Ground, sky, and fog
A ground plane with a bit of noise reads far better than a flat color. Displace vertices in a loop, and use FogExp2 so distant geometry fades out instead of hard-clipping at the far plane:
const groundGeo = new PlaneGeometry(60, 60, 40, 40); const pos = groundGeo.attributes.position; for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) { const x = pos.getX(i), y = pos.getY(i); pos.setZ(i, Math.sin(x * 0.15) * Math.cos(y * 0.15) * 0.4); } groundGeo.computeVertexNormals(); const ground = mesh(groundGeo, mat(0x8e7154)); ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; ground.name = 'Ground'; scene.fog = new FogExp2(0x0a0e18, 0.02);
3 A structure, built as a group
Group related parts under one named Group so the Outliner stays readable and you can move/animate the whole thing as one object. A simple shelter — four posts and a roof slab — demonstrates the pattern everything bigger (a bus, a fence, a robot) also follows:
const shelter = new Group(); shelter.name = 'Shelter'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, shelter)); const post = mat(0x526765, { metalness: 0.5, roughness: 0.65 }); for (const x of [-1.5, 1.5]) for (const z of [-1, 1]) { box(0.12, 2.4, 0.12, post, x, 1.2, z, shelter); } box(3.4, 0.15, 2.6, mat(0x815840), 0, 2.5, 0, shelter);
Why parent instead of always AddObjectCommand. The top-level group gets one undo-tracked AddObjectCommand; its children are just parent.add(...) since they're not independently addressable objects in the scene graph — the same pattern the built-in helpers use for a bus with 80+ parts, so undo/redo stays one step instead of eighty.
4 Light it for night
A dim HemisphereLight for ambient sky/ground fill, a low-intensity DirectionalLight standing in for moonlight, and one warm PointLight as the actual subject of the shot — the thing a viewer's eye goes to:
const hemi = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0x0a1428, 0x161208, 0.1); hemi.name = 'Hemisphere'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, hemi)); const moon = new DirectionalLight(0xaac4ff, 0.16); moon.position.set(-40, 90, -30); moon.name = 'Moonlight'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, moon)); const lamp = new PointLight(0xffc37e, 2.4, 12, 2); lamp.position.set(0, 2.6, 0); lamp.castShadow = true; lamp.name = 'Lamp'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, lamp));
The mistake that undoes all of this. Strata's Scene tab has an Environment dropdown defaulted to Default — a bright, generic image-based-lighting environment map. It lights every MeshStandardMaterial in the scene independently of every light object above, and at its default intensity it will wash out a night scene no matter how dim you make your lights. Set it to None (or editor.signals.sceneEnvironmentChanged.dispatch('None') from the Shell) before judging your lighting — this single setting was the difference between a bright "dusk" look and a real night look while building the reference scene.
A couple of intensity numbers are easy to get wrong the first time too: if a light is going to flicker or pulse later via a per-frame script, its authored intensity should be the steady-state value the flicker oscillates around — not whatever placeholder you happened to construct it with. A PointLight(color, 47, ...) that a script immediately overwrites to 2.4 * flicker every frame should be authored at 2.4, since Strata's timeline bakes keyframes rather than running a per-frame callback.
Pasting a block into the Shell — autocomplete lists everything in scope (editor, THREE, scene, the Command classes, and every bare geometry constructor).
5 Animate something along the timeline
Give the shelter (or any object) a moving companion — a lit box standing in for a vehicle works fine to demonstrate the grammar. $S(selector).at(seconds).animate(...) places one keyframe event; chain more calls to build a multi-leg move:
const rig = box(1, 1, 3, mat(0x365854, { metalness: 0.3 }), 0, 0.5, -30); rig.name = 'Rig'; $S('#Rig').at(0).animate({ to: { positionZ: -8 } }, 8000, 'linear'); $S('#Rig').at(8).animate({ to: { positionZ: -8 } }, 1000); // a short hold $S('#Rig').at(9).animate({ to: { positionZ: 20 } }, 4000, 'ease-in');
Scrub the Animations tab's timeline to preview — $S(...).at(t) events are absolute seconds on one shared clock for the whole scene, so a camera, a light's intensity, and this rig can all be choreographed against the same numbers. See the animation guide for the full grammar (fades, lookAt, per-axis targets, class-based batch selectors).
Mid-timeline: the lamp's warm pool of light is doing most of the compositional work in a dark scene.
6 Cut in a static hero camera
Your main camera can stay wherever you like — animated, or just parked at a default angle. For one moment worth a dedicated, hand-framed shot (say, the rig's closest pass to the lamp), add a second, non-animated camera and schedule it in the Render tab's Camera Sequence rather than re-keyframing the main one:
const heroCam = new PerspectiveCamera(38, 16 / 9, 0.1, 500); heroCam.name = 'HeroCam'; heroCam.position.set(4, 1.6, -4); heroCam.lookAt(0, 1, 0); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, heroCam)); editor.scene.userData.renderShots = [ { id: 'shot-intro', at: 0, camera: editor.camera.uuid, transition: 'cut', transitionDur: 0.5 }, { id: 'shot-hero', at: 8, camera: heroCam.uuid, transition: 'fade', transitionDur: 0.8 }, { id: 'shot-return', at: 12, camera: editor.camera.uuid, transition: 'fade', transitionDur: 0.8 }, ]; editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch();
A shot runs from its at until the next shot's at (or the timeline's end) — with zero shots, the render always falls back to the single camera picked at the top of the Render tab, so this is purely additive. Preview any camera by temporarily pointing the viewport at it:
editor.viewportCamera = heroCam; editor.signals.viewportCameraChanged.dispatch();
Keep it out of the way. A static camera parked directly in a moving object's path gets driven through mid-shot. Offset it to the side or elevate it so the subject passes near the lens, not through it, for the whole window it's active.
The Render tab's Camera Sequence lane after adding a hero-camera cut-in — see the dedicated tutorial for more on this feature.
7 Render it
Open the Render tab, pick a resolution and FPS. The Camera Sequence lane shows your shots as colored blocks — click one to retarget its camera or nudge its timing without touching the Shell again. Click Render & Export — rendering is real-time, so a 20s timeline takes about 20s.
This tutorial is a distillation, not the full scene. The actual "Last Stop" reference this is based on has ~500 objects: a noise-displaced road with painted stripes, a fence with sagging wire (CatmullRomCurve3 + TubeGeometry), a field of procedurally-scattered rocks and cacti, an articulated robot figure (cylinders connected end-to-end via quaternion alignment, same idea as the rod() helper above), a bus with real glass materials and working headlight beams, and a full multi-shot camera choreography over a 45-second timeline. Every one of those is the same handful of patterns from this tutorial — a helper function, a loop, a named Group, a $S(...).at(t).animate(...) call — just repeated and combined more times.

posts.title: Editing captured motion as data
posts.text:
Editing captured motion as data
All tutorials
A two-performer capture runs 170.17 s and has a 53-second dead middle. Cut it to 52.9 s with a few hundred bytes of edit list — the capture itself is never modified.
The idea. Motion is data you can edit. A cut is not a re-bake: it is an edit list — a handful of spans over the captured clip — stored on the timeline next to everything else. Clear the list and the full capture plays again, byte for byte. A generated video clip cannot do this; a captured, rigged performance can.
What you'll need. A scene with two rigged performers that were captured together (so they share one world frame), each with a baked clip, on the Universal Timeline — for example $S('#a').at(0).play('clip-a') and the same for #b. Everything below is pasted into the Shell tab; nothing needs the viewport, so an agent can author the same cut headlessly.
1 Register the pair
Two performers captured in one metric frame are only coherent together. Registering them as a group makes every edit apply to both, atomically — same spans, same blend windows.
const sparring = $M.group('sparring', ['#a', '#b']); sparring.collision(); // baseline over the full capture
The baseline report says how close the two hips ever get on the floor. For the capture used here: min 0.80 m, never under the 0.6 m floor for non-contact sparring.
2 Find the exchanges
In the measured capture, the close approaches cluster into 18 exchanges. They are front-loaded: ten land between 2.6 s and 43.2 s, then nothing from 43.2 s to 98.5 s. Padding each cluster by −1.0 s / +1.2 s and merging gaps under 0.4 s gives eight spans:
# in out dur closest E01 1.60 9.00 7.40 s 0.94 m E02 14.60 22.10 7.50 s 0.96 m E03 30.80 44.40 13.60 s 0.80 m E04 97.50 103.40 5.90 s 1.11 m E05 104.80 110.80 6.00 s 0.93 m E06 113.70 117.60 3.90 s 1.08 m E07 134.70 140.60 5.90 s 1.10 m E08 158.40 161.10 2.70 s 1.17 m
That removes 44.4 – 97.5 s (53.1 s) and keeps 52.9 s — 31% of the source.
3 Splice them
splice joins the spans. A blend is mandatory: over the transition window (0.25 s ≈ 8 frames by default) every rotation is slerped from the outgoing pose to the incoming one, and the root is offset so the hips continue from where they were — otherwise the body pops or teleports at every cut.
sparring.splice([ [1.6, 9.0], [14.6, 22.1], [30.8, 44.4], [97.5, 103.4], [104.8, 110.8], [113.7, 117.6], [134.7, 140.6], [158.4, 161.1], ].map(([from, to]) => ({ from, to })), { blend: 0.25 }); editor.timeline.duration; // 52.9 (once the cameras are remapped — step 5) sparring.asCommand(); // the declarative form of this cut
Why the pair moves as one. The continuity offset at each cut is computed from the pair's centroid and applied to both performers, so their separation survives the cut. Per-performer timeOffset and speedOf are refused until you call breakRegistration() — it warns what is lost (they can clip through each other) and is undoable. A directive on a single member, e.g. $S('#a').play('clip-a', { from: 1, to: 5 }), is refused for the same reason.
4 Check for collisions
No renderer will warn you that the fighters now overlap. The collision report measures the hip-to-hip floor distance over the edited timeline and flags every span under the floor:
console.log(sparring.collision()); // { min, minAt, ok, violations: [...], spans: [...] } sparring.collision({ floor: 0.6 }); // the default floor, in metres
For this cut: ok: true, no span under 0.6 m. The closest approach sits inside a blend window (0.74 m) — the blend interpolates the two performers' positions, so it can bring them closer than either source span does; the check is what tells you.
5 Remap the cameras
Shots authored against the 170 s source need the new timebase. remapShots() keeps every event that lies wholly inside one kept span, moves it to the cut's clock, and drops (and reports) the rest:
const r = sparring.remapShots(); r.kept; r.dropped; // what survived the cut editor.timeline.duration; // 52.9
6 Slow a beat, hold a pose
Everything is composed from the same span primitive and applies to both performers:
sparring.hold(20, 0.4); // freeze the pose at cut-time 20 s for 0.4 s sparring.retime([[30.8, 1], [38, 0.5]]); // from source 38 s on, run at half speed sparring.rootYaw(15); // turn the whole performance 15° about its centre sparring.rootOffset([0.5, 0, 0]); // move it in the world, same vector for both
7 Undo, clear, commit
Every call above is one Undo step — the same stack as the Animations tab. sparring.clear() drops the edit list; the full 170.17 s capture plays again, untouched. Open the Animations tab: the cut is one teal block per performer with a tick at every span boundary, and a Collision check / Clear cut bar underneath. Drag a block and both performers move together; the code panel shows the same cut as a $M('sparring').cut(...) line you can edit and save. Commit from the Git tab. The scene is written compact (no pretty-printing) with the animation floats quantized — see below.
Honest note on what is and isn't modified. The captured clip on the scene is only ever read. The cut is compiled in memory from the edit list each time it is needed (and for glTF export), the way the Timeline clip is, and is never saved. Saving the scene writes the capture as it was plus a few hundred bytes of edit list. Saved animation values are quantized (quaternions 5 decimals, positions and times 4) — a deliberate, deterministic, lossy size saving applied at save, independent of any edit.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Pavan Turaga (asset) Assegid Kidane (asset) Assets Sparring capture: clips st1_1072026Skeleton and st2_1072026Skeleton (170.17 s): Recorded with an OptiTrack system in "Martial Arts and Motion Capture" (GAME 294), Arizona State University; course run by Pavan Turaga, recorded by Assegid Kidane; the two performers are not named Licence: not stated. posts.title: Build a fighting-game arena scene
posts.text:
Build a fighting-game arena scene
All tutorials
Two fighters, a stage, a health-bar HUD and a round timer — and no game logic. Like the paddle game and bubble shooter tutorials, the scene's job is to hand later code well-named, class-tagged things to find and drive. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order — or just load the finished fight.json (File → Open, or drop it on the viewport).
The whole scene: plank stage, tavern backdrop, two fighters, and a HUD with portraits, health and mana bars, and a round timer.
Build the data the logic needs, not the logic itself. A fighting game needs to find each fighter, shrink a health bar, and tick a timer. So the scene provides exactly that: $S('.p1') and $S('.p2') for the fighters, P1 Health Fill / P2 Health Fill meshes whose scale.x is the bar, and a Round Timer plane. Hit boxes, moves and AI would be guesses at rules nobody has written yet.
Pasting long blocks into the Shell: if you paste a long block and Enter seems to do nothing, press Esc first (it closes the autocomplete dropdown that was swallowing the keypress), then Enter. On a non-empty scene, run clearScene() first.
1 Build the arena
One Group holds the plank floor (planks run along the depth axis, so the camera sees them converge), a plaster back wall with a doorway, stairs, pillars, two wagon wheels, four barrels and the banner. A canvas-painted texture draws the crossed swords — no image files. One AddObjectCommand adds the whole group, so it is one undo step:
const arena = new Group(); arena.name = 'Fighting Arena'; const plankMats = [ 0xb5562a, 0x9c4521, 0xc8693a ].map(c => new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: c, roughness: 0.75 })); const floor = new Group(); floor.name = 'Stage Floor'; for (let i = 0; i < 26; i++) { const plank = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(1.15, 0.2, 18), plankMats[i % 3]); plank.name = 'Plank ' + (i + 1); plank.position.set(-14.375 + i * 1.15, -0.1, 0); plank.receiveShadow = true; floor.add(plank); } arena.add(floor); const stoneMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x8a7d70, roughness: 0.9 }); const plasterMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xc9a67a, roughness: 0.9 }); const darkWood = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4a2c18, roughness: 0.85 }); const whiteStone = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xe6e0d4, roughness: 0.6 }); const wall = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(44, 12, 0.6), plasterMat); wall.name = 'Back Wall'; wall.position.set(0, 6, -15); arena.add(wall); const doorway = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(4.5, 5, 0.7), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x1a2a2a, roughness: 0.6 })); doorway.name = 'Doorway'; doorway.position.set(0, 3.2, -14.6); arena.add(doorway); for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { const step = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(9 - i * 0.6, 0.3, 1.1), stoneMat); step.name = 'Stair ' + (i + 1); step.position.set(0, 0.15 + i * 0.3, -8.6 - i * 1.0); arena.add(step); } [-5.5, 5.5, -11, 11].forEach((x, i) => { const pillar = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.55, 0.65, 11, 16), whiteStone); pillar.name = 'Pillar ' + (i + 1); pillar.position.set(x, 5.5, -14.4); pillar.castShadow = true; arena.add(pillar); }); // Wagon wheels and barrels flank the stage function makeWheel(name, x, z, ry) { const wheel = new Group(); wheel.name = name; const rim = new Mesh(new TorusGeometry(1.5, 0.14, 8, 28), darkWood); wheel.add(rim); const hub = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.28, 0.28, 0.3, 12), darkWood); hub.rotation.x = Math.PI / 2; wheel.add(hub); for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) { const spoke = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.14, 3, 0.12), darkWood); spoke.rotation.z = i * Math.PI / 6; wheel.add(spoke); } wheel.position.set(x, 1.5, z); wheel.rotation.y = ry; return wheel; } arena.add(makeWheel('Wagon Wheel Left', -10.5, -9, 0.5)); arena.add(makeWheel('Wagon Wheel Right', 10.5, -9, -0.5)); const barrelMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x7a4a26, roughness: 0.8 }); const bandMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2a2a2a, roughness: 0.5, metalness: 0.6 }); [[-8, -7], [-9.2, -6.2], [8.5, -7], [9.6, -6]].forEach(([x, z], i) => { const barrel = new Group(); barrel.name = 'Barrel ' + (i + 1); const body = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.7, 0.7, 1.4, 14), barrelMat); body.position.y = 0.7; body.castShadow = true; barrel.add(body); [0.3, 1.1].forEach(y => { const band = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.72, 0.72, 0.1, 14), bandMat); band.position.y = y; barrel.add(band); }); barrel.position.set(x, 0, z); arena.add(barrel); }); // Centre banner: pole, crossbar, canvas-painted crossed swords const pole = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.1, 0.12, 7, 8), darkWood); pole.name = 'Banner Pole'; pole.position.set(0, 3.5, -6); pole.castShadow = true; arena.add(pole); const crossbar = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(2.6, 0.12, 0.12), darkWood); crossbar.name = 'Banner Crossbar'; crossbar.position.set(0, 6.6, -6); arena.add(crossbar); const bc = document.createElement('canvas'); bc.width = 256; bc.height = 320; const bx = bc.getContext('2d'); bx.fillStyle = '#8c2f1a'; bx.fillRect(0, 0, 256, 320); bx.strokeStyle = '#d9b36a'; bx.lineWidth = 8; bx.strokeRect(10, 10, 236, 300); bx.strokeStyle = '#f2f2f2'; bx.lineWidth = 14; bx.lineCap = 'round'; bx.beginPath(); bx.moveTo(60, 70); bx.lineTo(196, 250); bx.moveTo(196, 70); bx.lineTo(60, 250); bx.stroke(); const banner = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(1.8, 2.25), new MeshStandardMaterial({ map: new THREE.CanvasTexture(bc), roughness: 0.9, side: THREE.DoubleSide })); banner.name = 'Banner'; banner.position.set(0, 5.4, -5.95); arena.add(banner); arena.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh && !o.name.startsWith('Plank')) o.receiveShadow = true; }); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, arena));
2 Place two fighters
The fighters are deliberately primitive stand-ins — swap in real models later and keep the names and classes. The important detail is the axis: build each fighter facing +z (shoulders and boots on local ±x), then turn the whole group with rotation.y. Rotating by ±π/2 makes local +z point along world ±x, so the two face each other across the stage. Fighter 2 is scaled 1.25 so they read as different sizes. Tag each with a shared .fighter class plus .p1 / .p2:
function makeFighter(name, o) { const f = new Group(); f.name = name; const robe = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: o.robe, roughness: 0.6 }); const trim = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: o.trim, roughness: 0.35, metalness: 0.5 }); const dark = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: o.dark, roughness: 0.7 }); const add = (mesh, n, x, y, z) => { mesh.name = n; mesh.position.set(x, y, z); mesh.castShadow = true; f.add(mesh); return mesh; }; add(new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.5, 0.85, 1.7, 16), robe), 'Robe', 0, 0.95, 0); add(new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(1.0, 0.5, 0.6), trim), 'Chest Plate', 0, 1.65, 0); add(new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.42, 16, 16), trim), 'Shoulder Left', -0.6, 1.95, 0); add(new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.42, 16, 16), trim), 'Shoulder Right', 0.6, 1.95, 0); add(new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.36, 16, 16), dark), 'Head', 0, 2.3, 0.05); add(new Mesh(new ConeGeometry(0.42, 0.7, 16), o.hood ? dark : trim), o.hood ? 'Hood' : 'Helm', 0, 2.62, 0.02); add(new Mesh(new CapsuleGeometry(0.13, 0.8, 4, 8), robe), 'Arm Left', -0.75, 1.4, 0.3).rotation.x = -0.9; add(new Mesh(new CapsuleGeometry(0.13, 0.8, 4, 8), robe), 'Arm Right', 0.75, 1.4, 0.4).rotation.x = -1.1; add(new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.06, 0.06, 2.0, 8), dark), 'Weapon Shaft', 0.75, 1.5, 0.85).rotation.x = 0.25; add(new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.45, 0.45, 0.8), trim), 'Weapon Head', 0.75, 2.45, 0.95); add(new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.4, 0.18, 0.8), dark), 'Boot Left', -0.3, 0.09, 0.1); add(new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.4, 0.18, 0.8), dark), 'Boot Right', 0.3, 0.09, 0.1); f.position.set(o.x, 0, 0); f.rotation.y = o.facing; f.scale.setScalar(o.scale); return f; } const fighter1 = makeFighter('Fighter 1', { x: -3.4, facing: Math.PI / 2, scale: 1.0, robe: 0xb8391c, trim: 0xf0a030, dark: 0x1e1a1a, hood: true }); const fighter2 = makeFighter('Fighter 2', { x: 3.4, facing: -Math.PI / 2, scale: 1.25, robe: 0x3a3a8c, trim: 0xd6b45a, dark: 0x2e4a3a, hood: false }); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, fighter1)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, fighter2)); tagClass(fighter1, 'fighter'); tagClass(fighter1, 'p1'); tagClass(fighter2, 'fighter'); tagClass(fighter2, 'p2');
A bug worth checking for. The first version put the shoulders, arms and boots on local ±z — fine in the editor's default orientation, but after the π/2 turn they pointed at the camera instead of out to the sides, and the fighters looked like they were facing front. If a rotated rig looks wrong, check which local axis its "left and right" parts are on.
3 Add the HUD
The HUD is a 3D group hung behind the fighters, not a screen overlay — so it is scaled (0.78) until both portraits fit inside the camera frustum. Each bar fill's geometry is translated so its origin sits on the portrait-side edge; later code only has to set fill.scale.x between 0 and 1 and the bar drains toward the centre, with no position math:
// Fills have their geometry origin on the portrait-side edge, so game logic can // just set fill.scale.x (0..1) and the bar drains toward the centre. const hud = new Group(); hud.name = 'HUD'; hud.position.set(0, 8.4, -4); hud.scale.setScalar(0.78); const gold = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xd9b36a, roughness: 0.35, metalness: 0.7 }); const slot = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x15171c, roughness: 0.6 }); const emissive = c => new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: c, emissive: c, emissiveIntensity: 0.35, roughness: 0.5 }); function makeHudSide(prefix, sign, healthColor, manaColor, portraitColor) { const side = new Group(); side.name = prefix + ' HUD'; const frame = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(7.4, 1.5, 0.15), slot); frame.name = prefix + ' Frame'; frame.position.set(sign * 6.6, 0, 0); side.add(frame); const barW = 6.4, edge = sign * 9.75; [['Health', 0.42, healthColor], ['Mana', -0.12, manaColor]].forEach(([n, y, c]) => { const g = new BoxGeometry(barW, 0.38, 0.1); g.translate(-sign * barW / 2, 0, 0); const fill = new Mesh(g, emissive(c)); fill.name = prefix + ' ' + n + ' Fill'; fill.position.set(edge + 0, y, 0.12); side.add(fill); }); const ring = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(1.0, 1.0, 0.18, 32), gold); ring.name = prefix + ' Portrait Ring'; ring.rotation.x = Math.PI / 2; ring.position.set(sign * 10.6, 0, 0); side.add(ring); const face = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.85, 0.85, 0.2, 32), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: portraitColor, roughness: 0.5 })); face.name = prefix + ' Portrait'; face.rotation.x = Math.PI / 2; face.position.set(sign * 10.6, 0, 0.02); side.add(face); [0, 1].forEach(i => { const gem = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.5, 0.5, 0.1), slot); gem.name = prefix + ' Round Slot ' + (i + 1); gem.position.set(sign * (3.0 + i * 0.7), -0.95, 0.05); side.add(gem); }); return side; } const hudP1 = makeHudSide('P1', -1, 0x22a82a, 0x2a5fd9, 0xb8391c); const hudP2 = makeHudSide('P2', 1, 0x22a82a, 0x2a2a60, 0x3a3a8c); hud.add(hudP1); hud.add(hudP2); const tc = document.createElement('canvas'); tc.width = 256; tc.height = 160; const tx = tc.getContext('2d'); tx.clearRect(0, 0, 256, 160); tx.textAlign = 'center'; tx.textBaseline = 'middle'; tx.fillStyle = '#ffffff'; tx.font = 'bold 120px Georgia'; tx.fillText('99', 128, 84); const timer = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(2.6, 1.6), new MeshBasicMaterial({ map: new THREE.CanvasTexture(tc), transparent: true })); timer.name = 'Round Timer'; timer.position.set(0, 0, 0.1); hud.add(timer); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, hud)); tagClass(hud, 'hud');
4 Light the stage and set the mood
Warm ambient fill, a shadow-casting key light, exponential fog and a clay-coloured background:
editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, new AmbientLight(0xffd9b0, 0.7))); const sun = new DirectionalLight(0xffe2bb, 1.6); sun.name = 'Key Light'; sun.position.set(-6, 14, 10); sun.castShadow = true; sun.shadow.camera.left = -14; sun.shadow.camera.right = 14; sun.shadow.camera.top = 12; sun.shadow.camera.bottom = -12; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sun)); setFog('FogExp2', '#8a5a3a', 0, 0, 0.012); setBackground('#7a4f35');
5 Stand the camera at the front of the stage
A low, close camera makes the fighters feel large. The same technique as the other tutorials — set the position, aim it, and update the controls' centre so orbiting pivots around the action:
const cam = editor.camera; cam.position.set(0, 2.6, 12); cam.fov = 50; cam.lookAt(0, 3.2, 0); cam.updateProjectionMatrix(); editor.controls.center.set(0, 3.2, 0); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(cam); editor.signals.objectChanged.dispatch(cam);
6 Sanity-check before handing off
Confirm the things later game code depends on, rather than eyeballing the viewport. The last two lines prove the bar anchors correctly — at half scale the left edge stays put and only the right edge moves:
$S('.fighter').count(); // 2 $S('.p1').count(); // 1 const fill = findObject('P1 Health Fill'); const bounds = () => { fill.updateMatrixWorld(true); const b = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(fill); return [b.min.x, b.max.x]; }; fill.scale.x = 1; bounds(); // [-7.61, -2.61] fill.scale.x = 0.5; bounds(); // [-7.61, -5.11] (left edge pinned) fill.scale.x = 1; // put it back
7 Save it as fight.json
Use File → Save (the disk icon) to download the project as JSON, or load the ready-made one: fight.json. Opening it restores the names, the .fighter / .p1 / .p2 / .hud classes, the painted textures, the fog and the camera exactly as built here. Drop the file on the viewport, or use File → Open.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script, scene) Assets None used. Tools None used.
