posts.title: FutureFlux: From a Mesa heat map to a tree-shade proposal
posts.text:
FutureFlux: From a Mesa heat map to a tree-shade proposal Build a short heat tour in Strata, from Landsat observations to a tree-shade proposal with animated walkers and independently selectable English and Spanish narration and subtitles.
All tutorials · Build the base GIS scene by hand · Planner guide and shade results
Build a three-site heat tour and a tree-shade proposal for Red Mountain Multigenerational Center in Mesa, Arizona. Start with mapped geometry, keep satellite observations separate from the design, and check each step before moving on. Dub is optional if you export without narration.
Watch in English or Español
One film, two narration tracks on the same timeline. Each English line and its Spanish counterpart use the same cue window, not one after the other. Use Audio in the upper-right corner to choose English or Español; only the selected track plays. Use the subtitles control to choose either language independently or turn subtitles off.
Open the short cut in Strata’s video player
The short cut also has a 720p compatibility version for VS Code’s Integrated Browser, with the same audio and subtitle choices.
1:10.5, 1080p at 30 fps. The synthetic narration and green overlay illustrate the proposal; they do not report the geometric shade analysis below or measured cooling.
Explore the 1:10.5 bilingual cut in Strata
Open the final Strata project. The editable timeline runs 1:08.5, plus a two-second hold on export.
To shorten the cut without speeding up the voices, use the longer of the English and Spanish recordings to set each shared cue window, then retime the camera moves, character walks, and tree reveals to match. Each language has 12 cues, with no overlaps or overruns; the tightest cue has 0.34 seconds to spare. Both subtitle tracks use the same cue boundaries, and the last cue ends at 0:58.5, just as the camera begins to rise.
Explore the interactive scene
Open the pinned scene in Strata
The live call card is not available inside the embedded scene. Watch it in the film above or open the pinned scene in Strata to see it there.
Before starting: Save unrelated work and use a separate Strata project. The original Mesa scene is the older rehearsal fixture, not the finished film. Use the linked base tutorial for complete Shell blocks that construct the original mapped site from an empty scene.
1. Build the site from Mesa GIS
Start with the City of Mesa REST catalogue. Use ParkFinder layer 19 path records 30121 (community center) and 30046 (park loop), and CommunityMaps layer 6 building footprint 53258. Keep those IDs on the scene groups so you can trace the meshes back to the source records.
Project WGS84 records to local meters with origin [-111.667328704, 33.431791272]: x east, y up, z south. Turn each centerline into flat path sections and extrude the mapped footprint vertically. The 3.3 m paths and 6 m shell are assumptions, not surveyed dimensions. Keep OpenStreetMap service roads, parking, and sports fields in a separate context group so they do not replace the Mesa features.
Human check: Orbit the scene. The center walkway should sit south of the footprint, the park path should curve north of it, and the roof should sit about 6 m above ground. Hide the OSM group: both paths and the building should stay in place.
2. Add the comparison neighborhoods and heat overlays
Use Mesa’s municipal boundary for the opening and registered neighborhood records for Encanto (#301) and Alta Mesa (#6). Encanto here is in Mesa, not Phoenix. Put the boundary, title, study-area locator, and credit under a single opening group so they can fade together.
Use the July 29, 2025 Landsat 9 Collection 2 Level-2 scene LC09_L2SP_037037_20250729_02_T1. Read ST_B10 with QA_PIXEL; drop invalid, cloud, shadow, and snow pixels before taking the mean. Use equal 17 × 17 native product-grid windows. Convert valid digital numbers to Celsius with DN * 0.00341802 + 149 - 273.15. Project the cell corners into the scene’s local coordinates and draw the cells as a separate flat layer.
Use one shared 40–60 °C palette (green → yellow → red). Keep the source cells unchanged, and round only the displayed sample means: Encanto 58.5 °C, Alta Mesa 49.1 °C, Red Mountain 51.5 °C. These are surface temperatures from one overpass, not air temperatures or averages for entire neighborhoods.
Human check: Toggle each heat group and compare its edges with mapped context. Identical temperatures must get identical colors. At Alta Mesa, orbit at a shallow angle and make sure water does not flicker against the ground. The water-only depth fix should not affect the heat layer.
The opening uses Mesa’s municipal boundary to locate the study area before the camera moves toward Encanto.
3. Lay out the route and measure it
Order the route Encanto → Alta Mesa → Red Mountain. Draw a red double-headed arrow between each pair of sample centers. Compute horizontal distance in local meters with Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.z - a.z) and divide by 1609.344 for miles. Place the text where it will be readable during the camera pullbacks.
Human check: Look for 1.48 miles between Encanto and Alta Mesa and 2.56 miles between Alta Mesa and Red Mountain. Both should say straight-line distance, not imply a walkable route. Red Mountain is the design site, not the hottest observation.
The comparison view uses one temperature palette across Encanto, Alta Mesa, and Red Mountain. The arrows show straight-line distances.
4. Finish the center and stage the trees
Keep the original footprint and 6 m shell. Use repeating albedo, normal, and roughness maps on the stucco and mineral roof. The finished scene uses six embedded 256 × 256 procedural maps and separate glazing, frames, sills, coping, and base trim. These additions provide visual detail; they are illustrative, not survey records.
Use two shared mesquite variants (tree4 and tree5) for the eight baseline trees and eighteen proposed trees. Simplify the shared meshes rather than each instance; in this pass the tree geometry in the saved scene dropped from 51.3 MB to 24.5 MB. Use dark olive-green leaves and warm brown bark, and preserve each tree’s dimensions, position, and contact with the ground. Stage the proposed trees as cumulative groups of 3, 8, and 18.
Human check: Reload a saved copy. Trees should not change size, sink into the ground, or appear before their reveal. At eye level the material maps should still load and the façade should not change the mapped footprint.
5. Make the shade visible without changing the observation
For a dated observation, use derived sun by default. Bind the directional key and the acquisition time label to the same gisLayer.date on the thermal layer. Strata computes the geometric sun locally with NOAA GML equations; store UTC, and format the display in America/Phoenix. The capture hour is the relevant light for evaluating the design at the capture hour. Use explicitly labelled illustrative lighting only when there is no data instant.
On a copy of the Mesa scene, import ./js/scene/futureFluxSun.js relative to the editor root (/editor/) and call configureFutureFluxSun(editor.scene). This disables the old illustrative directional fill and cooling graphics. Scrub past the last planting reveal, then call analyzeFutureFluxShade(editor.scene, instants, 0.4) with UTC instants for a day or for different dates at the same local hour. Inspect the results separately from the thermal legend. The solver samples the actual walkway slabs and checks for direct-sun occlusion by the modeled trees; it does not fetch irradiance. Revisit irradiance only before making claims about absorbed solar energy, mean radiant temperature, or cooling.
Human check: At the acquisition instant the key is about 65.12° up and 121.15° clockwise from north. A vertical post should cast a WNW shadow about 0.464 times its height. Check the planner results, rather than assuming more trees must improve shade at this hour.
37 s · An earlier preview of the walkway before proposed planting. 45 s · An earlier preview after all 18 proposed mesquites appear. These two stills predate the final walkers and walkway border.
6. Animate and check the three shots
In Render → Video → Camera Sequence, use a city opening camera, a comparison camera, and an eye-level walkway camera. Animate the city camera down toward Encanto while fading the city group. Match the first two cameras’ position, aim, and field of view at the handoff so the viewport does not jump even when it is not compositing the export fade.
0:00–0:12: Open over Mesa, then fade to the matched comparison camera around 0:08.6 and push in on Encanto.
0:12–0:40.5: Start the site close-ups at 0:12 (Encanto), 0:23.5 (Alta Mesa), and 0:34.5 (Red Mountain). Keep each label readable through the shared narration window; pull back between sites to show the distance arrows.
0:40.5–0:58.5: Glide forward at eye level. Reveal three proposed trees at 0:45.5, eight total at 0:49.5, and eighteen at 0:53.5.
Human check: Enable the timeline’s follow-camera checkbox and use as render. Scrub backward and forward across the first handoff and all three planting beats. The opening should restore on rewind, the camera should not snap at the switch, and the planting counts should agree with the indicator.
7. Import, customize, and animate the walkers
Make Maya, Alex, and Jordan in Look (look.webcli.app). Start with a bundled base VRM or open your own, customize the character in Look, then export a .vrm for each walker. Import those three files into Strata, name the root groups, and place the walkers on the slabs at human scale. Remove the old placeholders only after checking that no timeline track targets them.
In Customize → Wardrobe, select each avatar by name and use Recolor on the existing top and bottom. Maya wears rust and navy, Alex sage and brown, and Jordan blue and charcoal. Recolor the existing garments instead of adding new meshes that would need skin weights.
Parse walk-cycle.bvh with Three.js BVHLoader. This file has 42 samples at about 24 fps. Map the source joints to the VRoid J_Bip_ bones: Hips to C_Hips, Ab to C_Spine, LeftShoulder to L_UpperArm, and LeftHip, LeftKnee, and LeftAnkle to L_UpperLeg, L_LowerLeg, and L_Foot, with equivalent right-side mappings. Include spine, collar, head, elbow, and wrist rotation. In this scene the BVH faces +Z while the avatars face local −Z, so convert the rotations with a half-turn about Y. Do not copy the BVH’s joint offsets or its raw hip height over the VRM rest skeleton.
Scale the source’s forward travel using each avatar’s leg length and direct it along the path. Offset the loop phases so their feet do not land together. Sample the shoe meshes when baking to calibrate root height to the pavement, then save the 19 bone-rotation tracks and two root-transform tracks per avatar. The extended cut retimes those clips to the walkway dolly, from 1:18.25 to 1:49.5. The motion was retargeted directly in Strata, not generated in Look or the Customize tab.
The imported meshes initially repeated unreferenced vertices across material groups. Compact each indexed group without changing the geometry it draws, then store in-range facial morph deltas with normalized 16-bit integers. The subsequent optimization reduced character geometry in the saved scene from 64.7 MB to 41.5 MB without removing expressions, textures, or rigs.
Maya, Alex, and Jordan walk along the Red Mountain path beside the illustrative cooling overlay.
Human check: Scrub several parts of the final shot and rewind. Check for moving knees, opposed arm swing, feet close to the pavement, distinct strides, and no walkers leaving the path. Reopen a copy and check that all three imported clips still target the correct bones.
8. Add bilingual subtitles, the call card, and export
Open Render → Subtitles and import timed SRT cues. The bilingual format uses English first and Spanish second. The three historical samples are 137.3 °F, 120.4 °F, and 124.7 °F in English and 58,5 °C, 49,1 °C, and 51,5 °C in Spanish. Close by explaining that the proposed trees provide shade, not a measured temperature drop.
After the final cue, keep the same walkway camera and rise to a site-wide overhead view. Hold from 1:01.25 to 1:03.25 to show the illustrative green ground overlay and the tree shadows. Then move down to the roof, where the transparent call card reads like black lettering painted on the surface. Hold the close-up from 1:05.5 through the authored end at 1:08.5. The two-second render tail brings the export to 1:10.5. The editor loads the call card live; the offline render bakes it into the film.
In Render → Video, leave Skip First at None. The short export uses 1080p at 30 fps (2,115 frames). Make one WAV and one SRT per language using the shared short-cut cue windows. Check that each spoken line fits its cue, then upload the English WAV and the Spanish WAV under Narration audio, with es as the alternate language. Add each SRT separately in the publish panel. Leave the rooftop shot free of cues so viewers have time to scan the QR code.
Human check: Save and reopen a copy. Confirm the three camera beats, embedded textures, tree stages, and caption units. Read the map legend and credits at output size before exporting.
Sources and credits
City of Mesa Open Data Terms — Sections 3(e)–(f) permit redistribution of open-licensed data with City attribution. The prior layer audit found no additional restriction on the paths and footprint. Needs clarification for the full package: confirm coverage for the boundary and neighborhood layers with Mesa Enterprise GIS before a new redistribution.
Whisper WebCLI source and licence — GPL-3.0.
© OpenStreetMap contributors — separately attributed context under ODbL.
USGS Landsat 9 Collection 2 Level-2 — historical land-surface-temperature observations; not a cooling model.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script, scene) Assets City of Mesa GIS: City of Mesa GIS paths, Enterprise GIS building footprint, city boundary, and neighborhood records. Licence: City of Mesa Data Terms of Use License Agreement; see dataset-specific notices. OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors; separately attributed context. Licence: Open Database License (ODbL). USGS Landsat 9 Collection 2 Level-2: Historical land-surface-temperature observations; not a cooling model. Licence: USGS public domain. Tools Three.js (MIT) Playwright (Apache-2.0) dub.webcli.app (GPL-3.0) whisper.webcli.app (GPL-3.0) Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct (Apache-2.0)
9. Optional: Playwright harness for distributed decision-making and suggestions
Here, distributed means different participants and components have different responsibilities. In a future session a resident would define the need; in this rehearsal no resident participated. A fixed script and synthetic speech stand in for that role. The current rehearsal is single-operator browser automation, not multiplayer editing, voting, or community approval.
Resident role (simulated): The fixed script supplies the request and clarification; Dub speaks both lines.
Dub and Whisper: Dub makes synthetic speech for this rehearsal. Whisper transcribes the actual WAV; Playwright forwards that transcript, not the original script.
Strata model: Suggest a structured operation from a closed vocabulary, or refuse. It does not write geometry.
FutureFlux host: Enumerate visible tagged candidates, check operation and target, and either return a named refusal or apply an undoable edit.
Playwright: Drive browser surfaces, wait for real results, assert the refusal and the later edit, and save a numbered report. It does not make the decision.
Run the English rehearsal
Use the FutureFlux demo folder, not the Strata Editor repository. Run these commands from that folder. The runner loads its own scene.json into an isolated demo/.browser/ profile; don’t point it at your working scene or normal profile.
npm ci
npm test
npx playwright install chromium
npm run rehearse
For installed Chrome, use FLUX_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome npm run rehearse. First use needs network access for the hosted apps and model downloads. Rehearsal writes evidence, not video footage.
Ask “What if we shaded this walkway?” With the community-center walkway and park loop both visible, the host returns ambiguous-path, highlights both, and asks which one. Nothing is added. The English runner holds the refusal visibly for at least 3.5 seconds.
Clarify “The one by the community center.” On success the validated shade.add adds one proposal to center-walk.
Read the newest takes/*-english.json. Check the actual transcript, refusal, resolved path, and edit journal. The older fixture rehearses a canopy; the 48-second tour uses trees. The fixture does not exercise the Landsat layer.
If it fails, check the transcript before looking at candidate selection and refusal reason. Don’t silently fix a transcript or substitute a successful model response. Spanish SRT playback and Spanish speech recognition are separate checks. Earlier Spanish speech attempts did not reliably resolve the landmark and were refused without an edit. No OBS footage or Spanish end-to-end pass is claimed.
Workshop extension: Suggest → Review → Apply
The existing rehearsal applies a valid clarified operation automatically. The following human review step is a proposed extension, not a feature already available in Strata.
Suggest: Collect options against the same scene revision, such as shading the center walkway first or comparing it with the park loop. Show the landmark, proposed change, rationale, and limits of the evidence. Preview separately; don’t change the shared baseline.
Review: Compare suggestions side by side. Clarify locations and discuss coverage, access, and maintenance. Record the facilitator’s reason and any unresolved objections rather than picking a winner automatically.
Apply: A designated facilitator approves one proposal. Recheck the target and scene revision before applying one undoable command. If the scene changed, require reconfirmation.
Use two isolated Playwright browser contexts for resident and reviewer roles against a disposable test project. Connect them through the prototype’s shared suggestion store: isolated contexts don’t share local editor state. Pin a scene fixture and compare affected objects before and after each step.
Ambiguous: Show both candidates and request clarification; no geometry changed.
Awaiting review: The reviewer sees the target and rationale; the shared scene stays unchanged.
Rejected: Record the reason; no edit occurs.
Approved: Apply one edit to the approved path; repeated approval doesn’t duplicate it; Undo restores the prior state.
Stale: A changed scene revision blocks the proposal until reconfirmed.
Transcription or model failure: Show a named failure; no fallback edit.
Use fixed transcripts or model outputs for fast approval-state tests and label them as fixtures. Keep a separate live rehearsal for actual speech and inference. Log suggestion ID, scene revision, candidate IDs, decision, and resulting edit ID. Use synthetic or consented speech and keep personal information out of shared reports.

posts.title: Build a GIS-grounded scene by hand
posts.text:
All tutorials
Build a GIS-grounded scene by hand
No model, prompt, speech recognition or generated code is required. Build the site with deterministic JavaScript, and inspect the evidence at every step.
Reconstruct the FutureFlux site at Red Mountain Multigenerational Center in Mesa, Arizona, using the JS Shell. The numbered steps below are complete, sequential snippets for the human-operated Shell, not requests to an AI. AI assistance and the original speech demo are separate, optional extensions at the end.
Open the cinematic, pinned scene · Browse the matching implementation
Open embed
The embed is the actual pinned Strata project, not a video. Orbit and inspect its scene tree, or use the full-size link above. It opens in authoring mode with timeline autoplay off; do not load a model or run the project's optional interaction script for the no-AI walkthrough. Use a separate, empty editor tab to build your own copy.
The Mesa scene with procedural gravel, paving, roof and stucco, warm low-angle light, cool fill and softened shadows, captured with Strata's Snapshot tool. City of Mesa GIS supplies the footprint and path centerlines; finishes and lighting are illustrative, not surveyed or a dated solar study. No proposal or heat result is shown. The thumbnail is a cropped, resized copy of this capture.
Before starting: save unrelated work and open a separate editor tab. In Settings → Renderer, choose WebGL, then use New for an empty scene. Open Shell, paste each complete block into the input marked JavaScript, no AI needed, and press Enter to run it (Shift+Enter inserts a newline). Do not use the AI input or Load AI. Run each numbered block once, in order, wait for its result, and stop if a check throws. No package installation or Strata build is needed.
1. Load and inspect the source records
The project saved GeoJSON extracts from the City of Mesa REST catalogue. The query envelope was -111.6692,33.4305,-111.6653,33.433, using spatial intersection with input and output spatial reference 4326.
Source layer Selected record Project use Parks/ParkFinder/MapServer/19 30121 / PKPTH2837 center-walk: walkway by the community center Same paths layer 30046 / PKPTH2771 park-loop: walkway along the park loop OpenData/CommunityMaps/MapServer/6 53258 Building footprint Parks/ParkFinder/MapServer/16 geodb_oid 1 Community-center location and identity
The extracts are in demo/data/; other paths in the envelope were deliberately omitted. The City's data terms apply. An empty copyright field in a REST response is not a public-domain licence. Record source, licence, attribution and modifications, as this project does in the updated PROVENANCE.md permission audit.
The raw-data blocks retain the earlier immutable extract pin below; those GeoJSON bytes are unchanged in the cinematic revision.
Why these extracts can be redistributed: Mesa's linked agreement, verified 2026-11-16 (MST), states in §3(e), Permitted Uses, that datasets are publicly available on an open-license basis, meaning there are no restrictions on copying, publishing, distributing, modifying or using the data for a commercial or non-commercial use. §3(f) requires listing the City as the source on products using the data or derivative work, including exported stills and footage. For the footprint, retain the layer credit: City of Mesa, Information Technology Department, Enterprise GIS. Additional source conditions also apply (§3(b)); §4 supplies the data as-is and disclaims accuracy, completeness and fitness. Read the full agreement, including its liability and indemnity terms. An accessible REST endpoint or an empty copyright field is not a licence, and fetching at generation time would not remove these obligations.
This first block downloads only pinned public GeoJSON, not executable project code. A named object on window retains state between Shell runs. The empty-scene guard prevents accidentally adding this tutorial to your other work.
(async () => { if (editor.scene.children.length || window.mesaTutorial) { throw new Error('Use an empty scene and a fresh tab before step 1.'); } const base = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tejaswigowda/test1/' + '7859f88a593617c16cccd96dddc5f905850a6f59/demo/data/'; const read = async name => { const response = await fetch(base + name); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(name + ': HTTP ' + response.status); return response.json(); }; const [paths, buildings] = await Promise.all([ read('mesa-paths.geojson'), read('mesa-buildings.geojson') ]); const check = (condition, message) => { if (!condition) throw new Error(message); }; const selected = [ { objectid: 30121, id: 'center-walk', label: 'Walkway by the community center', color: '#d2bc8e' }, { objectid: 30046, id: 'park-loop', label: 'Walkway along the park loop', color: '#dcd6c1' } ]; for (const spec of selected) { const feature = paths.features.find(f => f.id === spec.objectid); check(feature?.geometry.type === 'LineString', 'Missing ' + spec.id); } const footprint = buildings.features.find(f => f.id === 53258); check(footprint?.geometry.type === 'Polygon', 'Missing footprint 53258'); window.mesaTutorial = { paths, footprint, selected, check }; return selected.map(spec => { const f = paths.features.find(f => f.id === spec.objectid); return { id: spec.id, source: f.id, facility: f.properties.FACILITYID, points: f.geometry.coordinates.length }; }); })()
Human check: inspect the returned records: center-walk is source 30121 / PKPTH2837 with 5 points; park-loop is 30046 / PKPTH2771 with 13. Compare the saved coordinates and IDs with the linked source layers. If the download fails, stop and inspect the error; do not substitute invented paths.
2. Project the site into local metres
Longitude and latitude are not scene distances. Use the fixed origin below, with x east, y up and z south. This small-site approximation is for representative massing, not surveying. THREE and the editor command classes are already available in the JS Shell.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; m.origin = [-111.667328704, 33.431791272]; m.project = ([lon, lat], y = 0) => [ (lon - m.origin[0]) * 111320 * Math.cos(m.origin[1] * Math.PI / 180), y, -(lat - m.origin[1]) * 111320 ]; m.check(m.project(m.origin).every(v => v === 0), 'Origin must be zero'); const first = m.paths.features.find(f => f.id === 30121) .geometry.coordinates[0]; const local = m.project(first, 0.12); m.check(Math.abs(local[0] - 63.8344484391) < 0.000001, 'Check x'); m.check(Math.abs(local[2] - 31.0489561484) < 0.000001, 'Check z'); return { origin: m.project(m.origin), firstPathPointMetres: local }; })()
Human check: the origin becomes [0,0,0]. The first center-walk point is approximately [63.834448,0.12,31.048956] metres. Check the signs: east is positive x; south is positive z. All later meshes use this same conversion.
3. Build the ground and footprint
Set up a mesh helper and an undoable add helper. For a cinematic but reproducible finish, generate small, seeded grain textures in memory. Paving also has authored expansion joints. These are original procedural pixels, not downloaded photographs or AI-generated textures; the seed determines every pixel.
The footprint uses (x,-z) in its 2D shape. Rotating the mesh by -90 degrees around x makes its assumed 6 m extrusion vertical and preserves the orientation on reload.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; m.makeSurface = (name, color, repeat, seed, bumpScale, joints = false) => { const size = 64, data = new Uint8Array(size * size * 4); let state = seed; for (let y = 0; y < size; y++) { for (let x = 0; x < size; x++) { state = (Math.imul(state, 1664525) + 1013904223) >>> 0; const grain = state / 4294967296; const value = joints && (x < 1 || y < 2) ? 155 : Math.round(224 + (grain - 0.5) * 34); const i = (y * size + x) * 4; data[i] = data[i + 1] = data[i + 2] = value; data[i + 3] = 255; } } const map = new THREE.DataTexture(data, size, size, THREE.RGBAFormat); map.name = name + ' / seeded grain'; map.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; map.wrapS = map.wrapT = THREE.RepeatWrapping; map.repeat.set(...repeat); map.magFilter = THREE.LinearFilter; map.minFilter = THREE.LinearMipmapLinearFilter; map.generateMipmaps = true; map.anisotropy = 4; map.needsUpdate = true; return new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ name, color, map, bumpMap: map, bumpScale, roughness: 0.9, metalness: 0 }); }; m.sand = m.makeSurface('Procedural desert gravel', '#cfbda2', [36,36], 11, 0.12); m.planting = m.makeSurface('Procedural planted ground', '#7b895b', [24,7], 23, 0.08); m.roof = m.makeSurface('Procedural mineral roof', '#ddd4c4', [0.22,0.22], 37, 0.04); m.stucco = m.makeSurface('Procedural warm stucco', '#eee4d0', [0.75,0.75], 41, 0.055); m.foliage = m.makeSurface('Procedural foliage', '#56784d', [3,2], 53, 0.18); m.paving = m.makeSurface('Procedural jointed paving', '#e1d7c3', [1,1], 67, 0.025, true); m.mesh = (name, geometry, finish, position) => { const material = typeof finish === 'string' ? new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: finish, roughness: 0.94 }) : finish; const object = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material); object.name = name; object.position.set(...position); object.castShadow = object.receiveShadow = true; return object; }; m.add = objects => { for (const object of objects) editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, object)); }; const ground = m.mesh('Representative desert ground', new THREE.BoxGeometry(430, 1, 420), m.sand, [0, -0.6, -10]); const planted = m.mesh('Representative planted zone', new THREE.BoxGeometry(240, 0.1, 70), m.planting, [5, -0.03, -85]); const shape = new THREE.Shape(m.footprint.geometry.coordinates[0].map(p => { const [x, , z] = m.project(p); return new THREE.Vector2(x, -z); })); m.building = m.mesh('Community center / assumed 6m height', new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry(shape, { depth: 6, bevelEnabled: false }), [m.roof, m.stucco], [0, 0.05, 0]); m.building.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; m.building.userData = { source: 'City of Mesa building OBJECTID 53258', modifications: 'Assumed 6m height; not surveyed.' }; m.add([ground, planted, m.building]); const size = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(m.building) .getSize(new THREE.Vector3()); m.check(Math.abs(size.y - 6) < 0.00001, 'Building must be 6m high'); return { buildingSizeMetres: size.toArray() }; })()
Human check: the building is approximately 109.131 × 6 × 79.330 m in x/y/z, not an 80 m tall wall. Its extrusion material groups use mineral roofing for caps and stucco for walls. Inspect its rotation and materials in the Scene tree. Every texture is 64 × 64 RGBA pixels; repeating seed 11 produces identical gravel. Bump mapping changes shading, not surveyed geometry. Each object or path group is an undoable addition; undo all additions from a block before rerunning it.
4. Turn the two centerlines into walkways
Make one named group per source path. Each pair of points becomes a box, positioned at its midpoint and rotated along its direction. Width 3.3 m and thickness 0.18 m are assumptions. These boxes approximate a buffered centerline, not a surveyed paving polygon.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; m.pathGroups = m.selected.map(spec => { const feature = m.paths.features.find(f => f.id === spec.objectid); const points = feature.geometry.coordinates.map(p => m.project(p, 0.12)); const group = new THREE.Group(); group.name = spec.label; group.userData.fluxPath = { id: spec.id, label: spec.label, points, source: 'Mesa OBJECTID ' + spec.objectid + ' / ' + feature.properties.FACILITYID }; for (let i = 1; i < points.length; i++) { const a = new THREE.Vector3(...points[i - 1]); const b = new THREE.Vector3(...points[i]); const surface = m.paving.clone(); surface.map = m.paving.map.clone(); surface.map.repeat.set(1, a.distanceTo(b) / 3.3); surface.map.needsUpdate = true; surface.bumpMap = surface.map; const segment = m.mesh(spec.id + ' / ' + i, new THREE.BoxGeometry(3.3, 0.18, a.distanceTo(b) + 0.1), surface, a.clone().add(b).multiplyScalar(0.5).toArray()); segment.rotation.y = Math.atan2(b.x - a.x, b.z - a.z); group.add(segment); } return group; }); m.add(m.pathGroups); m.check(m.pathGroups[0].children.length === 4, 'Expected 4 center segments'); m.check(m.pathGroups[1].children.length === 12, 'Expected 12 park segments'); return m.pathGroups.map(g => ({ id: g.userData.fluxPath.id, segments: g.children.length, firstMidpoint: g.children[0].position.toArray() })); })()
Human check: expand both groups in the Scene tree: there are 4 and 12 segments. The first midpoints are approximately [58.150234,0.12,31.923832] and [33.105119,0.12,-84.984967]. Compare these with the average of each source's first two projected points. The community-center path is south of the footprint; the curved park path is north of it. Paving repeats are scaled by each segment's length, rather than stretching one joint pattern over every segment. Joint positions are illustrative, not GIS attributes.
5. Add representative trees and people
These are explicitly authored placements, not a tree inventory or observations of real people. The dimensions and positions below reproduce the original scene's context.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; const objects = []; for (const [x, z, radius] of [ [-68,-68,6], [-30,-94,5], [4,-93,5], [38,-100,6], [65,-75,4], [85,30,4], [-82,38,4], [68,62,4] ]) { objects.push(m.mesh('Arranged tree trunk / not surveyed', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.25, 0.4, 4, 8), '#8a7554', [x,2,z])); const crown = m.mesh('Arranged tree crown', new THREE.SphereGeometry(radius, 14, 9), m.foliage, [x,6.8,z]); crown.scale.y = 0.8; objects.push(crown); } for (const [x, z, color] of [ [39,39,'#305d70'], [42,40,'#b77f50'], [39,43,'#f1ead6'], [35,40,'#536d54'] ]) { objects.push(m.mesh('Arranged participant', new THREE.CapsuleGeometry(0.28, 1.05, 4, 8), color, [x,0.95,z])); objects.push(m.mesh('Participant head', new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.24, 10, 8), '#bf9979', [x,1.85,z])); } m.add(objects); m.check(objects.length === 24, 'Expected 16 tree and 8 participant meshes'); return { trees: 8, participants: 4, contextMeshes: objects.length }; })()
Human check: count eight crowns and four people, orbiting or zooming as needed. People should sit near the southern path, not at the scene origin. Trees are several metres high, while people are about two metres high.
6. Light and frame the site
Use derived sun by default when the scene has a dated observation. Bind the directional key and legend to the observation’s UTC timestamp and derive local display time with the site’s time zone. The capture hour is the relevant light for assessing shade at that hour; see the FutureFlux solar setup. This base geometry exercise has no data instant. The warm low-angle key below is therefore explicitly illustrative lighting, not a dated study. Only the key casts a shadow; the 2048-pixel PCF shadow map uses a radius of 3 for softened edges.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; const sky = new THREE.HemisphereLight('#bfd9ed', '#9d7954', 0.9); sky.name = 'Cool sky / warm ground bounce'; const sun = new THREE.DirectionalLight('#ffe0b0', 4.6); sun.name = 'Illustrative golden-hour key / not a dated solar study'; sun.position.set(-95, 55, 60); sun.castShadow = true; sun.shadow.mapSize.set(2048, 2048); Object.assign(sun.shadow.camera, { left: -160, right: 160, top: 160, bottom: -160, near: 1, far: 400 }); sun.shadow.bias = -0.00015; sun.shadow.normalBias = 0.08; sun.shadow.radius = 3; const rim = new THREE.DirectionalLight('#b5cce6', 0.65); rim.name = 'Cool edge fill / illustrative'; rim.position.set(90, 60, -100); m.add([sky, sun, rim]); editor.signals.sceneEnvironmentChanged.dispatch('None'); editor.scene.name = 'Mesa walkways / human-built representative scene'; editor.scene.background = new THREE.Color('#afc3d0'); editor.scene.fog = new THREE.Fog('#afc3d0', 390, 900); editor.backgroundType = 'Color'; editor.scene.userData.provenance = { source: 'City of Mesa GIS: paths 30121/30046, building 53258', licence: 'City of Mesa Data Terms of Use License Agreement', attribution: 'City of Mesa GIS / representative reconstruction', modifications: 'Local metres; assumed widths and height; arranged context, ' + 'seeded procedural finishes and illustrative golden-hour lighting.' }; editor.config.setKey( 'project/renderer/shadows', true, 'project/renderer/shadowType', THREE.PCFShadowMap, 'project/renderer/toneMapping', THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping, 'project/renderer/toneMappingExposure', 0.95 ); editor.camera.position.set(130, 115, 160); editor.camera.fov = 43; editor.camera.near = 0.1; editor.camera.far = 2000; editor.controls.center.set(0, 0, -16); editor.camera.lookAt(editor.controls.center); editor.camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); editor.camera.updateMatrixWorld(); editor.scene.updateMatrixWorld(true); editor.deselect(); editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(editor.camera); return { camera: editor.camera.position.toArray(), center: editor.controls.center.toArray(), objects: editor.scene.children.length }; })()
Human check: there are 32 top-level objects, two distinct paths, a horizontal building, eight trees and four people. Camera position is [130,115,160] and orbit center is [0,0,-16]. Choose as render in the viewport's shading menu to preview the export settings. Look for warm lit faces, cooler shaded faces, visible ground contact and softened tree/building shadows, without a clipped-white roof.
Preview and export must agree. Use Settings → Renderer → WebGL before loading or building: mixing a WebGPU authoring renderer with the WebGL export preview was observed to omit shadows in the preview. If you already built in WebGPU, save first, switch to WebGL and reload your saved JSON. The code sets the config consumed by Render → Snapshot and as render. Loading JSON alone does not reliably replace renderer preferences; when inspecting a loaded example, apply the four editor.config.setKey pairs above (not the whole construction block), then choose as render.
7. Verify the saved scene and capture it
Verify the serialized result, not just the working viewport. This block exports to memory and reloads a separate copy for inspection; it does not replace the live scene or run scripts.
(() => { const m = window.mesaTutorial; editor.scene.updateMatrixWorld(true); editor.camera.updateMatrixWorld(); const json = editor.toJSON(); m.check(Object.keys(json.scripts).length === 0, 'No scripts should be installed'); const copy = new THREE.ObjectLoader().parse(json.scene); copy.updateMatrixWorld(true); const groups = copy.children.filter(o => o.userData.fluxPath); m.check(groups.length === 2, 'Expected two reloaded paths'); for (const group of groups) { const points = group.userData.fluxPath.points.map(p => new THREE.Vector3(...p)); m.check(group.children.length === points.length - 1, 'Segment count changed'); group.children.forEach((segment, i) => { const middle = points[i].clone().add(points[i + 1]).multiplyScalar(0.5); const position = segment.getWorldPosition(new THREE.Vector3()); m.check(position.distanceTo(middle) < 0.000001, 'Lost path position'); const direction = points[i + 1].clone().sub(points[i]).normalize(); const axis = new THREE.Vector3(0,0,1).transformDirection(segment.matrixWorld); m.check(axis.dot(direction) > 0.999999, 'Lost path rotation'); }); } const building = copy.getObjectByName('Community center / assumed 6m height'); const size = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(building).getSize(new THREE.Vector3()); m.check(Math.abs(size.y - 6) < 0.00001, 'Lost building orientation'); m.check(json.controls.center.every((v, i) => v === [0,0,-16][i]), 'Camera center changed; reset editor.controls.center to [0,0,-16]'); m.check(json.scene.images.length === 6, 'Expected six embedded grain images'); m.check(json.environmentType === 'None' && copy.environment === null, 'Disable the default environment fill to retain the authored contrast'); m.check(json.scene.images.every(image => typeof image.url === 'object' && image.url.data.length === 64 * 64 * 4), 'Textures must be embedded

posts.title: Hardy–Weinberg as a square
Tutorials
posts.text:
Tutorials
Step-by-step walkthroughs for building scenes, games, animation and characters with Strata — by hand, no AI required. 28 tutorials.
Scenes8 Games4 Animation and rendering8 Characters5 Motion capture3
Scenes Build and label a scene, or cut a model into named parts. Build a GIS-grounded scene by hand Build a Mesa site scene from mapped paths and a footprint without AI, add procedural finishes and cinematic lighting, and verify every saved result. AI assistance remains optional and human-checked. Open example → FutureFlux: From a Mesa heat map to a tree-shade proposal Build a bilingual Mesa surface-heat tour from mapped geometry and Landsat observations, then stage proposed tree shade and animate the camera. Cut any textured mesh into named parts The editor's SEG tool on any one-piece textured model: read the UV islands and painted colours, decide what each piece is, and cut it into named, classed meshes in one undo step. An avocado is the easy case, a toy duck the hard one (ten islands, six parts), an animated fox shows a skinned mesh cut with its skeleton and clips intact, and the page says where the method stops working. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Cut a scene into named parts SEG on a furnished room: one mesh, 538 texture islands, no part that is one island. SEG joins the islands that touch into components, measures them in the world frame, places everything you did not name on the nearest anchor you did, and checks the cut; you supply the anchors and their names. Says where the checks fired on the first attempt. Built with the JS Shell. Name every part of a street-corner diorama SEG on a 71-mesh street-corner diorama whose biggest mesh has 3,297 texture islands: too many to anchor individually. An agent names 22 regions from orthographic views, cuts nine meshes into 124 named, classed parts, names the 62 meshes that were already separate, and selects one object across all its materials with a class. Says where SEG's own warning caught a second post box, and that the cut replays. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Cut an avocado into named parts, building the tool by hand The editor's SEG tool, written out by hand on a one-piece avocado: read the evidence the file carries (separate patches of the texture, and the colours painted on them), cut it into five named, classed meshes (skin, pit, cavity, flesh, edge) without losing a triangle, and check the cut. Says plainly where the method stops working. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Build a night scene from scratch The from-scratch workflow: helper functions, noise-displaced ground, night lighting, a moving object and a hero camera. Open example → Build a wizard hat and sculpt a face into it Assemble a hat from primitives, then sculpt a relief smiley into it as one undoable step. Games Build a scene, label it, and leave the behaviour to game code. Build a table-view paddle game scene Build a paddle game as a receding table, and verify the camera framing by projecting points to screen space. Build a bubble shooter scene A lane, one class-tagged bubble template for game code to clone, a rainforest backdrop and a score sign. Build a fighting-game arena scene A tavern stage, two class-tagged fighters and a health-and-mana HUD, built for game code to drive. Build a labelled racing circuit with a script Generate a whole circuit from corner points and name every object at creation so game engines can find it. Animation and rendering Timelines, cameras and shots. Make a Pythagorean-theorem short Build a 100-second animated demonstration that 3² + 4² = 5², extend it to two more triples with quarter turns of the camera, and add subtitles, using the JS Shell and the Universal Timeline. Open example → Build the (a + b)³ proof in 3D A 3D visual proof of (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ with no numbers: a whole cube falls apart into eight coloured blocks that line up under the expanded equation, with five cameras, an x-ray and subtitles, all from the JS Shell. Open example → Hardy–Weinberg as a square The Hardy–Weinberg law as a square: p² + 2pq + q² for one round of random mating, then a count of the alleles that shows p and q are unchanged, with the assumptions listed. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Why cells are small: surface area to volume Cubes of side 1, 2 and 3 have surface-to-volume ratios of 6, 3 and 2 per unit-cube width, falling as 1 / side in any units: why cells stay small and divide, and why mitochondria and lungs fold their membranes. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → A projectile: two motions, one path A thrown ball's curve is a sideways motion at constant speed plus an up-and-down motion under gravity. Orbit the path to see each alone, then put them back together. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → A crank, a rod and a piston: crank-slider kinematics A crankshaft, connecting rod and piston through one revolution: the dead centers, the stroke, and the mechanical advantage drawn as a gap that vanishes at the dead centers. Orbit the assembly to see what a flat view hides. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Why molecules are shaped differently: electron-pair repulsion Methane, ammonia and water built from coloured spheres and bonds: four electron pairs spread to the corners of a tetrahedron, and each lone pair, which has no atom on it, closes the angle a little more (109.5°, 107°, 104.5°). Orbit each molecule to see what a flat drawing hides. Built with the JS Shell. Open example → Add a static hero camera to a render sequence Cut a fixed hero camera into a render sequence to show a moment your main camera does not frame well. Characters Import, restyle, pose and animate a character. Make your own MetaHuman Import a MetaHuman GLB, restyle it, pose its 51 face blendshapes and capture a still. One dance, two characters Bake one Mixamo dance onto two different characters and stage them with an orbiting camera. Restyle a VRM into an explorer with the JS Shell Restyle a VRoid base model into an expedition explorer: retint, re-clothe, attach gear and pose a smirk. Animate a finished character: clips, a timeline and a camera Open a finished VRM that carries a baked body clip and a baked face clip, read what the file holds, start the body on cue and keep a camera on her as she walks. Character by portrait.webcli.app and look.webcli.app, rigged with rig.webcli.app. Open example → Authoring a face: gaze and idle Give two characters a face with timeline keys: gaze that follows, a seeded blink and held expressions. Motion capture Work from recorded performances. A martial-arts lesson, then a sparring match, in a bamboo dojo Two characters share one mocap clip in a bamboo dojo: a lesson, then a sparring match filmed by four cameras. Editing captured motion as data Cut a 170-second two-performer capture to 53 seconds with a non-destructive edit list. A sparring match from a two-person motion capture Turn a two-person sparring capture into a 53-second match, checked frame by frame for collisions.

posts.title: Make your own MetaHuman
posts.text:
Make your own MetaHuman
All tutorials
A MetaHuman is a photoreal rigged character — and metahuman-to-glb is an open-source (MIT) pipeline that exports one from Unreal Engine 5.7 as a single web-ready .glb with all 51 ARKit face blendshapes. This tutorial loads one of its sample characters, Bruce, straight from the project's GitHub Pages URL, then makes him yours: no hair, a new skin tone and outfit, a smile posed from the blendshapes, selector-friendly classes on every part, and a still image from the Render tab. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
The result of this tutorial, captured with the Render tab's Take Snapshot — Bruce, bald, in a blue leather jacket, smiling.
Where the character comes from. creategamecharacters/metahuman-to-glb is a five-stage pipeline (Unreal assemble → Sequencer ARKit bake → Blender shape keys → Draco GLB → three.js viewer). Its live demo hosts the finished characters, so you can import one with a plain fetch — no download, no account. To bring in your own MetaHuman, run that pipeline on it and fetch (or drag in) the resulting GLB exactly the same way. The sample files are about 80 MB, so the first load takes a moment.
1 Import Bruce straight from the URL
The host sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, so the browser can fetch the GLB directly. Wrapping the bytes in a File and handing it to the editor's own loader is the same path as File → Import or dragging a file onto the page — Draco and every other glTF extension are already handled:
const url = 'https://creategamecharacters.github.io/metahuman-to-glb/5.7/characters/bruce/bruce.glb'; const blob = await (await fetch(url)).blob(); editor.loader.loadFiles([new File([blob], 'bruce.glb', { type: 'model/gltf-binary' })]);
A progress banner shows reading, then parsing, and then the Import glTF dialog appears. Leave the defaults and click OK — geometry compression is for later, and see the note in step 7 before you turn it on for a rigged character.
Use fetch, not fetchAPI, for binary files. fetchAPI returns parsed JSON or text, which is right for APIs and wrong for a 80 MB model. Plain fetch(...).blob() keeps the bytes intact.
2 See what you imported
A MetaHuman GLB is a skinned body plus a pile of separate meshes. List them before touching anything — the names are how you'll address each part:
const rig = []; scene.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) rig.push(o.name + (o.isSkinnedMesh ? ' (skinned)' : ' (hair card)')); }); rig;
You'll see the skinned SKM_Bruce_FaceMesh_1…8 (skin, teeth, eyes, lashes), SKM_Bruce_BodyMesh001, the outfit pieces Bruce_Outfits_1/2/3 (jacket, pants, shoes), and flat card meshes for Hair_, Beard_, Mustache_ and Eyebrows_. The face also carries the 51 ARKit blendshapes:
const face = scene.getObjectByName('SKM_Bruce_FaceMesh_1'); Object.keys(face.morphTargetDictionary).length; // 51 Object.keys(face.morphTargetDictionary).slice(0, 5); // ['eyeBlinkLeft', 'eyeLookDownLeft', 'eyeLookInLeft', 'eyeLookOutLeft', 'eyeLookUpLeft']
3 Take the hair off
Hair, beard and moustache are separate card meshes, so removing them is just hiding three objects. The eyebrows are also cards, and stay:
['Hair_S_Casual_CardsMesh_Group0_LOD0', 'Beard_M_MuttonChops_CardMesh_Group0_LOD0', 'Mustache_S_Horseshoe_CardMesh_Group0_LOD0' ].forEach(n => { scene.getObjectByName(n).visible = false; });
Not every character has the same part names. Ada, for example, has Eyebrows_M_Thin… and no beard, and her outfit meshes are named differently. If you'd rather not type names, the repo's presets/rigParts.js classifies the parts by mesh and material name: const p = findParts(scene) gives you p.hair, p.face, p.shirt, p.shoes… for any MetaHuman export.
4 Change the skin and the clothes
Skin keeps its texture and is only tinted (the colour multiplies the map), so pores and detail survive. Clothes drop their texture for a flat colour. Both go through a small helper that edits a clone of the material and swaps it in — changing a material that has already been drawn can leave the WebGPU renderer with a stale uniform buffer, and a fresh material avoids that:
const restyle = (mesh, fn) => { const edit = old => { const m = old.clone(); fn(m); old.dispose(); return m; }; mesh.material = Array.isArray(mesh.material) ? mesh.material.map(edit) : edit(mesh.material); }; // Skin: tint only, keep the texture for (const n of ['SKM_Bruce_FaceMesh_1', 'SKM_Bruce_BodyMesh001']) { restyle(scene.getObjectByName(n), m => m.color.set(0xb98a6c)); } // Clothes: flat colour, no texture restyle(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_1'), m => { m.map = null; m.color.set(0x1b3a6b); m.roughness = 0.6; }); // jacket restyle(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_2'), m => { m.map = null; m.color.set(0x202428); m.roughness = 0.7; }); // pants restyle(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_3'), m => { m.map = null; m.color.set(0xf2f2f2); m.roughness = 0.5; }); // shoes
Change the hex values to change the person. Skin is the one to tune by eye: lighter tints read warmer under the default environment than they look as swatches.
5 Pose the face with the ARKit blendshapes
Each of the 51 shapes is a morph target with an influence from 0 to 1. The same shape names exist on the face, the eyebrow cards, and (here) the beard and moustache cards, so one helper sets a shape everywhere it exists:
const express = (shape, value) => scene.traverse(o => { const i = o.morphTargetDictionary?.[shape]; if (i !== undefined) o.morphTargetInfluences[i] = value; }); express('mouthSmileLeft', 0.8); express('mouthSmileRight', 0.8); express('cheekSquintLeft', 0.4); express('cheekSquintRight', 0.4); express('browInnerUp', 0.3);
Other useful ones: jawOpen, eyeBlinkLeft/eyeBlinkRight, mouthPucker, browDownLeft, eyeLookUpLeft. Because they're ordinary morph target influences, the Universal Timeline can keyframe them like any other number — a blink or a talking mouth is just a short clip.
6 Tag the parts with classes
The auto-derived classes on an imported rig are mostly material-name noise (.mifaceskinbakedlod0skmbrucefacemesh). Add a few meaningful ones with tagClass — it's a command, so it's undoable and travels with the scene — and the parts become addressable by selector:
tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('SKM_Bruce_FaceMesh_1'), 'head'); tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('SKM_Bruce_FaceMesh_1'), 'skin'); tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('SKM_Bruce_BodyMesh001'), 'skin'); tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_1'), 'jacket'); tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_2'), 'trousers'); tagClass(scene.getObjectByName('Bruce_Outfits_3'), 'shoes'); $S('.skin').count(); // 2 — head and body, both retinted together by one selector
7 Frame the shot and take a snapshot
Move the viewport camera to a head-and-shoulders view and project nothing by guesswork — set the position and look-at target, and tell the orbit controls the same target so the next mouse drag pivots around his face:
const cam = editor.camera; cam.position.set(0.35, 1.68, 1.15); cam.lookAt(0, 1.52, 0); editor.controls.center.set(0, 1.52, 0); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(cam);
Now open the Render tab. The Snapshot section at the top renders the scene once, offscreen, with no grid, gizmos or skeleton lines: pick Current view, a size (1280 × 720 for the picture above), PNG, and press Take Snapshot. It downloads the file and leaves a preview with Download again and Copy to clipboard buttons under it. Tick Transparent for a cut-out with no background.
Don't compress a rigged character on import. The Import glTF dialog's geometry options include Simplify mesh. Strata skips that step for skinned meshes and ones with morph targets (it would otherwise strip the skin weights and blendshapes), so on a MetaHuman it does nothing useful — and quantizing normals only helps non-skinned meshes. Leave compression off here.
8 The same edits from the Customize tab, or as a spec
Steps 3–6 are a customizer: they change how an existing rigged character looks and what its face is doing, and nothing else. The Customize tab runs exactly those edits from a panel (skin tint, hair and beard toggles, clothing recolor, expression sliders, a bone-attached prop), and the same edits can be written as a list of ops that replays deterministically — on this Bruce, on Ada, or on any other rigged GLB:
{ "customize": [ { "ops": [ { "op": "hide", "target": "part:hair", "optional": true }, { "op": "hide", "target": "part:beard", "optional": true }, { "op": "tint", "target": "part:skin", "color": "#b98a6c" }, { "op": "recolor", "target": "part:shirt", "color": "#1b3a6b", "roughness": 0.6 }, { "op": "recolor", "target": "part:bottom", "color": "#202428", "roughness": 0.7 }, { "op": "recolor", "target": "part:shoes", "color": "#f2f2f2", "roughness": 0.5 }, { "op": "blendshape", "shapes": { "mouthSmileLeft": 0.8, "mouthSmileRight": 0.8, "cheekSquintLeft": 0.4, "cheekSquintRight": 0.4, "browInnerUp": 0.3 } }, { "op": "tag", "target": "part:skin", "classes": ["skin"] } ] } ] }
Paste it into the Customize tab's Spec box and press Apply spec, or hand it to runCustomizeStage(scene, spec) from customize/customizeOps.js. "optional": true skips an op when the character has no such part (Ada has no beard), so one spec serves both.
Why it can only do these things. Every op here leaves the vertex set, the skin weights and the skeleton alone, which is what keeps the body skeleton and the 51 face morph targets working: the customized character still bakes and animates exactly as before (the tab shows a fingerprint of the rig and refuses to finish a run that changed it). Geometry edits, bone edits, swapping the body mesh, and adding a jacket or dress are therefore not customize ops — the spec validator rejects them. A rigid accessory such as sunglasses is allowed because it is parented to a bone; a new deformable garment must be skinned to the body first (the tab's Skin selected garment to body rig step), otherwise it z-fights and stays put when the character moves. Recoloring the clothing the character already has is the cheap, safe wardrobe.
9 Save it
Everything above is ordinary scene state — geometry, materials, classes, blendshape influences — so a normal commit captures it. Set your repository and token in the Git tab, then use Commit Scene. Expect a big commit for a MetaHuman: the face alone carries 51 full copies of its vertices per mesh, so the scene is stored as roughly a hundred megabytes of binary asset files plus a small scene.json that references them.
// Sanity-check what you're about to commit $S('.skin').count(); // 2 scene.getObjectByName('Hair_S_Casual_CardsMesh_Group0_LOD0').visible; // false editor.history.undos.length; // commands issued this session
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets Bruce (MetaHuman sample .glb): creategamecharacters, metahuman-to-glb; MetaHuman by Epic Games Licence: not stated for the character (the pipeline code is MIT); a MetaHuman is an Epic Games asset. Tools metahuman-to-glb (MIT)
