posts.title: Make a Pythagorean-theorem short
A martial-arts lesson, then a sparring match, in a bamboo dojo
posts.text:
A martial-arts lesson, then a sparring match, in a bamboo dojo
All tutorials
The finished scene, seen through the cam-wide camera at 30 s: the teacher demonstrates a kick while the student watches.
Two characters, one motion clip. A teacher performs a martial-arts routine in short chunks; after each chunk the student, who has been standing and watching, repeats it. Around them a bamboo hut with warm lanterns and a low sun, and four cameras that cut between over-the-shoulder, side and wide shots. Everything after the import is the JS Shell and the Render tab, and the finished scene is dojo.json in the tejaswigowda/test1 repo.
Part 2 (steps 11–14): the same hut with a second pair of characters, now sparring for 170 s — sparring.json, seen through cam-wide at 12 s.
Where the pieces come from. Both characters are VRM models made with facebind. They were rigged and given the animation with bodyrig-webCLI, which writes one GLB per character with the clip baked in. The motion itself is from Mesquite MoCap: Democratizing Real-Time Motion Capture with Affordable, Bodyworn IoT Sensors and WebXR SLAM (arXiv:2512.22690). Both characters carry the same clip, named p2, 46.83 s long. Part 2 (step 10 onwards) uses a second pair from the same pipeline whose two clips, st1_1072026Skeleton and st2_1072026Skeleton (170.17 s each), were captured together. That sparring capture was recorded with an OptiTrack system in the course “Martial Arts and Motion Capture” (GAME 294) at Arizona State University, run by Pavan Turaga and recorded by Assegid Kidane; see A sparring match from a two-person motion capture for what to do with it.
How to follow along. Open the editor, import your two GLBs (Import in the menu bar), open the Shell tab and paste each block in order. Every block goes through an undoable command, so Ctrl/Cmd+Z backs out a step. The selectors below (.vroidv110malev113bound-15p2glb) are derived from the imported object names; yours will differ, so check with scene.children.map(o => o.name) and adjust.
Each Shell command runs in its own scope. A const or function from one block is not visible in the next, so step 1 stores the shared pieces on window.dojo and every later block starts by pulling out what it needs with const { … } = window.dojo;. Only the bamboo-frame block in step 5 (and, in Part 2, the swap block in step 10 and the shot-list block in step 13) needs await, so only those are wrapped in (async () => { … })();; the Shell does not print what an async block returns, so they leave their results on window.dojo too. holdTimelineAt(t), used throughout, is a Shell global that jumps the whole scene to t seconds — exactly what scrubbing the timeline does.
1 Import and pick a teacher
Import both GLBs. They arrive as two top-level groups, each with its own copy of the clip p2, and the same clip name does not clash because a clip is bound to its own character. Make the bald one the teacher and the other the student; below, the teacher is the group whose name contains (15) and the student the one containing (11).
const T = scene.children.find(c => /\(15\)/.test(c.name)); // teacher const S = scene.children.find(c => /\(11\)/.test(c.name)); // student const bone = (root, re) => { let r = null; root.traverse(o => { if (!r && o.isBone && re.test(o.name)) r = o; }); return r; }; const wp = b => b.getWorldPosition(new THREE.Vector3()); const hips = ch => bone(ch, /J_Bip_C_Hips/); window.dojo = { T, S, bone, wp, hips, plan: [] };
Check it took: window.dojo.T.name and window.dojo.S.name should print the two character names.
Frame 0 of this clip is a T-pose. The routine starts from a relaxed stance at about 4.5 s into the clip, so everything below treats 4.5 as the "rest" time: both characters are held there before and between their turns.
2 Put them face to face
Imported clips carry root motion: the hips travel through the scene as the clip plays, and the clip's own root node can start well away from the group origin. Placing the groups by their position alone therefore leaves the characters wherever the clip puts them. Instead, measure where the hips are at rest time, then move each group so the hips land on the spots you want.
const { T, S, wp, hips } = window.dojo; // Hold the whole scene at the rest stance (this is what scrubbing does), then read where each pair of hips is. holdTimelineAt(4.5); scene.updateMatrixWorld(true); const s0 = wp(hips(S)), t0 = wp(hips(T)); // Teacher goes to the mirror image of the student across the origin on z. const target = new THREE.Vector3(s0.x, 0, -s0.z); const d = target.clone().sub(t0); d.y = 0; editor.execute(new SetPositionCommand(editor, T, T.position.clone().add(d)));
The pair now stand about 3.4 m apart on the z axis. Next, turn them to face each other. The chest line is the reliable way to measure facing — the angle between the shoulder normal and the direction to the partner — so use it to check, then nudge rotation.y until both read close to 0°:
const { T, S, bone, wp, hips } = window.dojo; const facingError = (a, b) => { const l = wp(bone(a, /J_Bip_L_UpperArm/)), r = wp(bone(a, /J_Bip_R_UpperArm/)); const f = l.sub(r).cross(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0)); f.y = 0; f.normalize(); const to = wp(hips(b)).sub(wp(hips(a))); to.y = 0; to.normalize(); return +(f.angleTo(to) * 180 / Math.PI).toFixed(1); }; [facingError(T, S), facingError(S, T)]; // aim for ~0 at the rest stance
Why measure instead of rotating by 180°. The clip's root node has its own orientation, so the group's rotation.y that makes a character face its partner is not a round number (the teacher ended up near +92° and the student near +272° here). Measure, then adjust — a few degrees either way is easy to see from above in the viewport.
While the routine plays, the performer turns and kicks, so the facing error grows mid-move. That is the clip, not the placement; at the rest stance both are within a degree or two.
3 Teach in chunks: the demo, then the repeat
The timeline is a list of directives. $S(selector).at(t).play(clip, { duration }) starts a clip, .seek(time) picks where in the clip to start, and .pause() freezes it. Before its first play a clip shows frame 0 (the T-pose), so first park both characters at the rest stance, then play the routine in three chunks:
The teacher demonstrates a chunk of the clip while the student stands at rest. One second later, the student plays the same chunk while the teacher watches at rest. A second after that, the next chunk begins.
const { plan } = window.dojo; // [who, start, end] windows on the timeline const teacher = $S('.vroidv110malev113bound-15p2glb'); const student = $S('.vroidv110malev113bound-11p2glb'); // Park both on the rest stance: play for 1 s, seek to 4.5 s, pause. for (const who of [teacher, student]) who.at(0).play('p2', { duration: 1000 }).seek(4.5).pause(); // Three chunks of the 46.8 s clip, in clip time. const chunks = [[4.5, 16.4], [16.4, 29.1], [29.1, 46.8]]; let t = 1; for (const [a, b] of chunks) { const len = +(b - a).toFixed(2); teacher.at(t).play('p2', { duration: len * 1000 }).seek(a); // teacher demos teacher.at(+(t + len).toFixed(2)).pause(); // ...and freezes student.at(+(t + len + 1).toFixed(2)).play('p2', { duration: len * 1000 }).seek(a); // student repeats student.at(+(t + 2 * len + 1).toFixed(2)).pause(); plan.push(['teacher', t, +(t + len).toFixed(2)], ['student', +(t + len + 1).toFixed(2), +(t + 2 * len + 1).toFixed(2)]); t = +(t + 2 * len + 2).toFixed(2); } editor.timeline.toJSON().duration; // 90.6
Open the Animations tab and scrub. The teacher moves from 1 s to 12.9 s while the student holds still, then the student performs the same moves from 13.9 s to 25.8 s, and so on. Each chunk starts where the last one ended in the clip (4.5 → 16.4 → 29.1 → 46.8), so the lesson walks through the whole routine once, demo then repeat, in 90.6 s.
Why .seek() after .play(). A later play restarts the clip's local time at 0, so the chunk's start has to be re-applied each time. duration is in milliseconds and sets how long the clip runs before the next directive can take over.
4 A floor with no grid
A wood base, a tatami mat on top and a boundary tape make the floor. The important detail is the mat's texture: tatami is usually drawn with dark seams, but those read as a grid under the characters, so paint plain straw with random fibres instead — and the texture still tiles.
const dojo = new THREE.Group(); dojo.name = 'Dojo Floor'; const wood = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(60, 60), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6b4a2b, roughness: 0.8 })); wood.name = 'Wood Floor'; wood.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; wood.position.y = -0.06; wood.receiveShadow = true; // Straw texture: a flat tan base with thin random fibres, no seams. const c = document.createElement('canvas'); c.width = c.height = 512; const g = c.getContext('2d'); g.fillStyle = '#c9b57c'; g.fillRect(0, 0, 512, 512); for (let i = 0; i < 2600; i++) { const x = Math.random() * 512, y = Math.random() * 512, len = 30 + Math.random() * 90; g.strokeStyle = `hsla(${42 + Math.random() * 8},${30 + Math.random() * 20}%,${48 + Math.random() * 18}%,0.35)`; g.lineWidth = 1 + Math.random(); g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x, y); g.lineTo(x + len, y + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2); g.stroke(); } const straw = new THREE.CanvasTexture(c); straw.wrapS = straw.wrapT = THREE.RepeatWrapping; straw.repeat.set(3, 3); straw.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; // Box faces are [+x, -x, +y, -y, +z, +z]: only the top (+y) gets the straw. const side = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xb8a56c, roughness: 0.9 }); const top = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ map: straw, roughness: 0.9 }); const mat = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(10, 0.06, 10), [side, side, top, side, side, side]); mat.name = 'Tatami Mat'; mat.position.y = -0.03; mat.receiveShadow = true; dojo.add(wood, mat); for (const [x, z, w, d] of [[0, -4.65, 9.3, 0.07], [0, 4.65, 9.3, 0.07], [-4.65, 0, 0.07, 9.3], [4.65, 0, 0.07, 9.3]]) { const tape = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(w, 0.004, d), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x9a2a2a })); tape.name = 'Boundary Tape'; tape.position.set(x, 0.002, z); dojo.add(tape); } editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, dojo)); scene.fog = new THREE.FogExp2(0xb9c29a, 0.035); // a soft green haze scene.background = new THREE.Color(0xb9c29a);
Check the characters' feet against the mat: both should be within a centimetre of y = 0. If one floats or sinks, nudge that group's position.y with SetPositionCommand.
5 A bamboo hut
The hut is built from the same trick everywhere: a pole is a thin cylinder stretched between two points, with a few short rings along it for the bamboo nodes. Collect all the poles into arrays, merge each array into one mesh, and the whole frame is a handful of draw calls instead of a thousand. The hut is 20 m long and 15 m wide with an open front, so the cameras fly through it freely, and the sun comes in through the open end.
(async () => { const { mergeGeometries } = await import('three/addons/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js'); const V3 = THREE.Vector3, UP = new V3(0, 1, 0); let seed = 11; const rnd = () => (seed = (seed * 16807) % 2147483647) / 2147483647; const std = o => new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial(Object.assign({ roughness: 0.75 }, o)); const mesh = (name, geom, material, cast = false) => { const m = new THREE.Mesh(geom, material); m.name = name; m.castShadow = cast; m.receiveShadow = true; return m; }; // A pole from a to b, plus node rings along it. const poles = { p: [], n: [] }; const addPole = (set, a, b, r, nodeEvery = 0.55) => { a = new V3(...a); b = new V3(...b); const dir = b.clone().sub(a), len = dir.length(); dir.normalize(); const q = new THREE.Quaternion().setFromUnitVectors(UP, dir); const pole = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(r, r * 1.05, len, 7, 1); pole.applyMatrix4(new THREE.Matrix4().compose(a.clone().add(b).multiplyScalar(0.5), q, new V3(1, 1, 1))); set.p.push(pole); for (let t = 0.3 + rnd() * 0.25; t < len - 0.08; t += nodeEvery + rnd() * 0.15) { const ring = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(r * 1.25, r * 1.25, 0.05, 7, 1); ring.applyMatrix4(new THREE.Matrix4().compose(a.clone().addScaledVector(dir, t), q, new V3(1, 1, 1))); set.n.push(ring); } }; const X0 = -10, X1 = 10, ZW = 7.5, EAVE = 3.5, RIDGE = 6.1, EZ = 8.2; // hut extents // Posts every 2.5 m on both long sides, with beams along the tops. for (let x = X0; x <= X1 + 1e-6; x += 2.5) for (const z of [-ZW, ZW]) addPole(poles, [x, 0, z], [x, 3.85, z], 0.1, 0.7); for (const z of [-ZW, ZW]) addPole(poles, [X0 - 0.2, 3.8, z], [X1 + 0.2, 3.8, z], 0.08, 1.0); // Ridge pole and rafters (one every metre, on both slopes). for (const x of [X0, X1]) addPole(poles, [x, 0, 0], [x, RIDGE + 0.1, 0], 0.11, 0.8); addPole(poles, [X0 - 1.2, RIDGE + 0.05, 0], [X1 + 1.2, RIDGE + 0.05, 0], 0.1, 1.0); for (let x = X0 - 0.5; x <= X1 + 0.5 + 1e-6; x += 1) for (const s of [-1, 1]) addPole(poles, [x, RIDGE, 0], [x, EAVE, s * EZ], 0.05, 1.2); // Back wall: vertical slats that follow the gable, with three lashed rails. for (let z = -ZW; z <= ZW + 1e-6; z += 0.28) addPole(poles, [X0 + 0.05, 0, z], [X0 + 0.05, RIDGE - 0.05 - Math.abs(z) * 0.317, z], 0.05, 0.6); for (const y of [0.5, 1.9, 3.2]) addPole(poles, [X0 + 0.15, y, -ZW], [X0 + 0.15, y, ZW], 0.04, 1.4); // Low railings along both long sides. for (const z of [-ZW, ZW]) { for (const y of [0.5, 1.0]) addPole(poles, [X0, y, z], [X1, y, z], 0.04, 1.4); for (let x = X0 + 0.4; x < X1; x += 0.45) addPole(poles, [x, 0, z], [x, 1.0, z], 0.03, 0.6); } const hut = new THREE.Group(); hut.name = 'Bamboo Hut'; hut.add(mesh('Bamboo Frame', mergeGeometries(poles.p), std({ color: 0xc7b256, roughness: 0.55 }), true)); hut.add(mesh('Bamboo Nodes', mergeGeometries(poles.n), std({ color: 0x74672a, roughness: 0.7 }))); // Hand everything the next blocks need over on window.dojo. Object.assign(window.dojo, { mergeGeometries, rnd, std, mesh, addPole, hut, K: { X0, X1, ZW, EAVE, RIDGE, EZ } }); })();
Nothing is in the scene yet: the hut group is held on window.dojo.hut until the next block adds the roof and the scroll and puts the whole thing in.
Now the thatch roof: two tilted boxes with a straw texture drawn on a canvas, and a rolled ridge cap. Then a calligraphy scroll on the back wall — drawn on a canvas too, with the characters 武道 ("martial way").
const { rnd, std, mesh, hut } = window.dojo; const { X0, EAVE, RIDGE, EZ } = window.dojo.K; // Thatch texture: brown base, 1600 random strands, a dark band every 32 px. const tc = document.createElement('canvas'); tc.width = tc.height = 256; const tx = tc.getContext('2d'); tx.fillStyle = '#8f6f37'; tx.fillRect(0, 0, 256, 256); for (let i = 0; i < 1600; i++) { const x = rnd() * 256, y = rnd() * 256, len = 20 + rnd() * 50; tx.strokeStyle = `hsla(${34 + rnd() * 10},${35 + rnd() * 20}%,${28 + rnd() * 30}%,0.55)`; tx.lineWidth = 1 + rnd() * 1.6; tx.beginPath(); tx.moveTo(x, y); tx.lineTo(x + (rnd() - 0.5) * 4, y + len); tx.stroke(); } for (let y = 0; y < 256; y += 32) { tx.fillStyle = 'rgba(40,28,10,0.35)'; tx.fillRect(0, y, 256, 3); } const thatch = new THREE.CanvasTexture(tc); thatch.wrapS = thatch.wrapT = THREE.RepeatWrapping; thatch.repeat.set(8, 3); thatch.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; const thatchMat = () => std({ map: thatch, roughness: 0.95 }); const tilt = Math.atan2(RIDGE - EAVE, EZ), slope = Math.hypot(RIDGE - EAVE, EZ); for (const s of [-1, 1]) { const roof = mesh('Thatch Roof ' + (s > 0 ? 'South' : 'North'), new THREE.BoxGeometry(22.8, 0.24, slope + 0.5), thatchMat()); roof.position.set(0, (RIDGE + EAVE) / 2 + Math.cos(tilt) * 0.17, s * (EZ / 2 + Math.sin(tilt) * 0.17)); roof.rotation.x = s * tilt; hut.add(roof); } const ridge = mesh('Ridge Roll', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.24, 0.24, 23, 10), thatchMat()); ridge.rotation.z = Math.PI / 2; ridge.position.set(0, RIDGE + 0.28, 0); hut.add(ridge); // Scroll on the back wall. const sc = document.createElement('canvas'); sc.width = 256; sc.height = 512; const sx = sc.getContext('2d'); sx.fillStyle = '#efe3c4'; sx.fillRect(0, 0, 256, 512); sx.strokeStyle = '#7a1d1d'; sx.lineWidth = 10; sx.strokeRect(14, 14, 228, 484); sx.fillStyle = '#16120d'; sx.textAlign = 'center'; sx.font = 'bold 170px "Hiragino Mincho ProN","Yu Mincho",serif'; sx.fillText('武', 128, 220); sx.fillText('道', 128, 410); const scrollTex = new THREE.CanvasTexture(sc); scrollTex.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; const scroll = mesh('Dojo Scroll', new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1.5, 3), std({ map: scrollTex, roughness: 0.9 })); scroll.position.set(X0 + 0.28, 2.0, 0); scroll.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2; hut.add(scroll); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, hut));
Keep the cameras inside. The hut is sized around the camera paths from step 7 — 20 × 15 m, rafters starting 3.5 m up. If you resize it, re-run the check at the end of that step: with the posts, rails and scroll in the way, a camera that moves through one at the wrong moment shows a bamboo trunk filling the frame.
6 A grove outside, and the lighting
The grove is the same pole helper again: 64 tall stalks scattered outside the hut footprint, leaning a little, with a leaf canopy on half of them, over a green ground plane. It shows through the slats and over the rails and gives the scene a surrounding. The floor from step 4 shrinks to the hut's footprint so the grove ground can take over outside it.
const { mergeGeometries, rnd, std, mesh, addPole } = window.dojo; const grove = { p: [], n: [] }, leaves = []; for (let placed = 0; placed < 64;) { const x = (rnd() * 2 - 1) * 20, z = (rnd() * 2 - 1) * 20; if (Math.abs(x) < 12 && Math.abs(z) < 10.8) continue; // keep the hut itself clear const h = 8 + rnd() * 5, lx = (rnd() - 0.5) * 0.9, lz = (rnd() - 0.5) * 0.9; addPole(grove, [x, 0, z], [x + lx, h, z + lz], 0.07 + rnd() * 0.05, 0.6); if (placed % 2 === 0) { const l = new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1.5, 1); l.scale(1.7, 0.8, 1.7); l.translate(x + lx, h - 0.4, z + lz); leaves.push(l); } placed++; } const groveGroup = new THREE.Group(); groveGroup.name = 'Bamboo Grove'; groveGroup.add(mesh('Grove Stalks', mergeGeometries(grove.p), std({ color: 0x8aa23f, roughness: 0.6 }))); groveGroup.add(mesh('Grove Nodes', mergeGeometries(grove.n), std({ color: 0x4d5a22 }))); groveGroup.add(mesh('Grove Leaves', mergeGeometries(leaves), std({ color: 0x5c8a33, roughness: 0.95 }))); const ground = mesh('Grove Ground', new THREE.PlaneGeometry(140, 140), std({ color: 0x7b8a47, roughness: 1 })); ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; ground.position.y = -0.075; groveGroup.add(ground); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, groveGroup)); // Shrink the wood floor to the hut footprint (scale on the plane's own x/y axes). editor.execute(new SetScaleCommand(editor, scene.getObjectByName('Wood Floor'), new THREE.Vector3(21.4 / 60, 16.6 / 60, 1)));
Lighting is five different jobs. A hemisphere light fills shadows with warm sky and brown ground bounce; a low warm sun through the open end casts the long soft shadows that make the floor read as a floor; a cool rim from behind separates the characters from the back wall; and four paper lanterns are both a visible mesh and a point light that pools orange on the mat.
const { std, mesh } = window.dojo; const lights = new THREE.Group(); lights.name = 'Hut Lighting'; const hemi = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xfff0d2, 0x3a3020, 0.85); hemi.name = 'Sky Fill'; lights.add(hemi); const sun = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffd59a, 2.6); sun.name = 'Sun Key'; sun.position.set(14, 5, 5); sun.castShadow = true; Object.assign(sun.shadow.camera, { left: -5, right: 5, top: 5, bottom: -5, near: 2, far: 40 }); sun.shadow.mapSize.set(2048, 2048); sun.shadow.bias = -0.0004; sun.shadow.normalBias = 0.03; // no acne on skin lights.add(sun); const rim = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0x9db9ff, 0.55); rim.name = 'Cool Rim'; rim.position.set(-12, 6, -5); lights.add(rim); [[-5, 4.8], [-5, -4.8], [3.5, 4.8], [3.5, -4.8]].forEach(([x, z], i) => { const glow = new THREE.PointLight(0xffa24a, 22, 13, 2); glow.name = 'Lantern Light ' + (

posts.title: Why molecules are shaped differently: electron-pair repulsion
posts.text:
Why molecules are shaped differently: electron-pair repulsion
All tutorials
Open embed
A 93-second film that builds methane, ammonia and water from coloured spheres and bonds and asks why three molecules that all look like "a central atom with hydrogens" have three different shapes. The answer is one idea: the electron pairs around the central atom repel one another and spread out in space, and a lone pair, which has no atom on it, still takes up room. The film shows the flat drawing, lets the bonds swing out into three dimensions, orbits each molecule, and compares the three angles side by side. Built with the JS Shell.
1 The idea
Around the central atom of each molecule sit four electron pairs: some are shared with a hydrogen (a bond), and some belong to the central atom alone (a lone pair). Pairs of electrons repel one another, so the four of them settle as far apart as they can get, and in three dimensions that means pointing at the corners of a tetrahedron, with 109.5° between any two. What we see as the molecule's shape is only where the atoms are, not where the pairs are. Methane has four bonds, so all four pairs hold an atom: a tetrahedron. Ammonia has three bonds and one lone pair, so the atoms make a pyramid. Water has two bonds and two lone pairs, so the atoms make a bent line. That is the key lesson: electron-pair repulsion predicts molecular geometry.
The 3D advantage. The angles are the concept, and a flat drawing hides or distorts them. Drawn on paper, methane is a cross with 90° between the bonds; in space the same four bonds are 109.5° apart, and the hydrogens are farther from one another (3.56 against 3.08 when each bond is 2.18 long). The film makes that point by letting the bonds swing out of the flat cross, and again by looking at ammonia from straight above, where the three hydrogens look flat, and then from the side, where the pyramid shows. The shadow each molecule throws on the floor is itself a flat drawing.
The numbers the film uses are the measured ones for the three molecules, so the film also shows an ordering the model explains: the angle gets smaller as lone pairs are added.
Molecule Pairs Bonds Lone pairs Atoms' shape H–X–H angle X–H bond Methane, CH4 4 4 0 tetrahedral 109.5° (cos⁻¹ −⅓) 0.109 nm Ammonia, NH3 4 3 1 trigonal pyramidal 107° 0.101 nm Water, H2O 4 2 2 bent 104.5° 0.096 nm
The units are scene units, 20 to the nanometre, so the bonds are 2.18, 2.02 and 1.92 long. Atoms are drawn at ball-and-stick size (hydrogen 0.42, carbon 0.65, nitrogen 0.62, oxygen 0.60), not at their true sizes. The plan for the clock, with the times the voice sets (the cues were timed first, and every beat sits on its cue), in seconds:
Time What happens 0.8 – 10 The question, and the three molecules built one after another: the central atom, then each bond and the hydrogen on its end 10.5 – 17.6 Methane as it is drawn on paper: the bonds swing into a flat cross, 90° apart 18 – 27.3 Every bond is a pair of electrons (a yellow glow, two dots); the pairs repel, so the bonds swing out of the plane 27.8 – 34.6 A tetrahedron: a gold cage through the four corners and a 109.5° arc, while the camera orbits 35 – 46 Ammonia: three bonding pairs, then the fourth pair, a lone pair with no atom on it, a fatter glow on top 46.5 – 56.7 The same cage; the atoms alone make a pyramid; the lone pair squeezes the bonds to 107° 57.2 – 63.7 The camera looks straight down at ammonia (three hydrogens that look flat), then comes down to the side (the pyramid) 64.2 – 74.1 Water: two bonding pairs, two lone pairs, the cage, bent, 104.5° 74.6 – 83.1 All three side by side: tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal and bent, with 0, 1 and 2 lone pairs 83.6 – 89.7 The lesson 89.7 Cut to the end card
2 The palette, a room and a floor
The ten materials of the film are made once, here, and every mesh that uses a colour is handed the same one: white is hydrogen and every label, charcoal is carbon (and the electrons' dots), blue is nitrogen, red is oxygen, grey is a bond, a soft translucent yellow is an electron pair, and gold draws the geometry (the tetrahedron and the angles). Seven in the palette, the room, the floor and the end card make ten. A shared material cannot fade one mesh without fading all of them, so this film reveals things by growing them from a scale of 0.001 and removes them by shrinking. One key light up and in front makes every molecule throw a shadow on the floor.
// The palette: every material of the film, made once and handed to every mesh that uses it (ten in all, with the room, the floor and the end card). // Atoms follow the usual colours: hydrogen white (the same white as the labels), carbon charcoal, nitrogen blue, oxygen red. Bonds are grey, electron pairs are // a soft yellow glow, and gold draws the geometry (the tetrahedron and the angles). const mat = (color, k = 0.4, extra = {}) => new MeshStandardMaterial({ color, emissive: color, emissiveIntensity: k, roughness: 0.45, metalness: 0.05, ...extra }); globalThis.PAL = { carbon: mat(0x4b5368, 0.3), nitrogen: mat(0x4f7dff, 0.4), oxygen: mat(0xff4d4d, 0.4), bond: mat(0xc4cbe0, 0.25), gold: mat(0xffb703, 0.55), pair: new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffe066, emissive: 0xffd23f, emissiveIntensity: 0.35, roughness: 0.4, metalness: 0, transparent: true, opacity: 0.42, depthWrite: false }), white: mat(0xffffff, 0.45) // hydrogen, and every label }; // a room around the scene and a floor under it, for the shadows to land on const room = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(100, 40, 70), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2b3680, roughness: 0.95, metalness: 0, side: THREE.BackSide })); room.name = 'Room'; room.position.set(0, 12, 0); room.receiveShadow = true; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, room)); const floor = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(100, 70), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x232d70, roughness: 0.9, metalness: 0 })); floor.name = 'Floor'; floor.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; floor.receiveShadow = true; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, floor)); // one key light up and in front, so every shadow falls on the floor behind its molecule; one soft fill const key = new PointLight(0xfff1dd, 4.5, 0, 0); key.name = 'KeyLight'; key.position.set(4, 24, 14); key.castShadow = true; key.shadow.mapSize.set(2048, 2048); key.shadow.bias = -0.0004; key.shadow.intensity = 0.6; key.shadow.radius = 4; key.shadow.camera.near = 0.5; key.shadow.camera.far = 120; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, key)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, Object.assign(new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xdde6ff, 0x6a78c8, 1.2), { name: 'FillLight' }))); Object.keys(PAL).length // 7
3 The three molecules
One builder makes all three, from the same few parts. Each electron pair gets a pivot, a group at the central atom turned to point where that pair points. A bonding pivot holds a bond (a cylinder from the nucleus outward), a hydrogen on its end and a pair of electrons (a glow with two dots, halfway along); a lone-pair pivot holds only a fatter glow and two dots. The directions are the geometry: methane's four bonds are at acos(−1/3) from one another; in ammonia the lone pair points straight up and the three bonds are placed so that the H–N–H angle is 107°; in water the bonds are 104.5° apart and the lone pairs 115° apart. Everything is made with make(name, geometry, material, { classes }), so each part has a name an author chose and a class from the start: ch4_nucleus, nh3_2_bond, h2o_lone1.
The gold cage joins the four pair directions with six edges (each a group at its first corner, so it grows from there), and a gold arc marks one bond angle, in the plane of the two bonds. The block also makes the flat 90° arc for the cross. The last line prints the three angles it built, which is the first check: 109.47, 107.00 and 104.50.
// The molecules. Each is a group at its own station (methane left, ammonia middle, water right), built from the same few parts: // a nucleus; one PIVOT per electron pair, turned to point where that pair points; inside a bonding pivot, a bond, a hydrogen and a pair of electrons // (a soft glow with two dots); inside a lone-pair pivot, a fatter glow with two dots and no atom; the gold cage that joins the four pair directions // (a tetrahedron; each edge is a group at its first corner holding a bar, so it grows from that corner); and the gold arc that marks one bond angle. // Everything starts collapsed (scale 0.001) and grows at its moment: a shared material cannot fade one mesh, so the film reveals by growing. globalThis.EV = []; globalThis.ev = (t, fn) => EV.push([t, fn, EV.length]); globalThis.flush = () => { EV.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[2] - b[2]); EV.forEach(([, fn]) => fn()); return EV.length; }; globalThis.show = (sel, t, dur = 450) => ev(t, () => $S(sel).at(t).animate({ to: { scaleX: 1, scaleY: 1, scaleZ: 1 } }, dur, 'ease-out')); globalThis.hide = (sel, t, dur = 350) => ev(t, () => $S(sel).at(t).animate({ to: { scaleX: 0.001, scaleY: 0.001, scaleZ: 0.001 } }, dur, 'ease-in')); const M = globalThis.MOL = { R: { H: 0.42, C: 0.65, N: 0.62, O: 0.6 }, // ball-and-stick sizes, not true atomic sizes L: { C: 2.18, N: 2.02, O: 1.92 }, // the measured bond lengths, 0.109, 0.101 and 0.096 nm, at 20 units per nm ANGLE: { C: 109.47, N: 107, O: 104.5 }, LONE_ANGLE_O: 115, // the measured bond angles (the tetrahedral angle is acos(-1/3)) TET: Math.acos(-1 / 3), Y: 5.2, X: { ch4: -12, nh3: 0, h2o: 12 } }; const V = (x, y, z) => new THREE.Vector3(x, y, z), UPV = V(0, 1, 0), rad = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad, deg = THREE.MathUtils.radToDeg; const polar = (theta, phiDeg) => { const p = rad(phiDeg); return V(Math.sin(theta) * Math.cos(p), Math.cos(theta), Math.sin(theta) * Math.sin(p)); }; M.euler = dir => { const e = new THREE.Euler().setFromQuaternion(new THREE.Quaternion().setFromUnitVectors(UPV, dir.clone().normalize()), 'XYZ'); return [e.x, e.y, e.z]; }; M.eulerDeg = dir => M.euler(dir).map(deg); // the directions of the electron pairs: methane has four bonds; ammonia a lone pair straight up and three bonds; water two bonds and two lone pairs const nTheta = Math.acos(-Math.sqrt((2 * Math.cos(rad(M.ANGLE.N)) + 1) / 3)); // the angle from the lone pair to each N-H bond, from the H-N-H angle const half = rad(M.ANGLE.O / 2), lone = rad(M.LONE_ANGLE_O / 2), turn = new THREE.Matrix4().makeRotationY(rad(-45)); const DIRS = { ch4: { bonds: [UPV.clone(), polar(M.TET, -30), polar(M.TET, 90), polar(M.TET, 210)], lone: [] }, nh3: { bonds: [polar(nTheta, -30), polar(nTheta, 90), polar(nTheta, 210)], lone: [UPV.clone()] }, h2o: { bonds: [V(Math.sin(half), -Math.cos(half), 0), V(-Math.sin(half), -Math.cos(half), 0)], lone: [V(0, Math.cos(lone), Math.sin(lone)), V(0, Math.cos(lone), -Math.sin(lone))] } }; DIRS.h2o.bonds.forEach(d => d.applyMatrix4(turn)); DIRS.h2o.lone.forEach(d => d.applyMatrix4(turn)); // turned 45 degrees about the vertical, so from the front both the bend and the two lone pairs show M.DIRS = DIRS; const gAtom = { H: new SphereGeometry(M.R.H, 32, 20), C: new SphereGeometry(M.R.C, 32, 20), N: new SphereGeometry(M.R.N, 32, 20), O: new SphereGeometry(M.R.O, 32, 20) }; const gDot = new SphereGeometry(0.085, 12, 8); const gBond = L => new CylinderGeometry(0.1, 0.1, L, 16).translate(0, L / 2, 0); // from the nucleus out to the hydrogen const gLobeBond = L => new SphereGeometry(1, 24, 16).scale(0.36, L * 0.34, 0.36); const gLobeLone = new SphereGeometry(1, 24, 16).scale(0.62, 0.85, 0.62); const MAT = { C: PAL.carbon, N: PAL.nitrogen, O: PAL.oxygen }; const NAME = { ch4: 'methane', nh3: 'ammonia', h2o: 'water' }; // a pair of electrons: a glow with two dots, collapsed until its moment function pair(name, parent, at, glow, dotX, classes) { const g = make(name, null, null, { classes: ['pair', ...classes], parent, position: [0, at, 0], scale: 0.001 }); make(name + '_glow', glow, PAL.pair, { classes: ['pair-glow', ...classes], parent: g, shadows: false }); make(name + '_ea', gDot, PAL.carbon, { classes: ['electron'], parent: g, position: [dotX, 0, 0], shadows: false }); make(name + '_eb', gDot, PAL.carbon, { classes: ['electron'], parent: g, position: [-dotX, 0, 0], shadows: false }); return g; } M.build = (id, centre) => { const L = M.L[centre], d = DIRS[id]; const mol = make(NAME[id], null, null, { classes: ['molecule', id], position: [M.X[id], M.Y, 0] }); make(id + '_nucleus', gAtom[centre], MAT[centre], { classes: ['atom', 'nucleus'], parent: mol, scale: 0.001 }); d.bonds.forEach((dir, k) => { const n = `${id}_${k + 1}`, e = M.euler(dir); const p = make(n + '_pivot', null, null, { classes: ['pivot', 'bonding'], parent: mol, rotation: e }); make(n + '_bond', gBond(L), PAL.bond, { classes: ['bond'], parent: p, scale: 0.001 }); make(n + '_h', gAtom.H, PAL.white, { classes: ['atom', 'hydrogen'], parent: p, position: [0, L, 0], scale: 0.001 }); pair(n + '_pair', p, L / 2, gLobeBond(L), 0.2, ['bonding-pair']); }); d.lone.forEach((dir, k) => { const n = `${id}_lone${k + 1}`; const p = make(n + '_pivot', null, null, { classes: ['pivot', 'lone'], parent: mol, rotation: M.euler(dir) }); pair(n, p, 0.95, gLobeLone, 0.24, ['lone-pair']); }); // the cage: an edge between every two of the four pair directions, each growing from its first corner const corners = [...d.bonds, ...d.lone].map(v => v.clone().multiplyScalar(L)); for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) for (let j = i + 1; j < 4; j++) { const delta = corners[j].clone().sub(corners[i]), len = delta.length(), n = `${id}_edge${i + 1}${j + 1}`; const edge = make(n, null, null, { classes: ['cage'], parent: mol, position: corners[i].toArray(), scale: 0.001 }); edge.quaternion.setFromUnitVectors(UPV, delta.normalize()); make(n + '_bar', new CylinderGeometry(0.04, 0.04, len, 8).translate(0, len / 2, 0), PAL.gold, { classes: ['cage'], parent: edge, shadows: false }); } // the bond angle: the pair of bonds that faces the front camera most squarely let best = null; for (let i = 0; i < d.bonds.length; i++) for (let j = i + 1; j < d.bonds.length; j++) { const n = d.bonds[i].clone().cross(d.bonds[j]).normalize(), face = Math.abs(n.z); if (!best || face > best.face) best = { i, j, face }; } const a = d.bonds[best.i], b = d.bonds[best.j], theta = a.angleTo(b), r = 1.2; const arc = make(id + '_arc', new TorusGeometry(r, 0.05, 10, 48, theta), PAL.gold, { classes: ['angle'], parent: mol, scale: 0.001, shadows: false }); const nz = a.clone().cross(b).normalize(), ny = nz.clone().cross(a); arc.quaternion.setFromRotationMatrix(new THREE.Matrix4().makeBasis(a, ny, nz)); M[id] = { group: mol, a, b, angle: deg(theta), mid: a.clone().add(b).normalize() }; return mol; }; M.build('ch4', 'C'); M.build('nh3', 'N'); M.build('h2o', 'O'); // the flat cross that methane is drawn as on paper, and the angle marker between two of its arms const flat = [UPV.clone(), V(1, 0, 0), V(0, -1, 0), V(-1, 0, 0)]; M.flatDeg = flat.map(M.eulerDeg); // the four arms, as the rotations the pivots turn to M.tetraDeg = DIRS.ch4.bonds.map(M.eulerDeg); make('ch4_flatarc', new TorusGeometry(1.2, 0.05, 10, 48, Math.PI / 2), PAL.gold, { classes: ['angle', 'flat'], parent: M.ch4.group, scale: 0.001, shadows: false }); const angles = ['ch4', 'nh3', 'h2o'].map(id => id + ' ' + M[id].angle.toFixed(2) + ' pair ' + M[id].a.toArray().map(x => x.toFixed(2)) + ' | ' + M[id].b.toArray().map(x => x.toFixed(2))); angles.join('\n')
8.5 seconds in: the question, and the three molecules just built, still without their electron pairs.
4 Seven cameras
One camera per idea: a wide one, then a close one for each molecule (field of view 28°, so the perspective is shallow and the angles read truly), one that comes down from straight above ammonia to its side, a wide one for the comparison, and the end card. The path() helper writes a move around a centre as a list of keys, each an azimuth, a radius and a height. The close cameras drift a few degrees on each molecule, so the depth shows in the parallax, and swing wider (−30° to +30°) while the tetrahedron is on screen. The block ends by putting the cuts in order.
// seven cameras, one per idea: a wide one for the three molecules, one for methane, one for ammonia, one that comes down from above ammonia to its side, // one for water, one for the comparison, and the end card (seven shots). Each looks at its molecule from a little above, and drifts around it a few degrees, // so the depth shows in the parallax. function addCamera(name, fov) { const cam = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(fov, 16 / 9, 0.1, 400); cam.name = name; cam.userData.customClasses = ['camera']; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, cam)); return cam; } // a move around a centre, written as a list of keys: [time, azimuth in degrees (0 = straight in front, looking along -z), radius, height] globalThis.path = (cam, pts, aim, center = [0, 0, 0]) => { const keys = pts.map(([t, az, r, y]) => ({ t, pos: [center[0] + r * Math.sin(THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(az)), y, center[2] + r * Math.cos(THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(az))], lookAt: aim })); $S('#' + cam.name).setKeys(keys, { smooth: true }); cam.position.set(...keys[0].pos); // where the camera waits before its move starts cam.lookAt(...aim); }; const camWide = addCamera('camWide', 40), camMethane = addCamera('camMethane', 28), camAmmonia = addCamera('camAmmonia', 28), camAbove = addCamera('camAbove', 28); const camWater = addCamera('camWater', 28), camCompare = addCamera('camCompare', 40), end = addCamera('camCard', 50); const Y = MOL.Y; path(camWide, [[0.001, -6, 31, Y + 2.9], [9.9, 6, 31, Y + 2.9]], [0, Y - 0.2, 0]); path(camMethane, [[9.9, -8, 19, Y + 2.3], [26.9, 8, 19, Y + 2.3], [30.2, -30, 19, Y + 2.3], [34.5, 30, 19, Y + 2.3]], [MOL.X.ch4, Y + 0.25, 0], [MOL.X.ch4, 0, 0]); path(camAmmonia, [[34.5, 8, 19, Y + 2.3], [46.4, -8, 19, Y + 2.3], [56.6, 24, 19, Y + 2.3]], [MOL.X.nh3, Y + 0.25, 0], [MOL.X.nh3, 0, 0]); // from straight above (the three hydrogens look flat) down to the side (the pyramid shows): a quarter of a circle round the nitrogen { const R = 19, pts = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 8; i++) { const t = i < 3 ? 57.15 + i * 1.5 : 60.15 + (i - 2) * 0.5; // held above for the first words, then down in the second half const el = i < 3 ? 86 : 86 - (i - 2) / 6 * 64; pts.push([t, 6, R * Math.cos(THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(el)), Y + R * Math.sin(THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(el))]); } path(camAbove, pts, [MOL.X.nh3, Y + 0.25, 0], [MOL.X.nh3, 0, 0]); } path(camWater, [[63.6, 30, 19, Y + 2.3], [70.0, 5, 19, Y + 2.3], [73.9, -30, 19, Y + 2.3]], [MOL.X.h2o, Y + 0.25, 0], [MOL.X.h2o, 0, 0]); path(camCompare, [[73.9, -6, 31, Y + 2.9], [89.6, 6, 31, Y + 2.9]], [0, Y - 0.2, 0]); end.position.set(0, 9, -17.5); // faces the end card, which hangs on the back wall end.lookAt(0, 9, -34); const cams = Object.fromEntries(['camWide', 'camMethane', 'camAmmonia', 'camAbove', 'camWater', 'camCompare', 'camCard'].map(n => [n, $S('#' + n).nodes[0]])); const cuts = [[0, 'camWide'], [9.9, 'camMethane'], [34.5, 'camAmmonia'], [56.6, 'camAbove'], [63.6, 'camWater'], [73.9, 'camCompare'], [89.6, 'camCard']]; editor.scene.userData.renderShots = cuts.map(([at, name], i) => ({ id: 'shot-' + name, at, camera: cams[name].uuid, transition: i === 0 ? 'cut' : 'fade', transitionDur: 0.6 })); editor.work.touch(); editor.scene.userData.renderShots.length // 7
5 The labels
Click the Text stencil (Stencils tab) once, and then paste this. Every label is a copy of that stencil, left-aligned; widths come from the font. The font has no subscript digits, so each formula is a few small labels (the letters, then a smaller, lowered digit). Labels are children of their molecule's group, so they sit in its own frame. The words are shown and cleared in step 7, and a molecule's labels are off while the camera is on another molecule, so they do not spill into the next frame.
// every label is a copy of the one Text stencil, so they share its font; they share a material per colour too, so each label cuts in (and out) // rather than fading, because a shared material cannot fade one label without fading them all. A label'

posts.title: Build a table-view paddle game scene
posts.text:
Build a table-view paddle game scene
All tutorials
A classic arcade paddle game is a flat vertical screen — both paddles the same distance from the camera, separated left/right. This tutorial builds the other kind: a physical table you stand at one end of, your own paddle close in the foreground and the opponent's paddle small in the distance — then swaps the generic arcade backdrop for a sunset desert without touching the table itself. The whole thing is one Group per section, assembled with plain .add() calls and added in a single undo step. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
Standing at your own end of the table — the blue Player Paddle fills the foreground, the red Computer Paddle is small at the far end.
Pick your depth axis before you place anything. The natural mistake is building the arcade layout — paddles on +x/-x, walls on +y/-y, camera parked on +z looking straight in — and then trying to fix the camera afterward to make one paddle look "far away." No camera angle can do that: both paddles are equidistant from the camera on that layout, so any attempt to view it obliquely just makes the thin flat parts (walls, table) foreshorten into confusing diagonal slabs. Decide up front which world axis is "the length of the table" and build paddles onto that axis (here, z) — the perspective camera then does the near/far size difference for free.
1 Lay out the table along z, not x
Keep y as true vertical (matches the camera's default up vector) and put the two paddles at opposite ends of z instead of x. Build every part into one Group with .add(), then add the whole group with a single AddObjectCommand:
const group = new Group(); group.name = 'Paddle Game'; const tableMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x1c5c3a, roughness: 0.7 }); const railMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff, roughness: 0.5 }); const playerMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2e7dff, roughness: 0.4 }); const compMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xff4444, roughness: 0.4 }); const ballMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff, roughness: 0.3 }); const table = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(12, 0.4, 24), tableMat); table.name = 'Table'; table.position.set(0, -0.2, 0); group.add(table); const railL = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.3, 0.5, 24.4), railMat); railL.name = 'Rail Left'; railL.position.set(-6.15, 0.25, 0); group.add(railL); const railR = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.3, 0.5, 24.4), railMat); railR.name = 'Rail Right'; railR.position.set(6.15, 0.25, 0); group.add(railR); const centerLine = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.12, 0.02, 24), railMat); centerLine.name = 'Center Line'; centerLine.position.set(0, 0.01, 0); group.add(centerLine); // The two paddles are on opposite ends of z — this is the whole trick. const playerPaddle = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(2.2, 0.7, 0.4), playerMat); playerPaddle.name = 'Player Paddle'; playerPaddle.position.set(0, 0.35, 10.5); group.add(playerPaddle); const compPaddle = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(2.2, 0.7, 0.4), compMat); compPaddle.name = 'Computer Paddle'; compPaddle.position.set(0, 0.35, -10.5); group.add(compPaddle); const ball = new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.35, 24, 24), ballMat); ball.name = 'Ball'; ball.position.set(0, 0.35, 0); group.add(ball); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, group));
2 Frame the far end
A backdrop, two pillars, and a scoreboard panel behind the computer's end give the camera something to look at beyond the far paddle — an empty background makes distance harder to read. Same pattern: one group, plain .add(), one command:
const scenery = new Group(); scenery.name = 'Background Scenery'; const floor = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(60, 50), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x333844, roughness: 0.9 })); floor.name = 'Floor'; floor.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; floor.position.set(0, -0.45, -2); scenery.add(floor); const backdrop = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(24, 12), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x14202c, roughness: 0.85 })); backdrop.name = 'Backdrop'; backdrop.position.set(0, 5.5, -14); scenery.add(backdrop); const pillarMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x777f8c, roughness: 0.6 }); const pillarL = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.4, 0.4, 12, 16), pillarMat); pillarL.name = 'Pillar Left'; pillarL.position.set(-8, 5.5, -14); scenery.add(pillarL); const pillarR = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.4, 0.4, 12, 16), pillarMat); pillarR.name = 'Pillar Right'; pillarR.position.set(8, 5.5, -14); scenery.add(pillarR); const board = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(6, 1.6, 0.3), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x101418, roughness: 0.5 })); board.name = 'Scoreboard'; board.position.set(0, 10.5, -14); scenery.add(board); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, scenery)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, new AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.5))); const dir = new DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 1.2); dir.position.set(4, 12, 10); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, dir));
3 Stand the camera behind your own paddle
Position it a little further back than the player paddle's z, raised in y for eye height, and lookAt a point near the far end — down and slightly beyond the computer paddle, not the paddle itself, so the whole length of the table stays in frame:
const cam = editor.camera; cam.position.set(0, 3, 21); cam.up.set(0, 1, 0); cam.fov = 60; cam.lookAt(0, 0.2, -8); cam.updateProjectionMatrix(); editor.controls.center.set(0, 0.2, -8); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(cam); editor.signals.objectChanged.dispatch(cam);
Verify framing with math, not just eyeballing. Perspective cameras are easy to misjudge by feel — a z offset that seems modest can put the camera nearly edge-on to a thin flat object (a wall, a table surface), foreshortening it into a huge confusing diagonal slab that looks like a bug but isn't. Before trusting a screenshot, project the key points you care about through the candidate camera and check their normalized device coordinates (both components should stay roughly within -1..1 to be on screen): const p = new Vector3(0, 0.35, 10.5).project(editor.camera); // Player Paddle console.log(p.x, p.y); // outside -1..1 means it's off-frame Comparing camera.position.distanceTo(...) to the near and far paddle also confirms the perspective ratio you're actually getting (here, roughly 2× — the far paddle is about twice as distant as the near one) before you spend time re-screenshotting.
4 Swap the arcade backdrop for a desert
The table itself never has to change — only what surrounds it. Remove the old Background Scenery group (and any stray lights left over from earlier experiments) with RemoveObjectCommand, the exact undo-tracked inverse of the AddObjectCommand that created them, then build a new Desert Scenery group the same way as step 2: a dune-displaced sand ground, a gradient sky plane, distant mesas, and a scatter of rocks and cacti kept clear of the rails:
const oldScenery = editor.scene.getObjectByProperty('name', 'Background Scenery'); if (oldScenery) editor.execute(new RemoveObjectCommand(editor, oldScenery)); const desert = new Group(); desert.name = 'Desert Scenery'; // Dune-displaced sand, reusing the noise-ground technique from "Build a night // scene from scratch" — the further a vertex is from the table, the more relief. const sandMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xd9b579, roughness: 0.95 }); const groundGeo = new PlaneGeometry(90, 90, 48, 48); const gp = groundGeo.attributes.position; for (let i = 0; i < gp.count; i++) { const x = gp.getX(i), y = gp.getY(i); const d = Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y); gp.setZ(i, Math.sin(x * 0.08 + 1.7) * Math.cos(y * 0.09) * 1.1 + Math.max(0, (d - 14)) * 0.02); } groundGeo.computeVertexNormals(); const ground = new Mesh(groundGeo, sandMat); ground.name = 'Sand Ground'; ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; ground.position.set(0, -0.46, -5); desert.add(ground); // A warm gradient painted onto a 4x256 canvas, stretched across a huge far plane — // cheaper than a sky dome and plenty convincing behind mesas at this distance. const skyCanvas = document.createElement('canvas'); skyCanvas.width = 4; skyCanvas.height = 256; const sctx = skyCanvas.getContext('2d'); const grad = sctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, 256); grad.addColorStop(0, '#3a3d6b'); grad.addColorStop(0.45, '#c9704f'); grad.addColorStop(0.75, '#f2a45c'); grad.addColorStop(1, '#fbd98b'); sctx.fillStyle = grad; sctx.fillRect(0, 0, 4, 256); const sky = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(140, 70), new MeshBasicMaterial({ map: new THREE.CanvasTexture(skyCanvas), fog: false })); sky.name = 'Sky'; sky.position.set(0, 24, -55); desert.add(sky); const mesaMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x8a4b34, roughness: 0.9 }); [[-30, 5, -40, 10, 10, 8], [-14, 7, -46, 8, 14, 7], [20, 6, -42, 12, 12, 9], [32, 4.5, -38, 7, 9, 6]] .forEach((s, i) => { const mesa = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(s[3], s[4], s[5]), mesaMat); mesa.name = 'Mesa ' + (i + 1); mesa.position.set(s[0], s[1], s[2]); mesa.rotation.y = i * 0.37; desert.add(mesa); }); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, desert)); // Warm sun replaces the neutral arcade lighting. editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, new AmbientLight(0xffd9a8, 0.55))); const sunLight = new DirectionalLight(0xffdca8, 1.4); sunLight.name = 'Sun Light'; sunLight.position.set(-18, 30, 10); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sunLight)); setFog('FogExp2', '#e2a565', 0, 0, 0.012); setBackground('#f2a45c');
Same table, same rails, same paddles — only Background Scenery was swapped for Desert Scenery.
Rocks, cacti, and mesas all stay outside |x| > 6.15 — the rails' own x position — so nothing overlaps the play area or blocks the sightline down the table. Placing scatter props is otherwise the same pattern as step 1/2: a small array of [x, y, z, ...params] tuples and a .forEach that builds one mesh per entry, named with an index so each stays individually addressable (findObject('Rock 3'), $S('#Mesa 1')).
5 Sanity-check the object count
Every editor.execute(...) above is undoable and shows up in editor.history.undos. After any batch of Shell edits, especially ones driven by automation rather than typing, compare the scene's object count against what you expect:
editor.scene.children.length; // top-level count editor.history.undos.length; // commands issued this session
Why this matters. A stray keystroke reaching the viewport instead of the Shell input (an unclosed autocomplete dropdown, focus lost between two automated steps) can trigger the app's global keyboard shortcuts — Delete removes whatever's currently selected. It's silent: the Shell shows no error, and the deletion is a normal RemoveObjectCommand sitting in the same undo stack as your real edits. Checking editor.history.undos for command types you didn't intend to run is the fastest way to catch it, and every entry there is individually undoable if something needs reverting.

posts.title: A crank, a rod and a piston: crank-slider kinematics
A projectile: two motions, one path
Build a labelled racing circuit with a script
posts.text:
Build a labelled racing circuit with a script
All tutorials
A whole racing circuit from one short list of corner points: a road ribbon on rolling terrain, a harbour setting built from a handful of shared shapes, and — the part that matters to a game — every object given a name and classes at the moment it is created, so a game engine can find the start line, the checkpoints and the pickups by name. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order, or run the whole generator, circuit-build.js (step 8).
The finished circuit running in strata-play: 19,052 triangles, ten shared materials, 436 named nodes.
Two Shell facts this page relies on. The Shell does not keep variables between pastes (a const from one block is gone in the next), so each block ends by storing what later blocks need on window.c1 and begins by reading it back. And if Enter seems to do nothing after a long paste, press Esc first (it closes the autocomplete dropdown that was swallowing the keypress), then Enter. On a non-empty scene, run clearScene() first.
1 Plan the lap as numbers
Decide the track before placing anything. The lap is thirteen corner points on a ground plane (x east, z south, metres). Every corner is rounded with an arc that is tangent to both straights, and a sign tells you which way it turns, so the turn balance is something you can read off instead of eyeball. The centreline is then sampled into points that carry their position, tangent and distance along the lap. Everything after this — road, kerbs, gates, start grid — is computed from those samples:
const P = [[-58,-40],[36,-30],[84,-74],[146,-56],[164,6],[128,60],[72,24],[22,12],[-30,30],[-66,70],[-126,66],[-166,18],[-122,-72]]; const ROAD_W = 14.5, CURB_W = 1.2, R_MAX = 70, n = P.length; const unit = (a, b) => { const dx = b[0] - a[0], dz = b[1] - a[1], l = Math.hypot(dx, dz); return [dx / l, dz / l, l]; }; const corners = P.map((p, i) => { const prev = P[(i + n - 1) % n], next = P[(i + 1) % n]; const [d0x, d0z, l0] = unit(prev, p), [d1x, d1z, l1] = unit(p, next); const turn = Math.atan2(d0x * d1z - d0z * d1x, d0x * d1x + d0z * d1z); // positive = right turn const phi = Math.abs(turn), sgn = Math.sign(turn), tanHalf = Math.tan(phi / 2); const r = Math.min(R_MAX, 0.45 * Math.min(l0, l1) / tanHalf), t = r * tanHalf; const A = [p[0] - d0x * t, p[1] - d0z * t], B = [p[0] + d1x * t, p[1] + d1z * t]; // arc start and end const inN = sgn > 0 ? [-d0z, d0x] : [d0z, -d0x]; return { i, p, d0: [d0x, d0z], phi, sgn, r, A, B, C: [A[0] + inN[0] * r, A[1] + inN[1] * r] }; }); const balance = { right: corners.filter(c => c.sgn > 0).length, left: corners.filter(c => c.sgn < 0).length }; if (Math.min(...corners.map(c => c.r)) < ROAD_W / 2 + CURB_W + 2) throw new Error('corner radius too tight for the road width'); // Sample the centreline: the straight before each corner, then its arc. s = metres along the lap. const pts = [], runs = []; let s = 0; corners.forEach((c, i) => { const from = corners[(i + n - 1) % n].B, len = Math.hypot(c.A[0] - from[0], c.A[1] - from[1]); const steps = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(len / 12)), [dx, dz] = c.d0; runs.push({ corner: i, s0: s, len }); for (let k = 0; k < steps; k++) { pts.push({ x: from[0] + dx * len * k / steps, z: from[1] + dz * len * k / steps, tx: dx, tz: dz, s }); s += len / steps; } const arcLen = c.r * c.phi, asteps = Math.max(3, Math.ceil(arcLen / 3)), a0 = Math.atan2(c.A[1] - c.C[1], c.A[0] - c.C[0]); for (let k = 0; k < asteps; k++) { const u = k / asteps, a = a0 + c.sgn * c.phi * u, h = c.sgn * c.phi * u; pts.push({ x: c.C[0] + c.r * Math.cos(a), z: c.C[1] + c.r * Math.sin(a), tx: c.d0[0] * Math.cos(h) - c.d0[1] * Math.sin(h), tz: c.d0[0] * Math.sin(h) + c.d0[1] * Math.cos(h), s }); s += arcLen / asteps; } }); const LAP = s, N = pts.length; // Position + tangent at any distance along the lap (binary search, then interpolate) const frameAt = (sq) => { sq = ((sq % LAP) + LAP) % LAP; let lo = 0, hi = N - 1; while (lo < hi) { const m = (lo + hi + 1) >> 1; if (pts[m].s <= sq) lo = m; else hi = m - 1; } const a = pts[lo], b = pts[(lo + 1) % N], sb = lo + 1 < N ? b.s : LAP, u = (sq - a.s) / Math.max(1e-6, sb - a.s); let tx = a.tx + (b.tx - a.tx) * u, tz = a.tz + (b.tz - a.tz) * u; const tl = Math.hypot(tx, tz); tx /= tl; tz /= tl; return { x: a.x + (b.x - a.x) * u, z: a.z + (b.z - a.z) * u, tx, tz }; }; window.c1 = { ROAD_W, pts, runs, LAP, N, frameAt }; ({ balance, lapMetres: Math.round(LAP), samples: N });
The result: 8 right turns, 5 left, a lap of about 816 m. Change a corner point and everything downstream moves with it; the guard throws if a corner is too tight for the road width instead of producing a kinked road. Why samples carry a tangent. Every object that has a direction (a gate, a grid slot) is later turned with rotation.y = atan2(tx, tz), so its local +z points along the lap. That one convention is what lets other engines know which way is forward (step 5).
2 One creation helper that labels at birth
The Shell's selector language, $S, edits and queries what exists; it cannot create the first object. Creation goes through the editor. Rather than create everything and then run a labelling pass, one small helper, make(), takes the id and classes as arguments and sets them before the object ever enters the scene. Ids are PascalCase and unique; classes are kebab-case words that say what a thing is (surface, trigger, checkpoint). Ten shared materials, no textures, and a seeded random generator so a layout is repeatable:
const mulberry = (a) => () => { a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0; let t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a); t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t; return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; const rand = mulberry(20241024); // every "random" layout choice comes from this, never Math.random() const mat = (name, o) => { const m = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ roughness: 0.9, metalness: 0, ...o }); m.name = name; return m; }; const M = { Asphalt: mat('M_Asphalt', { color: 0x3a3d42, roughness: 0.95 }), Grass: mat('M_Grass', { color: 0x4f8a3c, roughness: 1 }), Paint: mat('M_Paint', { vertexColors: true, roughness: 0.8 }), Sea: mat('M_Sea', { color: 0x1d6f9e, roughness: 0.08, metalness: 0.2 }), Concrete: mat('M_Concrete', { color: 0x9a9a94, roughness: 0.95 }), Glass: mat('M_Glass', { color: 0x7fd6ff, roughness: 0.1, metalness: 0.1, transparent: true, opacity: 0.35 }), PickupCore: mat('M_PickupCore', { color: 0xffb020, emissive: 0xff7a00, emissiveIntensity: 0.6, roughness: 0.3, metalness: 0.5 }), Gate: mat('M_GateVolume', { color: 0xff3df2, transparent: true, opacity: 0.14, roughness: 1, side: THREE.DoubleSide, depthWrite: false }), }; // THE creation primitive: id, classes and parent are given here, once. const make = (id, classes, geometry, material, parent, pos, ry) => { const o = geometry ? new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material) : new THREE.Group(); o.name = id; o.userData.label = id; o.userData.customClasses = classes.split(' '); if (pos) o.position.set(pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]); if (ry) o.rotation.y = ry; if (parent) parent.add(o); return o; }; const two = (v) => String(v).padStart(2, '0'); const withColor = (g, hex) => { const c = new THREE.Color(hex), a = new Float32Array(g.attributes.position.count * 3); for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i += 3) { a[i] = c.r; a[i + 1] = c.g; a[i + 2] = c.b; } g.setAttribute('color', new THREE.BufferAttribute(a, 3)); return g; }; // Two scene roots. Gameplay sits at the root with an identity transform, so its children's positions are world positions. const course = make('Circuit1', 'course'); const track = make('Track', 'surface', null, null, course); const trackside = make('Trackside', 'trackside', null, null, course); const environment = make('Environment', 'scenery', null, null, course); const gameplay = make('Gameplay', 'gameplay'); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, course)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, gameplay)); Object.assign(window.c1, { rand, M, make, two, withColor, track, trackside, environment, gameplay }); Object.keys(M).length; // 8
Why the M_ prefix. Selectors in a runtime such as strata-play also match material names, and they match the ancestors of a matching mesh. A material called plain Trigger made $S('.trigger') return one node too many — the whole Gameplay group — and an earlier strata-play gave that group a physics sensor the size of the circuit (current strata-play builds a body only for a mesh or a node that carries the class itself, but the extra match is still there for any selector). A material name can never collide with a class if it never looks like one. Why no labelling pass. A pass that runs afterwards has to guess what each mesh is from its shape and colour. Here the author already knows, so the answer is written once, at creation.
3 The road, the terrain and the sea
A ribbon is a strip along the centreline between two lateral offsets: two vertices per sample, one quad between neighbours, with uv.v running along the lap every 10 m. The ground follows the same height function H(x, z) as the road, so the road always sits on the terrain, and the relief fades to flat toward the edges:
const { ROAD_W, pts, N, make, M, track, environment } = window.c1; const smooth = (a, b, v) => { const t = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (v - a) / (b - a))); return t * t * (3 - 2 * t); }; const H = (x, z) => (3.2 * Math.sin(x / 62 + 0.6) * Math.cos(z / 58) + 1.6 * Math.sin((x + z) / 37)) * (1 - smooth(70, 98, Math.abs(z))); const rightOf = (p) => [-p.tz, p.tx]; // a strip along the lap between two lateral offsets (positive = right of travel) const ribbon = (o0, o1, dy) => { const pos = [], uv = [], idx = []; for (let k = 0; k < N; k++) { const p = pts[k], r = rightOf(p); for (const o of [o0, o1]) { const x = p.x + r[0] * o, z = p.z + r[1] * o; pos.push(x, H(x, z) + dy, z); } uv.push(0, p.s / 10, 1, p.s / 10); } for (let k = 0; k < N; k++) { const a = 2 * k, b = 2 * ((k + 1) % N); idx.push(a, a + 1, b, a + 1, b + 1, b); } const g = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); g.setAttribute('position', new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute(pos, 3)); g.setAttribute('uv', new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute(uv, 2)); g.setIndex(idx); g.computeVertexNormals(); if (g.attributes.normal.getY(0) < 0) { const ix = g.index.array; for (let i = 0; i < ix.length; i += 3) { const t = ix[i + 1]; ix[i + 1] = ix[i + 2]; ix[i + 2] = t; } g.computeVertexNormals(); } // wound the wrong way: flip return g; }; make('Road', 'surface road drivable', ribbon(-ROAD_W / 2, ROAD_W / 2, 0.03), M.Asphalt, track); // terrain: a plane displaced by the same height function const tg = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(400, 210, 40, 21).rotateX(-Math.PI / 2), tp = tg.attributes.position; for (let i = 0; i < tp.count; i++) tp.setY(i, H(tp.getX(i), tp.getZ(i)) - 0.12); tg.computeVertexNormals(); make('Terrain', 'surface grass offroad', tg, M.Grass, track); make('Sea', 'scenery water', new THREE.PlaneGeometry(900, 170).rotateX(-Math.PI / 2), M.Sea, environment, [0, -0.8, 190]); make('Quay', 'scenery', new THREE.BoxGeometry(400, 2, 14).translate(0, -0.2, 0), M.Concrete, environment, [0, 0, 98]); Object.assign(window.c1, { H, rightOf }); editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); ({ roadTriangles: $S('#Road').nodes[0].geometry.index.count / 3 });
The road is 454 triangles: one quad per ~3 m of arc and ~12 m of straight is all a drivable surface needs. The full script adds the kerbs, the centre dashes and the chequered start strip the same way, as extra ribbons and merged boxes (circuit-build.js, sections 7–8).
4 Shared geometry: the container stacks
The harbour is dozens of near-identical stacks of shipping containers. Define each shape once and place it many times: every mesh that uses the same geometry object shares one copy in memory and, later, one copy in the exported file. Colour comes from per-vertex colour on a single shared M_Paint material, so four colours cost four small geometries and still one material. The seeded rand() decides where gaps go, so the quay looks irregular but is identical every run:
const { rand, M, make, two, withColor, trackside } = window.c1; const colours = ['#c0392b', '#2471a3', '#d4a017', '#2e8b57']; const stackGeo = colours.map(hex => withColor(new THREE.BoxGeometry(12, 2.6, 2.4).translate(0, 1.3, 0), hex)); // four shapes, defined once let stack = 0; for (const zRow of [94.5, 100.5]) for (let x = -186; x <= 186; x += 13) { if (rand() < 0.25) continue; stack++; make('ContainerStack' + two(stack), 'trackside wall', stackGeo[Math.floor(rand() * 4)], M.Paint, trackside, [x, 0.8, zRow]); } editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); ({ stacks: stack, sharedGeometries: new Set($S('.trackside').nodes.filter(o => o.geometry).map(o => o.geometry)).size });
In the full script the same idea builds the crane, the grandstand with its crowd, the pit garage, thirty-six shrubs, tyre barriers and the hills: a few shared shapes, placed by the seeded generator.
5 The part a game engine wires: gates, grid, racing line, pickups
Everything a game needs to run a lap is an anchor: a named node at a known place. The scene contains no game logic; it only says where things are. All anchors live under the Gameplay root in world space:
a StartLine and seven Checkpoint01..07 gates, numbered in driving order; eight SpawnPoint01..08 grid slots (empty nodes: position and facing only); a RacingLine of 163 ordered empty nodes, one about every 5 m down the road centre, so a bot can follow the road without reading the road mesh; pickups: 18 item boxes (three parts each) and 5 boost pads in the full script, all classed pickup and trigger.
Anything with a direction gets forward: '+z' written into its data, which exports as extras.forward: the file states its own convention instead of leaving the next author to guess.
const { LAP, runs, frameAt, make, M, two, gameplay, H, rightOf } = window.c1; const yawOf = (p) => Math.atan2(p.tx, p.tz); // rotation.y that points local +z along the lap const fwd = (o) => { o.userData.forward = '+z'; return o; }; const startS = runs[1].s0 + runs[1].len * 0.3; // start line on the straight before the second corner // one gate shape, placed eight times const gate = new THREE.BoxGeometry(14.5 + 4, 5, 1.2); const f0 = frameAt(startS); fwd(make('StartLine', 'trigger start-line', gate, M.Gate, gameplay, [f0.x, H(f0.x, f0.z) + 2.5, f0.z], yawOf(f0))); for (let k = 1; k <= 7; k++) { const c = frameAt(startS + LAP * k / 8); fwd(make('Checkpoint' + two(k), 'trigger checkpoint', gate, M.Gate, gameplay, [c.x, H(c.x, c.z) + 2.5, c.z], yawOf(c))); } // eight grid slots behind the line, two abreast for (let k = 0; k < 8; k++) { const g = frameAt(startS - 9 - Math.floor(k / 2) * 7 - (k % 2) * 3.5), r = rightOf(g), o = (k % 2 ? 1 : -1) * 3.2; const x = g.x + r[0] * o, z = g.z + r[1] * o; fwd(make('SpawnPoint' + two(k + 1), 'spawn-point', null, null, gameplay, [x, H(x, z) + 0.3, z], yawOf(g))); } // racing line: empty nodes down the road centre in driving order; the last is followed by the first const count = Math.round(LAP / 5), line = make('RacingLine', 'racing-line', null, null, gameplay); for (let k = 0; k < count; k++) { const f = frameAt(startS + LAP * k / count); fwd(make('RacingLine' + String(k + 1).padStart(3, '0'), 'racing-line-point', null, null, line, [f.x, H(f.x, f.z) + 0.03, f.z], yawOf(f))); } line.userData.closed = true; // item boxes: one definition (a glass shell round a core), a row of four across the longest straight const shellGeo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1.7, 1.7, 1.7), coreGeo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.8, 0.8, 0.8).rotateY(Math.PI / 4); const itemBoxes = make('ItemBoxes', 'pickup-set', null, null, gameplay); const run = runs.filter((r, i) => i !== 1).sort((a, b) => b.len - a.len)[0]; const fm = frameAt(run.s0 + run.len / 2), rm = rightOf(fm); [-5.1, -1.7, 1.7, 5.1].forEach((o, i) => { const id = 'ItemBox' + two(i + 1), x = fm.x + rm[0] * o, z = fm.z + rm[1] * o; const b = make(id, 'pickup item-box trigger', null, null, itemBoxes, [x, H(x, z) + 1.5, z], yawOf(fm)); make(id + 'Shell', 'item-box-part', shellGeo, M.Glass, b); make(id + 'Core', 'item-box-part', coreGeo, M.PickupCore, b); }); editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); ({ gates: $S('.checkpoint').count(), grid: $S('.spawn-point').count(), racingLinePoints: count, itemBoxes: $S('.item-box').count() });
Why Gameplay is its own root, not a child of the circuit. strata-play's physics harness copies each labelled node's position straight onto a body and assumes the node is an untransformed child of the scene root. Keeping the anchors at the root with an identity transform makes their positions world positions in every runtime, so nothing has to guess an offset.
6 Light, and the $S passes
Now $S earns its keep: after creation, settings that apply to a class of things are one-liners. Receiving shadows belongs to everything classed surface; casting to scenery and trackside objects; the invisible trigger volumes do neither. The sun needs one extra line that is easy to miss, explained below:
const { environment } = window.c1; const sunlight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xfff1d6, 2.2); sunlight.name = 'Sunlight'; sunlight.userData.label = 'Sunlight'; sunlight.userData.customClasses = ['effect']; sunlight.position.set(-150, 220, -120); sunlight.lookAt(0, 0, 0); // see the note: the export needs a rotation, not just a position sunlight.castShadow = true; Object.assign(sunlight.shadow.camera, { left: -230, right: 230, top: 140, bottom: -140, near: 10, far: 600 }); sunlight.shadow.mapSize.set(2048, 2048); const sky = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xbfe3ff, 0x6a7f4a, 0.9); sky.name = 'SkyLight'; sky.userData.label = 'SkyLight'; sky.userData.customClasses = ['effect']; environment.add(sunlight, sky); setBackground('#a9d4ee'); $S('.surface').receiveShadow(true); $S('mesh.scenery').castShadow(true); $S('mesh.trackside').castShadow(true); $S('.trigger').castShadow(false); editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); 'ok';
The sun trap. A glTF directional light shines down its node's local −z. In the editor a light's direction comes from its target, so a light with only a position looks right on screen, but the exported file stores the node's rotation and the target is not exported. Without lookAt, the sun in the exported file points along −z, edge-on to the ground, and lights almost nothing. The exporter prints "Light direction may be lost" whether or not you added it, so the warning is not the check: read the file (step 9).
7 Check it
Before exporting, confirm the two properties a downstream engine depends on: every labelled object resolves by name, and the whole set can be listed from the scene alone. Two lines do it:
const names = []; editor.scene.traverse(o => { if (o !== editor.scene && o.userData.label) names.push(o.name); }); const notAddressable = names.filter(nm => $S('#' + nm).count() !== 1); ({ labelled: names.length, notAddressable: notAddressable.length, triggers: $S('.trigger').count(), gameplayIsATrigger: $S('.trigger').nodes.some(o => o.name === 'Gameplay') });
The full check, circuit-verify.js, adds a third property — totality: it fires 21 sampled operations at the scene (some deliberately wrong, such as scale with factor: 'big') and requires each to either apply to every matched node or fail cleanly, never half-apply and never write a NaN. It earned its place: its first run found that move, scale, rotate and duplicate reported success while writing NaN into transforms when an argument was missing or not a number. That was an editor bug, now fixed. The check tests this scene, not the editor in general: a pass does not prove the operations are safe everywhere.
8 Run the whole thing, and get the same bytes every time
The blocks above are the skeleton. circuit-build.js is the complete generator: the same code plus kerbs and markings, the harbour crane, grandstand and crowd, pit garage, shrubs, hills, tyre barriers, all 18 item boxes and 5 boost pads, and the camera. On a cleared scene, paste it into the Shell (it takes a few seconds). It i

posts.title: Add a static hero camera to a render sequence
posts.text:
Add a static hero camera to a render sequence
All tutorials
Your main camera is animated for the whole timeline — but sometimes one moment (an explosion, a headlight beam, a reveal) deserves its own fixed, carefully-framed shot cut into the middle of the video. This tutorial adds a second, non-animated camera and schedules it in the Render tab's Camera Sequence. Open the editor, load a scene with an existing timeline, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
Why a second camera, not more keyframes. The Camera Sequence is a completely separate mechanism from animating camera itself: it's a list of shots, each naming a camera object and a start time, persisted on scene.userData.renderShots. A shot's camera does not need any keyframes at all — it can simply sit wherever you put it for the whole time it's on screen. That's the point: a hero shot is often better hand-framed once than animated.
1 Find a moment worth a dedicated shot
Scrub the timeline to the moment you want to showcase and look at what your main camera shows there. Use holdTimelineAt to jump straight to a timestamp without pressing play:
const { holdTimelineAt } = await import('./editor/js/intelligence/timelineController.js'); holdTimelineAt(editor, 24); // seconds into the Universal Timeline
If the main camera's framing doesn't do that moment justice — too far, wrong angle, an object in the way — that's exactly the case for a second, purpose-built camera.
2 Add the new camera
A plain THREE.PerspectiveCamera, added like any other object. Give it a name — you'll use it to select the camera again later. Don't add any keyframes to it; point it once and leave it:
const heroCam = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(38, 16 / 9, 0.1, 500); heroCam.name = 'HeadlightHeroCam'; heroCam.position.set(-4.15, 3.2, 14); heroCam.lookAt(-4.15, 1.0, -40); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, heroCam));
Jump back to your target moment and check the framing from the new camera before wiring it into anything — swap the viewport over to it temporarily:
editor.viewportCamera = heroCam; editor.signals.viewportCameraChanged.dispatch(); holdTimelineAt(editor, 24);
Nudge heroCam.position / re-run .lookAt(...) and re-dispatch objectChanged until it reads well across the whole span you'll use it for — not just one instant. A bus or character can move a long way in a few seconds; check both ends of the window:
heroCam.position.set(-4.15, 3.2, 14); heroCam.lookAt(-4.15, 1.0, -40); editor.signals.objectChanged.dispatch(heroCam);
Keep it clear of anything that moves. A static camera parked directly in a moving object's path will get run over mid-shot. Offset it to the side, or elevate it, so the subject passes near — not through — the lens for the shot's entire duration.
3 Cut it into the Camera Sequence
The sequence is a plain array on scene.userData.renderShots: { id, at, camera: uuid, transition, transitionDur }. A shot runs from its at until the next shot's at (or the timeline's end). Build a three-shot sequence — main camera, then the hero shot, then back to the main camera:
const shots = [ { id: 'shot-intro', at: 0, camera: editor.camera.uuid, transition: 'cut', transitionDur: 0.5 }, { id: 'shot-headlight', at: 20, camera: heroCam.uuid, transition: 'fade', transitionDur: 0.8 }, { id: 'shot-return', at: 29, camera: editor.camera.uuid, transition: 'fade', transitionDur: 0.8 }, ]; editor.scene.userData = editor.scene.userData || {}; editor.scene.userData.renderShots = shots; editor.signals.sceneGraphChanged.dispatch(); // refreshes the Render tab's sequencer UI
Switch the viewport back to your main camera when you're done previewing:
editor.viewportCamera = editor.camera; editor.signals.viewportCameraChanged.dispatch();
4 Check it in the Render tab
Open the Render tab. The Camera Sequence lane now shows three colored blocks — one per shot, labeled with the camera name and its cut/fade transition. Click a block to select it; the detail row below lets you retarget its camera, nudge its start time, or change cut/fade and the fade duration — all without touching the Shell again. With zero shots, the render always falls back to the single camera picked in the Camera dropdown at the top — the sequence is opt-in, never required.
5 Render it
Pick a resolution/FPS and click Render & Export. The sequence plays back exactly as scheduled: your main camera's own animation runs during its shots, then the render cuts (or fades) to the static hero camera at 20s, holds its fixed framing for nine seconds, then cuts back.
Real example this tutorial is based on. A bus's headlight beams were nearly invisible from the main animated camera's angle at that distance. Rather than re-choreograph the whole approach, one static camera placed dead-center on the road — elevated above the bus's roofline, looking straight down the lane the headlights travel — was cut in for just the arrival. The beams read as two clean glowing cones converging on the lens, then the sequence handed back to the main camera for the stop and boarding. See the animation guide for the full $S(...) grammar this tutorial's main camera would otherwise use.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets None used. Tools None used.
