posts.title: Name every part of a street-corner diorama
posts.text:
Name every part of a street-corner diorama
All tutorials
A furnished room was one mesh with 538 islands and 14 things worth naming. This model is the opposite problem: 71 meshes, 141,802 triangles, and the one mesh that holds the city block has 3,297 islands in 2,841 components. Naming an anchor for each is out of the question. What works is to look at the model, write down the regions you can see, and let each component go to the region that holds it, once per material. Every one of the 186 pieces that come out has a name, a class, and a place in the record. Built with the JS Shell.
Who named this. Every region, part name and class on this page is agent output: an AI agent, working from SEG's reports and the rendered views below, wrote the 22 region names, the 124 part names they produce, and the 62 names in step 10 — not a human. A human gave the instruction ("segment and label every part") and ran the pasted commands; a human did not choose a single name. This is a standing fact about every tutorial on this site built with the JS Shell, stated here because this is the largest one.
Start with the other two SEG tutorials. This page uses SEG.describe, SEG.split, SEG.preview and the plan from Cut any textured mesh into named parts, and components from Cut a scene into named parts. The reference is guides/MESH_SEGMENT.md. What is new here is the plan: parts given by component, with the components chosen by where they are, and one class that selects the same object across every material it is made of; step 5 says why regions, not anchors. This page was made with SEG 1.6.0, in the editor at commit e02c076.
Littlest Tokyo by Glen Fox, imported and untouched. Every part you can see in this picture ends up with a name.
1 The model, its licence, and what changed
Littlest Tokyo by Glen Fox (glenatron), licensed Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. The file's own metadata says so, and names the Sketchfab page (sketchfab.com/models/94b24a60dc1b48248de50bf087c0f042); the three.js example that ships the file credits the same artist ("CC Attribution") and links ArtStation. This page loads the file from the three.js repository, at a pinned commit:
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/f405199a0ce26134efbf2d654a634efa5655b756/examples/models/gltf/LittlestTokyo.glb sha256 8375c2aa6808e28ad1cb9c0d43e1513f57ffd7865244bf66bbbd5bb0e907e06d 4,133,072 bytes
Changes made, as the licence asks. The model is cut into named parts, its meshes are renamed and given classes, and the skeleton nodes are named and classed. The geometry is only divided, never edited: the triangle count is 141,802 before and after. Textures are not changed. The artist has not endorsed this page or the segmented scene. The segmented scene is public as littletokyo.json in tejaswigowda/test1 under the same licence, with the same credit; the example link on the index card opens it.
2 Import it, and count what you have
Start from an empty scene (File, New). Download the .glb from the address above and drop it on the editor, or use File, Import. Accept the dialog's defaults. The Shell logs:
↳ Normalized "LittlestTokyo.glb": scaled ×0.00362, centered & grounded (reversible — undo to restore). ℹ Imported "LittlestTokyo.glb" with 71 separable parts. ℹ 67 part(s) are textured: setting a color will TINT the texture (map × color), not replace it.
The importer has made one mesh per material per node, so 71 is a count of mesh nodes, not of objects. Ask for the shape of it:
(() => { const rows = []; scene.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) rows.push([o.name, Math.round((o.geometry.index ? o.geometry.index.count : o.geometry.attributes.position.count) / 3)]); }); rows.sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]); return { meshes: rows.length, triangles: rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r[1], 0), biggest: rows.slice(0, 7).map(r => r.join(': ')) }; })()
{ "meshes": 71, "triangles": 141802, "biggest": [ "Object674_outline_0: 40734", "Object649_normal_0: 29276", "Object649_metalmat_0: 17350", "Object649_Plastic_Soft_0: 16935", "Object649_paintmat_0: 9438", "Object674_outline_0_1: 9124", "Object675_outline_0: 2966" ] }
Read it as a map of where the work is. Object649_* is the whole city block, which looks like one baked object split by material into eleven meshes. The three _outline_ meshes are Blender-style inverted hulls that draw the black outline (the two big ones alone are 49,858 of the 141,802 triangles, 35%; they have no UVs and nothing to cut, so they are named whole). Object675_* is the tram. The other fifty-odd meshes are small, already separate objects: birds, cables, lanterns. So the job has two halves: cut the meshes that hold many objects, and name the meshes that are already one object.
3 Fix the names a selector cannot reach
Seven meshes came in with a # in the name (Object649_Material_#5511_0). In a selector # means "id", so SEG.components('#Object649_Material_#5511_0') cannot reach it. Rename them:
scene.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh && o.name.includes('#')) o.name = o.name.replace(/#/g, '') })
[ "Object649_Material_#5511_0 -> Object649_Material_5511_0", "Object649_Material_#5512_0 -> Object649_Material_5512_0", "Object705_Material_#5516_0 -> Object705_Material_5516_0", "Object706_Material_#5518_0 -> Object706_Material_5518_0", … ]
4 Pin and hash the source
SEG.split will not cut without a source it can name exactly: the licence, the credit, and the hash of the file. SEG.source fetches the file and computes them; keep the result on window, because each Shell line is its own scope.
SEG.source('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/f405199a0ce26134efbf2d654a634efa5655b756/examples/models/gltf/LittlestTokyo.glb', { licence: 'CC-BY-4.0', attribution: 'Littlest Tokyo by Glen Fox (glenatron), https://sketchfab.com/models/94b24a60dc1b48248de50bf087c0f042' }).then(s => { window.src = s })
JSON.stringify(window.src, null, 1) { "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/f405199a…/examples/models/gltf/LittlestTokyo.glb", "page": "https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/f405199a…/examples/models/gltf/LittlestTokyo.glb", "commit": "f405199a0ce26134efbf2d654a634efa5655b756", "sha256": "8375c2aa6808e28ad1cb9c0d43e1513f57ffd7865244bf66bbbd5bb0e907e06d", "bytes": 4133072, "licence": "CC-BY-4.0", "attribution": "Littlest Tokyo by Glen Fox (glenatron), https://sketchfab.com/models/94b24a60dc1b48248de50bf087c0f042" }
The URL has to be the raw.githubusercontent.com form with a full commit, not the github.com/…/blob/… page and not a branch name: SEG refuses both and prints the address to use. The hash and size match the file in step 1, which is how anyone can check that the record describes the file they have.
5 Why anchors do not work here
In the room tutorial you named 14 components and SEG placed the other 268 on the nearest. Count what that would take here:
Mesh Islands Components Triangles Object649_normal_0 3,297 2,841 29,276 Object649_metalmat_0 655 407 17,350 Object649_Plastic_Soft_0 465 244 16,935 Object705_Material_5516_0 207 193 1,527 Object649_paintmat_0 267 178 9,438
In Object649_normal_0 the 1,291 largest components hold only 80% of the triangles: the long tail is tiles, leaves, sign lettering and cracks, thousands of pieces of a few triangles each. No component is "the building", and an anchor is a component you can justify naming. There is no short list of them to name. A rough line, from the two data points there are: anchors worked at the room's 282 components (14 named, 268 attached); they do not at this mesh's 2,841. Once a single mesh's components run into the thousands, no short list is worth naming and the grain below is the one to reach for instead.
But the evidence SEG gives for a scene still holds: every component has a centre in the world frame and a size. A pole, a tram and a cat are all somewhere, and the same somewhere in all eleven material meshes, because they share one set of coordinates. So name the places instead. This is not a mode SEG offers: there is no SEG.region, only SEG.attach for anchors. Regions — a plan made of named boxes instead of named components — were worked out for this cut, because anchors did not scale; nothing suggested them in advance.
6 Look at it, then write down the regions
The importer scaled the model to about 2 units across, centred and grounded: x runs −1 to 1 left to right, z −1 (back) to 1 (front), y up from 0 to 1.57. Look at it square-on with a grid. These two views are drawn with an orthographic camera and a grid every 0.25, so a pixel is a coordinate:
From the front: x across, y up. From above: x across, z down (the front is at the bottom).
From the two views, and a third and fourth from the back and the left, the agent wrote down 22 regions: the objects that stand out (the tram, the cat, two rooftop billboards, two post boxes, the cones, the poles, the panda signs), the three buildings plus the teal one cut into shopfront, upper floors and roof by height, the sidewalk with its benches, and the street. Each region is a box, a name and the classes it will carry. One is a rule instead of a box: a component at least 0.45 long and at most 0.03 thick on its second axis is a wire.
window.REGIONS = [ // name, classes, box: [x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1] in world units; the first region that holds a component's centre takes it { name: 'Overhead_Wires', rule: 'wire', classes: ['wire', 'utility'] }, { name: 'Traffic_Cones', classes: ['cone', 'street-furniture'], box: [0.15, 0.98, 0.0, 0.14, 0.8, 1.05] }, { name: 'Post_Box_Front', classes: ['post-box', 'street-furniture'], box: [0.58, 0.74, 0.0, 0.32, 0.66, 0.86] }, { name: 'Post_Box_Back_Left', classes: ['post-box', 'street-furniture'], box: [-0.52, -0.33, 0.0, 0.32, -0.26, -0.04] }, { name: 'Pole_Front', classes: ['pole', 'utility', 'street-furniture'], box: [0.72, 0.95, 0.0, 1.3, 0.68, 0.98] }, { name: 'Pole_Back', classes: ['pole', 'utility', 'street-furniture'], box: [0.72, 0.95, 0.0, 1.3, -1.0, -0.82] }, { name: 'Tram_Car', classes: ['tram', 'vehicle'], box: [0.22, 0.98, 0.0, 0.95, -1.03, -0.58] }, { name: 'Billboard_Purple_Screen', classes: ['billboard', 'sign', 'rooftop'], box: [-0.15, 0.35, 1.0, 1.5, -0.55, -0.25] }, { name: 'Billboard_Pink_Roof', classes: ['billboard', 'sign', 'rooftop'], box: [0.3, 0.62, 1.15, 1.55, 0.28, 0.42] }, { name: 'Cat_Statue', classes: ['cat', 'statue', 'rooftop'], box: [0.27, 0.72, 1.12, 1.8, 0.3, 0.8] }, { name: 'Panda_Signs', classes: ['panda', 'sign'], box: [-0.65, -0.03, 0.52, 1.3, -0.62, -0.08] }, { name: 'Building_B_Roof', classes: ['building', 'building-b', 'roof'], box: [0.25, 0.8, 1.12, 1.4, 0.2, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_B_Upper_Floors', classes: ['building', 'building-b', 'upper-floors'], box: [0.25, 0.8, 0.5, 1.12, 0.2, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_B_Shopfront', classes: ['building', 'building-b', 'shopfront'], box: [0.25, 0.8, 0.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_A_Roof', classes: ['building', 'building-a', 'roof'], box: [-0.55, 0.07, 1.05, 1.6, -0.02, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_A_Upper_Floors', classes: ['building', 'building-a', 'upper-floors'], box: [-0.55, 0.07, 0.5, 1.05, -0.02, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_A_Shopfront', classes: ['building', 'building-a', 'shopfront'], box: [-0.55, 0.07, 0.0, 0.5, -0.02, 0.8] }, { name: 'Building_C_Upper_Floors', classes: ['building', 'building-c', 'upper-floors'], box: [0.2, 0.8, 0.5, 1.3, -0.62, 0.2] }, { name: 'Building_C_Shopfront', classes: ['building', 'building-c', 'shopfront'], box: [0.2, 0.8, 0.0, 0.5, -0.62, 0.2] }, { name: 'Teal_Building_Upper_Floors', classes: ['building', 'teal-building', 'upper-floors'], box: [-0.5, 0.3, 0.5, 1.3, -0.62, -0.02] }, { name: 'Teal_Building_Shopfront', classes: ['building', 'teal-building', 'shopfront'], box: [-0.5, 0.3, 0.0, 0.5, -0.62, -0.02] }, { name: 'Sidewalk_Benches', classes: ['sidewalk', 'bench', 'street-furniture'], box: [-1.0, -0.55, 0.0, 0.35, -0.8, -0.2] }, { name: 'Street_Ground', classes: ['street', 'ground'], box: [-1.2, 1.2, -0.2, 0.09, -1.2, 1.2] }, ]
The order matters: small, specific regions come first so that a post box is a post box before it is "the street". A component whose centre is in no box goes to the nearest box, so nothing is left over (SEG would refuse a plan that leaves a component out). The numbers are what the agent read off the grid; they are coarse on purpose, and step 9 shows where.
7 The helper, and the first cut
Two functions turn the plan into a SEG.split call. regionOf is the rule above. cutMesh asks SEG for the components of one mesh, sorts their numbers into regions, and makes one part per region, named Region_Material and carrying the region's classes plus the material's, so the same region in two meshes gets two parts with the same classes.
window.regionOf = c => { const p = c.centre; for (const r of REGIONS) { if (r.rule === 'wire') { const s = [...c.size].sort((a, b) => a - b); if (s[2] >= 0.45 && s[1] <= 0.03) return r; continue; } const b = r.box; if (p[0] >= b[0] && p[0] <= b[1] && p[1] >= b[2] && p[1] <= b[3] && p[2] >= b[4] && p[2] <= b[5]) return r; } const d = r => { let t = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { const v = p[i], lo = r.box[2*i], hi = r.box[2*i+1]; if (v < lo) t += (lo - v) ** 2; else if (v > hi) t += (v - hi) ** 2; } return t; }; return REGIONS.filter(r => r.box).sort((a, b) => d(a) - d(b))[0]; // in no box: the nearest one } window.cutMesh = (mesh, suffix, group) => { const by = {}; for (const c of SEG.components('#' + mesh)) { const r = regionOf(c); (by[r.name] = by[r.name] || { r, ids: [] }).ids.push(c.component); } const parts = Object.values(by).map(({ r, ids }) => ({ component: ids, name: r.name + '_' + suffix, classes: [...r.classes, suffix.toLowerCase()] })); return SEG.split('#' + mesh, { group, source: window.src, parts }); }
Start with the smallest of the big meshes, the paint (178 components), and read the components first:
SEG.describe('#Object649_paintmat_0')
component 0: 406 triangles (1 island: 0), size 0.094,0.210,0.097, centre 0.650,0.162,0.746, at 0.83,0.08,0.88, colours rgb(222,91,87) 75% rgb(173,63,58) 24% rgb(250,146,142) 1% component 1: 406 triangles (1 island: 1), size 0.096,0.210,0.096, centre -0.408,0.162,-0.140, at 0.27,0.08,0.43, colours rgb(222,91,87) 75% rgb(173,63,58) 24% rgb(250,146,142) 1% component 2: 198 triangles (4 islands: 16,17,246,262), size 0.258,0.292,0.591, centre -0.353,0.267,0.273, at 0.30,0.16,0.64, colours rgb(32,23,22) 84% … … (267 islands joined into 178 components where they touch in space; world frame, y up. …)
Look at components 0 and 1: the same 406 triangles, the same size to a millimetre, the same red. Two identical red objects, one at the front right and one at the back left. They are post boxes. In the first plan only the front one had a region. The first cut:
cutMesh('Object649_paintmat_0', 'Paint', 'Paint_Parts')
Post_Box_Paint: 836 triangles | Teal_Building_Shopfront_Paint: 808 triangles | Building_A_Shopfront_Paint: 1030 triangles | Building_B_Shopfront_Paint: 1827 triangles | … ⚠ absorbed: Teal_Building_Shopfront_Paint: it is assembled from 8 components and 95% of its texture is one colour (#d3504c): it has probably absorbed a run of similar pieces ✨ Scene updated — 1 command executed
The cut worked and every triangle was kept, and SEG still said something was wrong with it. absorbed fires when a part is made of many components and nearly all one colour: a run of similar things that were swallowed by a neighbour. Eight red components in the teal building's volume, 95% one red: the second post box had been given to the teal building because no region claimed it. SEG.split made the whole cut as one undo step, so editor.undo() took it back. Add the second post box to the plan (it is in the list above as Post_Box_Back_Left), and cut again:
Post_Box_Front_Paint: 836 triangles | Post_Box_Back_Left_Paint: 660 triangles | Building_A_Shopfront_Paint: 1030 triangles | … | Teal_Building_Shopfront_Paint: 148 triangles | … ✨ Scene updated — 1 command executed
The warning is gone, and the teal building's paint went from 808 triangles to 148: the 660 that left it are the back post box, now its own part.
8 Cut the other eight
cutMesh('Object649_normal_0', 'Surface', 'Surface_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_metalmat_0', 'Metal', 'Metal_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_Plastic_Soft_0', 'SoftPlastic', 'SoftPlastic_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_Material_5511_0', 'Mat5511', 'Mat5511_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_Material_5512_0', 'Mat5512', 'Mat5512_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_alpha_glass_0', 'AlphaGlass', 'AlphaGlass_Parts') cutMesh('Object649_glassmat_0', 'Glass', 'Glass_Parts') cutMesh('Object705_Material_5516_0', 'Mat5516', 'Mat5516_Parts')
Paste them one at a time. Each call is its own undo step, and in these runs, in a browser with software rendering, each finished within the 20 seconds allowed for it (the largest mesh, with 2,841 components, is the slow one). The suffix is the glTF material's own name (normal, metalmat, Plastic_Soft, paintmat) in a readable form, or its number for the three that have only a number (Mat5511): what those materials are meant to be is not stated anywhere, so none of it was guessed. The metal cut printed two warnings, absorbed: Pole_Front_Metal (14 components, 96% one dark grey) and absorbed: Sidewalk_Benches_Metal (9 components, 94% one blue-grey). Both are what they say: the poles and the benches really are runs of the same metal, so they were left, as the room tutorial leaves its warning. The other eight cuts printed none.
absorbed fired three times across this whole cut, counting step 7's. Put together, it is a number worth having before the next cut:
Part Components Dominant colour Verdict Teal_Building_Shopfront_Paint 8 95% #d3504c true error — a second post box had no region, fixed in step 7 Pole_Front_Metal 14 96% #535a65 correct: one run of metal, kept Sidewalk_Benches_Metal 9 94% #73839a correct: one run of metal, kept
One true positive in three. That is the first measurement this project has of what the warning is worth, from a cut large enough to fire it more than once: treat it as roughly a one-in-three bet, worth checking rather than ignoring or obeying outright. It is also the assertion's first time firing on a real cut — the room tutorial's cut triggered oversize and orphan sink, not this one; absorbed had only been exercised by a planted test case (Plant_Cluster, in meshSegment.test.mjs) before this.
9 Check the cut
SEG.preview paints each part of one group a flat colour, in one undoable step, and SEG.restore() puts the textures back (it printed textured materials restored).
SEG.preview('#Paint_Parts')
SEG.preview('#Paint_Parts'): each of the 17 paint parts a flat colour, the rest of the model still textured. Both post boxes are parts of their own now.
One group at a time shows one material. To see all the regions at once, every cut part is drawn in a colour taken from its region name, so the same region is one colour in all nine meshes, from the front and from above. (This figure is a throwaway offscreen render, not a Strata command; grey parts are the ones that were never cut.)
From the front, by region. From above, by region.
Where the volumes are rough. A component belongs to the region that holds its centre, so a long thing that crosses a boundary goes wholly to one side. The street is cut by boxes, so the pavement in front of building A is Building_A_Shopfront and the road is Street_Ground. The cat's region includes the red bamboo stand under it. The "post box" regions include the plant and the signpost standing beside them. And a region is a box, not an object: the panda signs' box also holds a little of the teal facade behind them. The parts are regions of the model, by material, not outlines of individual objects; for an object-by-object cut you would need anchors, and the room tutorial shows how.
10 Name what was already separate
The 62 meshes that are one object each need no cutting, only a name an author would choose and a class. tagClass(node, 'bird') is the same undoable class call the Shell uses everywhere. T

posts.title: Cut an avocado into named parts, building the tool by hand
posts.text:
Cut an avocado into named parts, building the tool by hand
All tutorials
Open embed
The editor now has this tool built in. What this page builds by hand, a block called CUT here, ships in the editor as SEG (SEG.describe, SEG.split, SEG.preview, SEG.restore), with more checks: it refuses meshes it cannot cut safely (skinned, several materials, morph targets), reads the texture's own transform, welds on position and UV, and cuts in one undo step. To cut a model of your own, use the general tutorial, Cut any textured mesh into named parts, which uses SEG, and has this avocado as its quick example and a toy duck as its hard one. This page is kept because writing the tool once shows exactly what it does. It uses the name CUT so that it does not clash with the built-in SEG.
Models usually arrive as one mesh with one material, so nothing in the scene says "this is the seed". This tutorial imports an avocado half, looks for the evidence the file does carry (which pieces of the texture are separate patches, and what colours are painted on them), cuts the mesh into five separate meshes named skin, pit, pit cavity, flesh and skin edge, and checks the cut. Afterwards $S('#Avocado_Pit') or $S('.flesh-cut') reaches exactly those parts. Built with the JS Shell.
1 The idea, and how far it goes
A mesh has no idea what its triangles are. Two things in the file do carry hints. UV islands: an artist unwraps a model into patches of one texture image, and the patches that touch no other patch (they share no vertices, once the exporter has split vertices along the seams) are often whole parts. Painted colour: inside one patch, a ring of orange and a ring of cream are different things even though the triangles are the same size. The method is to look at both, decide what each piece is, then cut by that decision. It is not automatic recognition: the names come from you (or from an AI that is shown the description), and the tool never loses a triangle or invents one that is not on the surface.
When it works: one indexed mesh, with UVs and a base-colour texture, whose parts are laid out as separate islands or are painted in clearly different colours. The avocado is the good case. When it does not: a mesh with no UVs, or with only vertex colours or a flat colour (there is no evidence to read); a part that shares an island and a colour with its neighbour (a boundary no one painted cannot be found); and a model whose islands are not parts. The same description, run on a second textured sample model (a toy duck with one yellow body), gave ten islands of which most were pieces of the same yellow body, so island to part would have produced ten meaningless names. A person merges them, which the plan allows (island takes a list; the general tutorial does exactly that), and this is the real limit: the method makes a decision cheap to check, it does not make the decision.
The 3D advantage. The seed, the flesh and the skin are one fruit; the parts are only separable because the object is three-dimensional data, and you can isolate each one, look at it from behind, and see where the cut really is. A flat picture of the fruit would give you only the colours.
2 Import the model
The model is the Avocado sample from the Khronos glTF sample models (Avocado.glb), made by Microsoft and released under CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication); retrieved 27 October 2026, 8.3 MB, one mesh of 682 triangles and three 2048 × 2048 textures. Download it, then use File → Import (or drop it in the viewport). Accept the import dialog's defaults. The scene now has one object, Avocado, with one material.
3 The tool: CUT
One block defines CUT, six small functions on globalThis so that the following blocks (the Shell keeps no variables between pastes) can use them. CUT.islands finds the connected pieces of a mesh. CUT.describe prints each piece's size, where it sits in the texture, how big it is in space and its main colours (a small, deterministic k-means over colours sampled across each triangle). CUT.split cuts by a plan. CUT.preview gives every part its own flat colour so you can see the cut, and CUT.restore puts the textured material back.
Two details matter. A flat patch is made of a few large triangles, far larger than the rings painted on it, so a part that is divided by colour is first subdivided (each triangle into 4n, the same surface and texture, only more triangles) and then each small triangle goes to the palette colour nearest the texture at its centre. And the cut refuses to run if a piece of the mesh has no destination or is used twice: every triangle lands in exactly one part. The new meshes share the original material, so the model looks exactly as before, and the original mesh, with the empty wrapper nodes the importer left around it, is replaced in one undoable step.
// CUT: cut one textured mesh into named, addressable parts. // Meshes arrive as a single object with a single material, so nothing in them says "this is the pit". Two things in the file do, though: // 1. the UV islands: connected pieces of surface that the texture artist laid out as separate patches of the texture // (an exporter splits vertices along a UV seam, so a piece is a set of triangles joined by shared vertices); // 2. the colours painted on the texture: inside one island, a ring of orange and a ring of cream are different things. // CUT.describe() lists both, so you can look and decide what each one is. CUT.split() then cuts by your decisions, and never loses a triangle. const CUT = globalThis.CUT = {}; // the colour of the texture at a point (u, v), read from a copy of the image drawn once CUT.reader = map => { const img = map.image, w = img.width, h = img.height; const cv = document.createElement('canvas'); cv.width = w; cv.height = h; const cx = cv.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true }); cx.drawImage(img, 0, 0); const px = cx.getImageData(0, 0, w, h).data; return (u, v) => { u -= Math.floor(u); v -= Math.floor(v); const x = Math.min(w - 1, Math.floor(u * w)), y = Math.min(h - 1, Math.floor((map.flipY ? 1 - v : v) * h)), p = (y * w + x) * 4; return [px[p], px[p + 1], px[p + 2]]; }; }; // the triangles of each island, largest first CUT.islands = geometry => { const idx = geometry.index.array, n = idx.length / 3; const par = Int32Array.from({ length: geometry.attributes.position.count }, (_, i) => i); const find = a => { while (par[a] !== a) { par[a] = par[par[a]]; a = par[a]; } return a; }; for (let t = 0; t < n; t++) { const r = find(idx[t * 3]); par[find(idx[t * 3 + 1])] = r; par[find(idx[t * 3 + 2])] = r; } const by = new Map(); for (let t = 0; t < n; t++) { const r = find(idx[t * 3]); if (!by.has(r)) by.set(r, []); by.get(r).push(t); } return [...by.values()].sort((a, b) => b.length - a.length); }; // colours sampled across a triangle's face on a small grid of barycentric points, so that even a few large triangles give many samples const samples = (uv, idx, t, read, k = 5) => { const a = idx[t * 3], b = idx[t * 3 + 1], c = idx[t * 3 + 2], out = []; for (let i = 0; i <= k; i++) for (let j = 0; i + j <= k; j++) { const x = i / k, y = j / k, z = 1 - x - y; out.push(read(uv.getX(a) * x + uv.getX(b) * y + uv.getX(c) * z, uv.getY(a) * x + uv.getY(b) * y + uv.getY(c) * z)); } return out; }; // k-means on colours, started from the colour farthest from those already chosen, so the same input always gives the same answer const kmeans = (cols, k) => { const d2 = (p, q) => (p[0] - q[0]) ** 2 + (p[1] - q[1]) ** 2 + (p[2] - q[2]) ** 2; const c = [cols[0]]; while (c.length < k) c.push(cols.reduce((best, p) => (Math.min(...c.map(q => d2(p, q))) > Math.min(...c.map(q => d2(best, q))) ? p : best), cols[0])); let groups = []; for (let it = 0; it < 12; it++) { groups = c.map(() => []); cols.forEach(p => groups[c.reduce((bi, q, i) => (d2(p, q) < d2(p, c[bi]) ? i : bi), 0)].push(p)); groups.forEach((g, i) => { if (g.length) c[i] = [0, 1, 2].map(a => g.reduce((s, p) => s + p[a], 0) / g.length); }); } return c.map((m, i) => ({ rgb: m.map(Math.round), share: +(groups[i].length / cols.length).toFixed(2) })).sort((a, b) => b.share - a.share); }; // what is in a mesh: each island's size, where it sits in the texture and in space, and its main colours CUT.describe = (node, k = 3) => { const g = node.geometry, idx = g.index.array, uv = g.attributes.uv, pos = g.attributes.position; const read = CUT.reader(node.material.map); return CUT.islands(g).map((ts, i) => { const cols = ts.flatMap(t => samples(uv, idx, t, read)), lo = [9, 9, 9], hi = [-9, -9, -9], u = [9, -9], v = [9, -9]; ts.forEach(t => { for (let q = 0; q < 3; q++) { const a = idx[t * 3 + q]; u[0] = Math.min(u[0], uv.getX(a)); u[1] = Math.max(u[1], uv.getX(a)); v[0] = Math.min(v[0], uv.getY(a)); v[1] = Math.max(v[1], uv.getY(a)); for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) { const p = [pos.getX(a), pos.getY(a), pos.getZ(a)][c]; lo[c] = Math.min(lo[c], p); hi[c] = Math.max(hi[c], p); } } }); return `island ${i}: ${ts.length} triangles, texture u ${u.map(x => x.toFixed(2))} v ${v.map(x => x.toFixed(2))}, size ${hi.map((x, c) => (x - lo[c]).toFixed(3))}, colours ${kmeans(cols, k).map(c => `rgb(${c.rgb}) ${Math.round(c.share * 100)}%`).join(' ')}`; }).join('\n'); }; // cut by a plan: // { group, classes, parts: [ { name, island, classes }, a whole island (or a list of them) becomes one mesh // { island, subdivide, palette: [ { name, color: [r, g, b], classes } ] } ] } an island is divided by colour; entries // with the same name make one part // A palette part is first subdivided (each triangle becomes 4^subdivide smaller ones, same surface, same texture) because the triangles of a flat // patch are far bigger than the rings painted on it; then each small triangle goes to the palette colour nearest the texture colour at its centre. CUT.split = (node, plan) => { const g = node.geometry, idx = g.index.array, A = g.attributes, names = Object.keys(A); const islands = CUT.islands(g), read = CUT.reader(node.material.map); const used = new Set(); const vertex = i => names.flatMap(n => Array.from({ length: A[n].itemSize }, (_, c) => A[n].array[i * A[n].itemSize + c])); const tri = t => [0, 1, 2].map(k => vertex(idx[t * 3 + k])); const mid = (a, b) => a.map((x, k) => (x + b[k]) / 2); const subdivide = (t, n) => { if (!n) return [t]; const [a, b, c] = t, ab = mid(a, b), bc = mid(b, c), ca = mid(c, a); return [[a, ab, ca], [ab, b, bc], [ca, bc, c], [ab, bc, ca]].flatMap(s => subdivide(s, n - 1)); }; const UV = names.slice(0, names.indexOf('uv')).reduce((s, n) => s + A[n].itemSize, 0); const colour = t => read((t[0][UV] + t[1][UV] + t[2][UV]) / 3, (t[0][UV + 1] + t[1][UV + 1] + t[2][UV + 1]) / 3); const d2 = (p, q) => (p[0] - q[0]) ** 2 + (p[1] - q[1]) ** 2 + (p[2] - q[2]) ** 2; const made = []; // [name, classes, triangles] for (const part of plan.parts) { const ids = [].concat(part.island); ids.forEach(i => { if (!islands[i]) throw new Error('there is no island ' + i); if (used.has(i)) throw new Error('island ' + i + ' is used twice'); used.add(i); }); const ts = ids.flatMap(i => islands[i]).map(tri); if (!part.palette) { made.push([part.name, part.classes, ts]); continue; } const bins = new Map(); // several palette colours may share one name (a part with a gradient in it) part.palette.forEach(p => { if (!bins.has(p.name)) bins.set(p.name, { classes: p.classes, tris: [] }); }); ts.flatMap(t => subdivide(t, part.subdivide || 0)).forEach(t => { const c = colour(t); bins.get(part.palette.reduce((best, p) => (d2(c, p.color) < d2(c, best.color) ? p : best), part.palette[0]).name).tris.push(t); }); bins.forEach((bin, name) => { if (bin.tris.length) made.push([name, bin.classes, bin.tris]); }); } if (used.size !== islands.length) throw new Error('every island must go to a part: ' + (islands.length - used.size) + ' left over'); const group = new Group(); group.name = plan.group; group.userData.customClasses = plan.classes; node.updateWorldMatrix(true, false); node.matrixWorld.decompose(group.position, group.quaternion, group.scale); // the new group sits where the mesh was in the world for (const [name, classes, tris] of made) { const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry(), n = tris.length * 3; let at = 0; names.forEach(an => { const a = A[an], arr = new a.array.constructor(n * a.itemSize); tris.forEach((t, i) => t.forEach((v, k) => { for (let c = 0; c < a.itemSize; c++) arr[(i * 3 + k) * a.itemSize + c] = v[at + c]; })); at += a.itemSize; geo.setAttribute(an, new THREE.BufferAttribute(arr, a.itemSize, a.normalized)); }); geo.setIndex([...Array(n).keys()]); geo.computeBoundingBox(); geo.computeBoundingSphere(); const m = new Mesh(geo, node.material); // the same material, so the object looks exactly as it did m.name = name; m.castShadow = node.castShadow; m.receiveShadow = node.receiveShadow; m.userData.customClasses = classes; group.add(m); } // the mesh goes, and so do the empty wrappers the importer left around it (a file name, a root node), so nothing nameless is left behind let gone = node; while (gone.parent && gone.parent !== editor.scene && gone.parent.children.length === 1) gone = gone.parent; editor.execute(new RemoveObjectCommand(editor, gone)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, group)); return made.map(([n, , t]) => n + ': ' + t.length + ' triangles').join(' | '); }; // check a cut: give every part of a group its own flat colour (one undoable command each), then CUT.restore() puts the textured material back const PREVIEW = ['#e6194b', '#3cb44b', '#4363d8', '#f58231', '#911eb4', '#46f0f0', '#f032e6', '#bcf60c', '#008080', '#9a6324']; CUT.preview = group => { CUT.saved = CUT.saved || new Map(); group.children.forEach((m, i) => { if (!CUT.saved.has(m)) CUT.saved.set(m, m.material); editor.execute(new SetMaterialCommand(editor, m, new MeshBasicMaterial({ color: PREVIEW[i % PREVIEW.length] }))); }); return group.children.map((m, i) => PREVIEW[i % PREVIEW.length] + ' ' + m.name).join('\n'); }; CUT.restore = () => { CUT.saved.forEach((material, m) => editor.execute(new SetMaterialCommand(editor, m, material))); CUT.saved.clear(); return 'textured materials restored'; }; 'CUT ready: ' + Object.keys(CUT).join(', ')
4 Look before you cut
Ask for the description of the mesh, with four colours per island:
// look before cutting: every island of the mesh, with its size and its main colours const mesh = $S('#Avocado').nodes[0]; CUT.describe(mesh, 4)
island 0: 483 triangles, texture u 0.01,0.67 v 0.01,0.76, size 0.043,0.063,0.022, colours rgb(51,99,7) 51% rgb(70,118,26) 28% rgb(93,148,44) 20% rgb(97,172,4) 1% island 1: 158 triangles, texture u 0.70,0.97 v 0.00,0.33, size 0.019,0.027,0.006, colours rgb(126,62,19) 36% rgb(187,127,56) 32% rgb(159,90,34) 23% rgb(210,159,88) 9% island 2: 41 triangles, texture u 0.54,0.98 v 0.35,1.00, size 0.042,0.061,0.000, colours rgb(52,107,2) 39% rgb(203,227,119) 29% rgb(247,212,86) 18% rgb(113,185,21) 14%
Read it like evidence. Island 0 is the biggest (483 triangles), 0.043 × 0.063 × 0.022 in size, and dark green throughout: the skin. Island 1 is a small patch, 0.019 × 0.027 × 0.006, all brown: the pit. Island 2 has 41 triangles and a thickness of 0.000, so it is flat; its colours are dark green, cream, yellow and lime: the cut face, which is painted with a dark rim, a cream and lime flesh and a yellow hollow. Looking at the texture image itself agrees: a green sphere-like patch, a brown egg, and a half fruit.
Units are the model's own: the fruit is about 0.06 tall, so the sizes are in metres (6 cm). The unit is a property of the file, not of this tutorial.
5 Cut by what you decided
Islands 0 and 1 become whole parts. Island 2, the cut face, is divided by colour: yellow and orange to the cavity the seed sat in, cream and lime to the flesh, dark green to the edge where the peel meets the cut. Several palette colours can share one name, because the cavity has a gradient. Each part gets a name and classes: skin and peel, pit and seed, and so on, with flesh-cut on the three parts that are the cut face, so one class selects them together.
// cut the avocado. Island 0 is the big shell (the outside), island 1 the small egg-shaped patch (the seed), island 2 the flat half-fruit patch (the cut face). // The cut face is divided by colour into the hollow around the seed (yellow and orange), the flesh (cream and lime) and the dark edge where the peel meets it. const mesh = $S('#Avocado').nodes[0]; CUT.split(mesh, { group: 'Avocado_Fruit', classes: ['fruit', 'avocado'], parts: [ { island: 0, name: 'Avocado_Skin', classes: ['skin', 'peel'] }, { island: 1, name: 'Avocado_Pit', classes: ['pit', 'seed'] }, { island: 2, subdivide: 4, palette: [ { name: 'Avocado_Pit_Cavity', classes: ['cavity', 'flesh-cut'], color: [247, 212, 86] }, { name: 'Avocado_Pit_Cavity', classes: ['cavity', 'flesh-cut'], color: [245, 175, 70] }, { name: 'Avocado_Flesh', classes: ['flesh', 'edible', 'flesh-cut'], color: [203, 227, 119] }, { name: 'Avocado_Flesh', classes: ['flesh', 'edible', 'flesh-cut'], color: [113, 185, 21] }, { name: 'Avocado_Skin_Edge', classes: ['skin', 'peel-edge', 'flesh-cut'], color: [52, 107, 2] } ] } ] })
Avocado_Skin: 483 triangles | Avocado_Pit: 158 triangles | Avocado_Pit_Cavity: 2286 triangles | Avocado_Flesh: 6195 triangles | Avocado_Skin_Edge: 2015 triangles
The cut face went from 41 triangles to 10,496 (41 × 44), and the whole fruit from 682 to 11,137: that is the price of a boundary that follows the paint. A smaller subdivision is cheaper and the boundary is more ragged.
6 Check the cut
A cut is only as good as the decision behind it, so look at it. CUT.preview paints each part a different flat colour (one undoable command per part); isolate hides everything but one selector.
CUT.preview($S('#Avocado_Fruit').nodes[0]) // each part its own flat colour isolate('#Avocado_Pit') // only the pit showAll() CUT.restore() // the textured material, back
Before and after look the same: the five parts share the original material.
Previewed: orange is the flesh, blue the cavity around the seed, green the seed, purple the thin edge. The boundary between the cavity and the flesh follows the paint, so it is ragged.
Isolated: the pit.
Isolated: the pit cavity, the yellow-orange hollow where the seed sat.
Isolated: the flesh, a ring that the cavity and the pit fill.
Isolated: the skin edge, a thin dark green rim, nearly invisible on its own.
Isolated, from behind: the skin, the outer shell, which hides the cut face from this side.
From behind there is no cut face: the fruit is closed on this side.
7 Lights, and the gate
A directional light and a soft fill, named and classed like everything else, and then requireLabels(true). That marks the scene: from now on a commit is refused while any object is unnamed, duplicated or without a class, and lint() lists what is wrong. This is the second reason to name the parts well: the importer's own wrapper nodes had no class, and the block would not run until they were gone, which is why CUT.split removes them with the mesh.
// a light to see it by, and the names and classes that make every object reachable const sun = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xfff1dd, 2.6); sun.name = 'KeyLight'; sun.position.set(0.4, 0.8, 0.9); sun.userData.customClasses = ['light']; const sky = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xdde6ff, 0x6a78c8, 1.4); sky.name = 'FillLight'; sky.userData.customClasses = ['light']; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sun)); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sky)); requireLabels(true) // from here on a commit is refused while any object is unnamed, duplicated or classless
8 A view to open with
The camera, straight on, with the fruit filling the middle of the frame. The scene is at a scale of centimetres, so the camera is about 11 cm away.
// the view the scene opens with: the cut face, straight on, the fruit filling the middle of the frame const FRONT = [0, 0.032, 0.115], AIM = [0, 0.031, 0]; editor.camera.position.set(...FRONT); editor.controls.center.set(...AIM); editor.camera.lookAt(...AIM); editor.signals.cameraChanged

posts.title: Cut a scene into named parts
posts.text:
Cut a scene into named parts
All tutorials
An avocado has three texture islands and each one is a part. A furnished room is one mesh with 538 islands, most of them a few triangles of trim or the label on a prop, and no island is "the bed". SEG handles the part of the job that needs no judgment: it joins the islands that touch into components, measures them in the world frame, places everything you did not name on the nearest thing you did, and checks the result. What is left for you, or for a model, is the one step that never reduced to a rule: naming the anchors. Built with the JS Shell.
Who named this. The anchor names on this page (Dark_Console_Unit and the rest) are agent output, not a human's: an AI agent read the component report and chose them. A human gave the instruction and ran the pasted commands, not the names. See Name every part of a street-corner diorama for the case where a short list of anchors is not possible at all.
Start with the object tutorial. This page assumes Cut any textured mesh into named parts (the avocado and the duck): SEG.describe, SEG.split, SEG.preview, the plan, and the record. The reference is guides/MESH_SEGMENT.md. An older page, building the tool by hand, is for the object case and uses the name CUT.
1 Same tool, different evidence
The object tutorial's evidence was mostly colour: the cut face of the avocado is cream and orange, the beak of the duck is orange. A room has almost none to give. Its texture is a dark green-black atlas shared by a few hundred pieces, and the two lines that matter most for telling a ceiling from a floor are not colours at all: they are where a piece is and how big. The tool is the same; the evidence that carries the weight is different, and the report changes with it.
An object (avocado, duck) A scene (the room) Grain the island the component: islands that touch in space The report leads with texture position, then colours size and position in the world, colours last What tells parts apart paint: rings, eyes, a beak position, size, how much detail: a slab at the bottom is a floor, a 1,892-triangle figure 0.7 high is a cat Who places the small pieces you, island by island the host, by distance, from the anchors you name
Who chooses the grain. The host does, from the mesh: when there are at most three components for every four islands (the room has 538 islands and 282 components), SEG.describe and SEG.data report components; otherwise islands. A caller can say which: SEG.describe('#Mesh', 3, { grain: 'islands' }). The choice is stated in the last line of the report, and the grain the plan was written against is recorded.
2 The model, and its licence
Cyberpunk micro-apartments by Mikita_Hubanau, from Sketchfab, licensed Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial. Download the glTF and import the .glb with the dialog's defaults. The file has three meshes: Object_4 (12,151 triangles, textured, the room), Object_5 (7,794 triangles, one flat material) and Object_6 (a two-triangle glass pane). This page cuts Object_4.
The segmented scene is not published with this page. A segmentation is a derivative work, and this model's licence does not allow commercial use, so the scene is not committed to the public repository and there is no embedded player. If you publish your own cut, give the licence and the credit in the plan's source; SEG will not cut without them.
3 Read the components
SEG.describe('#Object_4')
component 0: 2270 triangles (12 islands: 0,5,7,9,12,13,…), size 0.754,1.489,0.258, centre -0.919,2.989,-2.331, at 0.41,0.50,0.23, colours rgb(14,17,14) 72% rgb(25,30,24) 18% rgb(43,52,40) 10% component 1: 1892 triangles (13 islands: 1,2,3,18,19,62,…), size 0.285,0.698,1.159, centre 0.340,1.362,-1.106, at 0.53,0.23,0.37, colours rgb(63,68,65) 48% rgb(107,120,114) 37% rgb(171,198,191) 15% … component 21: 118 triangles (4 islands: 36,84,123,251), size 5.694,0.471,7.736, centre 1.660,5.691,0.475, at 0.67,0.96,0.55, colours rgb(197,240,225) 59% rgb(55,80,71) 21% rgb(132,170,156) 20% component 29: 75 triangles (11 islands: 122,186,245,246,247,248,…), size 9.193,1.007,7.028, centre 0.355,0.522,0.769, at 0.54,0.09,0.59, colours rgb(14,18,14) 42% rgb(28,36,27) 40% rgb(48,61,48) 18% … (538 islands joined into 282 components where they touch in space; world frame, y up. Pass { grain: 'islands' } for the islands. Name anchors: { name, classes, component: [..] }, and let SEG.attach place the rest)
282 lines instead of 538, and each one says what a person asks first: how big, where, how detailed. Component 21 is 118 triangles, 5.7 × 0.47 × 7.7, with at.y 0.96: a thin slab at the very top, a ceiling. Component 29 is 75 triangles, 9.2 × 1.0 × 7.0, at.y 0.09: a slab at the bottom, the floor deck. Component 1 is 1,892 triangles, 0.29 × 0.70 × 1.16, low and in the middle: far too detailed and too small to be furniture. Its colours are grey and white. A cat.
Why "world frame" is a line of its own. The model is Z-up, and the importer turns it upright with a rotation. In the mesh's frame the ceiling has at.z 0.04 and the floor 0.91: "up" is on the wrong axis and runs the wrong way, and every number looks fine. SEG.components and the scene report apply the node's world matrix, so y is up and 0.96 is high. SEG.describe on an object still reports in the mesh's frame, as its tutorial says; a record says which it used (attach.parameters.frame).
The same numbers as objects, for a script or a model: SEG.components('#Object_4'). Each has component, islands, triangles, size, centre, at and colours.
4 Name the anchors
This is the step that does not reduce to a rule, and the only one that is yours. An anchor is a component you can name from the evidence. Start with the biggest and most distinctive; the rest will follow them. Say what each name rests on: position, size, colour, or shape when all you can honestly offer is a description of the form. It is recorded, and a record with many shape names is a different claim from one with none.
Component Evidence Name Basis 1 1,892 triangles, 0.3 × 0.7 × 1.2, low, grey and white Cyber_Cat position, size 2 574 triangles, light, on the bed at the right Bed_Pillow position, size, colour 7, 47, 68 thin brown pieces that run the length of the room: the arch round the doorway, and trim Doorway_Frame_And_Trim, class trim position, size 21 a thin slab at the very top Ceiling_Panel position, size 29 a slab 1.0 thick at the bottom, spanning the floor plan Floor_Deck position, size 14, 19, 28 tall thin plates at the edges Wall_Left_Pillar, Wall_Right_Unit, Wall_Front_Right_Column position, size 16 a long low frame, 5.2 × 1.0 × 2.9, brown Bed_Frame position, size 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 17 eight components in one cluster at the left front, standing on the deck, about 1.4 across: the crates and what is on them Crate_Stack position, size, colour 23 greenish, 0.9 wide and 1.7 high, along the right edge Plant_Cluster position, colour 22 the counter at the back, with its small items near it Kitchen_Counter position, size 4 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.3, blue, beside the bed Blue_Mug position, size, colour 0 2,270 triangles, near-black, 0.75 × 1.5 × 0.26, high on the wall; a small bright panel sits against it in the render Dark_Console_Unit shape
The last row is the honest one. Nothing in the evidence says what that unit is, so the name describes what can be seen and the basis says shape. It is better than a confident Fridge.
Before cutting, ask where everything else would go:
SEG.attach('#Object_4', [ { name: 'Floor_Deck', classes: ['floor'], component: 29 }, { name: 'Cyber_Cat', classes: ['cat'], component: 1 }, { name: 'Ceiling_Panel', classes: ['ceiling'], component: 21 } ], { maxDistance: 0.5 })
It returns parts (each anchor with what would be attached), unattached (what is too far), tie_broken, the parameters used and, per part, how many components it would take and how far the furthest was. Nothing is cut.
5 What attaching does, exactly
The rules are fixed and written down, so a run can be repeated and a result can be questioned.
Distance is to triangles, not vertices. A floor is a few huge triangles, and its four corner vertices are metres from anything standing on it. Each unnamed component is sampled at the centres of up to six triangles per island, and the distance is the shortest from a sample to any triangle of the anchor. The nearest anchor wins, but near-ties go to the smaller thing. Every anchor within tie (0.05 world units) of the nearest is tied with it, and the one with the smaller bounding box wins, so a mug that touches both the counter and the floor belongs to the counter. A prop beats the structure it stands against. On the room the rule decided seven components, each given to a smaller anchor than the strictly nearest one. tie is a recorded parameter, in world units: change it if your scene is a hundred times bigger. Beyond maxDistance, nothing is attached. There is always a nearest anchor, so without a limit a lamp standing alone across the room would join the nearest wall, and a component that is really an object of its own would be absorbed without a word. The limit defaults to a tenth of the scene's diagonal (1.448 on this room, which is 14.48 across) and the value used is recorded. A component beyond it is returned to you, named with its nearest anchor and the distance, and the cut refuses to run until you name it as an anchor of its own, or describe it the way Dark_Console_Unit is described, or raise the limit.
SEG.split('#Object_4', { group: 'Cyber_Room_Parts', source: { … }, anchors: [ … ], attach: { maxDistance: 0.3 } }) // with the first plan's anchors: // SEG.split: 5 components are further than maxDistance (0.3) from every anchor: component 272 (nearest "Kitchen_Counter", 0.38659), // component 273 (nearest "Bed_Frame", 0.55048), component 274 (nearest "Bed_Frame", 0.498), component 275 (nearest "Wall_Front_Right_Column", 0.56101), // component 281 (…). Name each as an anchor of its own (component: [n]) or raise attach.maxDistance. Nothing was changed
6 Cut
The plan is the anchors, their classes, what each name rests on, and the source. That is all a model has to write.
SEG.split('#Object_4', { group: 'Cyber_Room_Parts', classes: ['room', 'interior'], source: { url: 'https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/cyberpunk-micro-apartments-fd8011e2af0e43288f5445600197ea77', fetchable: false, // a model page behind a login: the file cannot be re-fetched, so its hash and size are what identify it sha256: 'b2026982a0cd825a2046e2e1c5dc49ad5af56ad36e7aba1954118b12ce85ec73', bytes: 2266956, licence: 'CC Attribution-NonCommercial (as stated on the Sketchfab model page)', attribution: 'Mikita_Hubanau (Sketchfab: cyberpunk micro-apartments)' }, anchors: [ { name: 'Cyber_Cat', classes: ['animal', 'cat'], component: 1, basis: ['position', 'size'] }, { name: 'Bed_Pillow', classes: ['bedding', 'pillow'], component: 2, basis: ['position', 'size', 'colour'] }, { name: 'Doorway_Frame_And_Trim', classes: ['structure', 'doorway', 'trim'], component: [7, 47, 68], basis: ['position', 'size'] }, { name: 'Ceiling_Panel', classes: ['structure', 'ceiling'], component: 21, basis: ['position', 'size'] }, { name: 'Floor_Deck', classes: ['structure', 'floor'], component: 29, basis: ['position', 'size'] }, // … Wall_Left_Pillar 14, Wall_Right_Unit 19, Wall_Front_Right_Column 28, Bed_Frame 16, Crate_Stack [3,5,8,9,10,12,15,17], // Plant_Cluster 23, Kitchen_Counter 22, Blue_Mug 4 … { name: 'Dark_Console_Unit', classes: ['appliance', 'console'], component: 0, basis: ['shape'] } ] })
Cyber_Cat: 1892 triangles | Bed_Pillow: 643 triangles | Doorway_Frame_And_Trim: 350 triangles | Ceiling_Panel: 140 triangles | Floor_Deck: 95 triangles | Wall_Left_Pillar: 251 triangles | Wall_Right_Unit: 496 triangles | Wall_Front_Right_Column: 89 triangles | Bed_Frame: 428 triangles | Crate_Stack: 2367 triangles | Plant_Cluster: 1130 triangles | Kitchen_Counter: 1340 triangles | Dark_Console_Unit: 2590 triangles | Blue_Mug: 340 triangles ⚠ orphan sink: Plant_Cluster: it received 167 of the 259 components that were attached (64%): it is the nearest anchor to everything that has no anchor of its own. Name more anchors
The triangles add up to the mesh's 12,151, the parts share the original material so the room looks as it did, and one Undo puts Object_4 back. Then check it as before: SEG.preview('#Cyber_Room_Parts') and isolate('#Crate_Stack'), from every side.
7 The checks, and the cut they caught
The first cut of this room was wrong in a way the picture did not show. The thin brown trim that runs round the whole room was attached to the nearest anchor, which was Wall_Front_Right_Column, and the column came out room-sized. What gave it away was a number, not the picture: the part's box spanned 70%, 92% and 99% of the room on x, y and z while it carried 14% of the surface. That is now an assertion, and it fires on exactly that plan.
Assertion Fires when oversize a part's box spans at least 60% of the scene on every axis while it carries less than 25% of the surface: trim, or several objects, swallowed engulfing a part's box contains at least half of the other parts' centres while it carries less than 10% of the surface absorbed a part assembled from at least 8 components whose main colour holds at least 85% of its texture footprint orphan sink one part received at least half of the components that were attached, out of at least 10
A part that declares itself spread out (a class of trim, frame, cable, pipe, wire, rail, network, edge or outline) is exempt from oversize and engulfing, which is how the fix is expressed: name the room-wide trim as one part and say so, as in step 6. Fewer than four parts are not judged. All the thresholds are in ASSERTIONS in meshSegment.js and are recorded with every cut.
A fired check does not stop the cut and does not change it. The cut is one undo step, and the right response to a failed check, undo and cut again with a better plan, is a decision for whoever wrote the plan. The check says which assertion, which part, and the numbers.
The one still firing is real. On the corrected cut, orphan sink still says Plant_Cluster took 167 of the 259 attached components (64%). It did: its 168 components average about seven triangles each, they lie along the right edge, and no anchor claims them, so the plant is the nearest. What they are (leaves, curtain folds, clutter) was not checked. The cut is usable, but "Plant_Cluster" is the room's catch-all, and the warning is the tool saying so. The remedy is the one in the message: name more anchors for what is there, and cut again. The tutorial leaves the warning in place on purpose.
8 What the record keeps
const rec = $S('#Cyber_Room_Parts').nodes[0].userData.segmentation rec.grain // 'components' rec.plan // the anchors, names, classes, basis, source: as given rec.describe.components // the 282-line report the decision was made from rec.attach.parameters // { max_distance: 1.448, max_distance_default: true, tie: 0.05, samples_per_island: 6, weld_digits: 4, scene_diagonal: 14.48, frame: 'world' } rec.attach.per_part // per part: components, how many were attached, and the median, 90th percentile and maximum distance rec.attach.tie_broken // the seven components the tie-break gave to a smaller anchor than the nearest rec.attach.unattached // [] : nothing was left over rec.signals.components_per_part // Plant_Cluster 168, Crate_Stack 24, Cyber_Cat 1, …: a part made of 168 components is a different claim from one made of 1 rec.signals.names_by_basis // { evidence: 13, shape: 1, unstated: 0 } rec.signals.assertions // what fired, with the numbers; rec.signals.assertion_parameters says what the thresholds were
SEG.replay('#Object_4', rec) recomputes the components and the attachment from the recorded plan and parameters, and refuses to run if the mesh is not the one the record describes (different triangle counts, or different islands in a component). Run on a fresh import, it gave the same 14 parts, triangle for triangle, and the same attachment record.
9 Your own scene
SEG.describe('#mesh'). If it reports islands, the mesh is an object: use the object tutorial. If it reports components, read size, centre and at first. Name the 8 to 20 components that you can justify, biggest first. Give each a basis. Use shape for what you can only describe. SEG.attach('#mesh', anchors) to see where everything goes and what is left over. Name what is left, or raise maxDistance if you mean it. SEG.split. Read every ⚠. Declare trim as trim. If a part took most of what was attached, name more anchors. SEG.preview and isolate from every side; then lint() and requireLabels(true).
What was checked, and what was not. The functions behind this page are tested in node on a synthetic room of boxes (components, the world frame, the tie-break, the limit, each assertion and a recorded plan run again) and on the real room, from the .glb file alone with no browser and no model: 538 islands become 282 components; the 14 anchors of the first cut give the same triangles and islands per part as that cut did when it was made by hand; the first plan fires oversize on Wall_Front_Right_Column and orphan sink on Plant_Cluster; a limit of 0.3 leaves exactly five components unattached. In the editor served from this repository, on a fresh import of the model, these were run: the report, the SEG.attach call of step 4, the cut of step 6 with its record, an undo, and the replay. The refusal at maxDistance: 0.3 was checked in node, not in the browser. SEG.preview and isolate were not run on this cut: look at it yourself. Not checked: whether these particular anchor names are good ones (they are the agent's reading of the evidence, not a measurement, and are not scored against a ground truth the way STOA's recovery run scores plans against 49 sample models' own part names); the thresholds, which were set on one room and one failure; and Object_5 and Object_6, which were left whole.
What a record cannot do. It cannot prove that the licence or attribution you give is right (SEG only refuses to run without them); it cannot say that the names are correct, only what they were made from, and now also by what rule everything else was placed.
The model. Cyberpunk micro-apartments, Mikita_Hubanau, on Sketchfab, Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial. No copy of the model or of its segmentation is in this repository.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets cyberpunk micro-apartments (room .glb): Mikita_Hubanau (Sketchfab: cyberpunk micro-apartments). Not for commercial use, so the segmented scene is not published Licence: CC BY-NC (as stated on the Sketchfab model page). Fox.glb: Low poly fox by PixelMannen; rigging and animation by @tomkranis; glTF conversion by @AsoboStudio and @scurest Licence: CC0 1.0 (the model); CC BY 4.0 (the rigging and animation, credited next). Fox rigging and animation (Sketchfab): @tomkranis on Sketchfab. Attribution is required, and applies to the Fox.glb above Licence: CC BY 4.0. Tools None used.

posts.title: Cut any textured mesh into named parts
posts.text:
Cut any textured mesh into named parts
All tutorials
Open embed
A model usually arrives as one mesh with one material, so nothing in the scene says "this is the beak". The editor's SEG tool cuts such a mesh into separate named, classed meshes in one undo step, from the evidence the file carries: which pieces of the texture are separate patches, and what colours are painted on them. This page uses it three times: on an avocado, where the file practically labels itself; on a toy duck, where you have to read the evidence and decide; and on an animated fox, a skinned mesh, where the cut must leave the skeleton and its animations alone. It also says where the method stops. Built with the JS Shell.
The tool is in the editor; this page uses it. SEG is a Shell global, with no setup. If you want to see what it does written out by hand, the older tutorial Cut an avocado into named parts, building the tool by hand builds the same thing step by step. The reference is guides/MESH_SEGMENT.md.
A whole room is a different case. This page is for objects, where each island is about one part. A furnished scene is one mesh with hundreds of islands and no island is "the bed"; for that, SEG.describe reports components in the world frame and SEG places the unnamed pieces itself. See Cut a scene into named parts.
1 The idea, and how far it goes
A mesh has no idea what its triangles are, but two things in the file do carry hints. UV islands: an artist unwraps a model into patches of one texture image, and a patch that shares no vertices with any other is often a whole part (a seed, a beak, a wing). Painted colour: inside one patch, a ring of orange and a ring of cream are different things even though the triangles are all alike. SEG reports both, you decide what each piece is, and SEG.split cuts exactly there. It does not recognise anything: the names come from you (or from an AI that you show the report to), and it never loses a triangle.
The 3D advantage. The parts are only separable because the object is three-dimensional data: you can isolate the beak, see from behind that the cut is where you think it is, and tell the left wing from the right by where its centre sits in space. The report says that in one column.
It works when the model is one indexed mesh with UVs and a base-colour texture, and its parts are laid out as separate islands or are painted in clearly different colours. It does not work when the mesh has no UVs, or only vertex colours or one flat colour (there is no evidence to read); when a part shares an island and a colour with its neighbour (a boundary nobody painted cannot be found); or when the model has several materials or morph targets (SEG refuses these, and says why, rather than break them; a mesh with several materials is better cut with SEG.byMaterial, step 10). A skinned mesh is cut, with its skeleton kept (step 5), but cannot be divided by colour with subdivide. And even when it works, it does not decide what an island is: the duck below has ten islands for about six parts, and you have to merge them.
2 The models, and their licences
All three are from the Khronos glTF Sample Models archive, retrieved 27 and 28 October 2026. Download the .glb files, then File → Import (or drop one in the viewport), accepting the import dialog's defaults. Import one at a time into an empty scene.
Model Source Licence Avocado Avocado.glb, Microsoft; 8.3 MB, one mesh of 682 triangles, three 2048 × 2048 textures CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication) Duck Duck.glb, Copyright 2006 Sony Computer Entertainment Inc.; 120 KB, one mesh of 4,212 triangles, one 512 × 512 texture SCEA Shared Source License 1.0: free to use, modify and redistribute, derivatives must carry the licence and notices and identify the modifications, as is, with no warranty Fox Fox.glb, low poly fox by PixelMannen, rigging and animation by @tomkranis, glTF conversion by @AsoboStudio and @scurest; 163 KB, one skinned mesh of 576 triangles, 24 bones, three clips, one texture Two licences in one file: the model is CC0 1.0; the rigging and animation are CC BY 4.0 and need attribution, which a record's source.attribution carries
The duck scene is a modified copy, and says so. duck.json in tejaswigowda/test1 is committed with the full licence text (licenses/SCEA-Shared-Source-License-1.0.txt) and a notice (licenses/duck-NOTICE.md) that gives the copyright line and lists the modifications: the one mesh cut into ten, two eyes subdivided, a light added. The texture and material are unchanged. If you publish a scene made from the duck, do the same. The avocado needs nothing, but the page credits it.
3 The easy case: the avocado
Import Avocado.glb. The scene holds one mesh, Avocado, inside a wrapper node named after the file. Ask for the report:
SEG.describe('#Avocado')
island 0: 483 triangles, texture u 0.01,0.67 v 0.01,0.76, size 0.043,0.063,0.022, at 0.50,0.50,0.61, colours rgb(54,102,10) 65% rgb(85,139,38) 34% rgb(96,170,4) 1% island 1: 158 triangles, texture u 0.70,0.97 v 0.00,0.33, size 0.019,0.027,0.006, at 0.50,0.45,0.12, colours rgb(132,66,22) 48% rgb(181,119,51) 41% rgb(207,155,85) 11% island 2: 41 triangles, texture u 0.54,0.98 v 0.35,1.00, size 0.042,0.061,0.000, at 0.49,0.50,0.22, colours rgb(220,221,107) 46% rgb(52,107,2) 39% rgb(113,186,22) 14%
Read it as evidence. Island 0 is the biggest, dark green: the skin. Island 1 is small and brown: the seed. Island 2 has a thickness of 0.000 (the third number of size), so it is flat, and it holds cream, dark green and lime: the cut face. Its 41 triangles are far too coarse to follow the rings painted on it, so the plan subdivides it and sorts the small triangles by colour. The at column is the island's centre across the whole mesh, 0 to 1 on x, y, z: the seed sits at the back of the mesh (z 0.12), the cut face just in front of it.
// Island 0 (483 triangles, dark green, the biggest) is the outside: the skin. Island 1 (158, brown, small, at the back of the mesh in z) is the seed. // Island 2 has thickness 0.000: it is flat, so it is the cut face, painted dark green (the rim), cream and lime (the flesh) and yellow-orange (the hollow). // The flat face is far too coarse (41 triangles) to follow those rings, so it is subdivided four times (41 x 256) and each small triangle goes to the // nearest palette colour; two colours may share one name. // The source is required: a segmentation is a derivative work, and its record says what it derives from and under what licence. SEG.split('#Avocado', { group: 'Avocado_Fruit', classes: ['fruit', 'avocado'], source: { url: 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KhronosGroupArchives/glTF-Sample-Models/d7a3cc8e51d7c573771ae77a57f16b0662a905c6/2.0/Avocado/glTF-Binary/Avocado.glb', sha256: '85ae91e60ed519f53a7e2096508837fedd446dcc450f8e05678b7a204679bd12', bytes: 8328156, licence: 'CC0 1.0 Universal', attribution: 'Microsoft (Khronos glTF Sample Models: Avocado)' }, parts: [ { island: 0, name: 'Avocado_Skin', classes: ['skin', 'peel'] }, { island: 1, name: 'Avocado_Pit', classes: ['pit', 'seed'] }, { island: 2, subdivide: 4, palette: [ { name: 'Avocado_Pit_Cavity', classes: ['cavity', 'flesh-cut'], color: [247, 212, 86] }, { name: 'Avocado_Pit_Cavity', classes: ['cavity', 'flesh-cut'], color: [245, 175, 70] }, { name: 'Avocado_Flesh', classes: ['flesh', 'edible', 'flesh-cut'], color: [203, 227, 119] }, { name: 'Avocado_Flesh', classes: ['flesh', 'edible', 'flesh-cut'], color: [113, 185, 21] }, { name: 'Avocado_Skin_Edge', classes: ['skin', 'peel-edge', 'flesh-cut'], color: [52, 107, 2] } ] } ] })
Avocado_Skin: 483 triangles | Avocado_Pit: 158 triangles | Avocado_Pit_Cavity: 2286 triangles | Avocado_Flesh: 6195 triangles | Avocado_Skin_Edge: 2015 triangles
The cut face went from 41 triangles to 10,496 (41 × 44); that is the price of a boundary that follows the paint, and the boundary is as ragged as the paint is. SEG.preview('#Avocado_Fruit') paints each part a flat colour so you can check it (step 7 does this on the duck); here the cavity, flesh, seed and rim were all where they should be. The finished scene is avocado.json, and a tutorial that builds the whole tool by hand on this avocado is here.
The avocado previewed: orange is the flesh, blue the cavity around the seed, green the seed, purple the thin edge.
4 The hard case: the duck
Start again with an empty scene and import Duck.glb. First look at what the importer gave you, then at the report:
// What did the importer give us? One mesh, wrapped in two nameless nodes, and a camera the file carried. // Then the description of the mesh: one line per island, largest first, with its size, where its centre sits across the whole mesh (0 to 1 on x, y, z) // and its main colours. const list = []; scene.traverse(o => { if (o !== scene) list.push(o.type + ' ' + (o.name || '(unnamed)')); }); list.join('\n') + '\n\n' + SEG.describe('#LOD3spShape')
Group Duck.glb Object3D (unnamed) Mesh LOD3spShape PerspectiveCamera (unnamed)
island 0: 2532 triangles, texture u 0.83,0.97 v 0.46,0.60, size 153.687,154.041,115.150, at 0.47,0.50,0.50, colours rgb(255,216,0) 100% island 1: 882 triangles, texture u 0.84,0.98 v 0.64,0.80, size 35.060,33.478,46.304, at 0.89,0.73,0.40, colours rgb(255,127,0) 98% rgb(255,163,0) 2% rgb(255,189,0) 0% island 2: 160 triangles, texture u 0.03,0.72 v 0.02,0.49, size 63.264,45.328,12.817, at 0.41,0.24,0.94, colours rgb(255,214,0) 58% rgb(255,188,0) 23% rgb(255,200,0) 20% island 3: 160 triangles, texture u 0.03,0.72 v 0.03,0.49, size 63.248,44.110,12.691, at 0.41,0.23,0.06, colours rgb(255,214,0) 54% rgb(255,188,0) 25% rgb(255,201,0) 20% island 4: 138 triangles, texture u 0.63,0.98 v 0.03,0.44, size 10.149,13.927,10.728, at 0.80,0.83,0.65, colours rgb(0,0,0) 66% rgb(255,255,255) 33% rgb(142,142,142) 1% island 5: 138 triangles, texture u 0.63,0.98 v 0.03,0.44, size 13.382,14.072,6.043, at 0.72,0.82,0.22, colours rgb(0,0,0) 66% rgb(255,255,255) 33% rgb(113,113,113) 1% island 6: 76 triangles, texture u 0.03,0.42 v 0.44,0.96, size 30.104,52.185,46.208, at 0.09,0.38,0.32, colours rgb(255,215,0) 78% rgb(255,198,0) 12% rgb(255,189,0) 11% island 7: 62 triangles, texture u 0.04,0.42 v 0.44,0.96, size 31.217,52.005,43.767, at 0.09,0.38,0.69, colours rgb(255,216,0) 77% rgb(255,191,0) 15% rgb(255,203,0) 8% island 8: 36 triangles, texture u 0.46,0.86 v 0.53,0.98, size 28.316,29.575,44.034, at 0.20,0.45,0.33, colours rgb(255,214,0) 64% rgb(255,200,0) 26% rgb(255,188,0) 11% island 9: 28 triangles, texture u 0.48,0.85 v 0.53,0.98, size 28.674,27.768,41.070, at 0.21,0.46,0.68, colours rgb(255,214,0) 67% rgb(255,202,0) 21% rgb(255,190,0) 11%
Ten islands, for a toy with a body, a head, a beak, two wings, a tail and two eyes. Reading them is the work, and the report gives you what you need:
Island Evidence Decision 0 2,532 triangles, 154 high, at 0.47, 0.50, 0.50: the middle of the mesh in every direction; one colour, yellow, 100% The body and the head, as a single island: the file does not separate them, and the tool cannot 1 882 triangles, orange 98%, at x 0.89: the front The beak 2, 3 160 triangles each, 63 long but only 12.7 wide (flat), yellow, at z 0.94 and 0.06: one on each side The wings. The duck faces +x with y up, so its right is +z: island 2 is the right wing, 3 the left 4, 5 138 triangles each, black 66%, white 33%, at y 0.83, z 0.65 and 0.22: high on the head, one on each side The eyes, each painted with a black eye and a white highlight. Divide each by colour 6, 8 and 7, 9 76 + 36 and 62 + 28 triangles, yellow, at x 0.09 to 0.21: the back, z 0.32 and 0.69 The tail, in two pieces on each side: merge each pair with a list, island: [6, 8]
Two things in this table are the real lesson. The islands do not map one to one onto the parts: the tail is four islands and the body and head are one. And two of the decisions rest on the at column (left from right) and on a colour split (the eyes) that no amount of automatic cutting could have guessed. Now the plan:
// Reading the description. The beak island is the orange one (882 triangles, centre at x 0.89, the front). The two big flat ones at z 0.06 and 0.94 // are the wings, one a side. The two 138-triangle islands (black and white in the texture) are the eyes, at z 0.22 and 0.65. The small pairs at x 0.09 // and 0.20 are the tail, in two pieces on each side. The biggest island, 2532 triangles at the middle of the mesh, is the body and the head in one. // The duck faces +x with y up, so its right is +z and its left -z, which is how the "at" column tells left from right. // Each eye is divided by colour: the black is the eye itself, the white is the highlight painted on it. // The source is required: a segmentation is a derivative work, and its record says what it derives from and under what licence. SEG.split('#LOD3spShape', { group: 'Duck', classes: ['toy', 'duck'], source: { url: 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KhronosGroupArchives/glTF-Sample-Models/d7a3cc8e51d7c573771ae77a57f16b0662a905c6/2.0/Duck/glTF-Binary/Duck.glb', sha256: '65bf938f54d6073e619e76e007820bbf980cdc3dc0daec0d94830ffc4ae54ab5', bytes: 120484, licence: 'SCEA Shared Source License 1.0', attribution: 'Copyright 2006 Sony Computer Entertainment Inc.' }, parts: [ { island: 0, name: 'Duck_Body_And_Head', classes: ['body', 'head'] }, { island: 1, name: 'Duck_Beak', classes: ['beak'] }, { island: 3, name: 'Duck_Wing_Left', classes: ['wing', 'left'] }, { island: 2, name: 'Duck_Wing_Right', classes: ['wing', 'right'] }, { island: [6, 8], name: 'Duck_Tail_Left', classes: ['tail', 'left'] }, { island: [7, 9], name: 'Duck_Tail_Right', classes: ['tail', 'right'] }, { island: 5, subdivide: 2, palette: [ { name: 'Duck_Eye_Left', classes: ['eye', 'left'], color: [1, 1, 1] }, { name: 'Duck_Eye_Highlight_Left', classes: ['eye-highlight', 'left'], color: [253, 253, 253] } ] }, { island: 4, subdivide: 2, palette: [ { name: 'Duck_Eye_Right', classes: ['eye', 'right'], color: [1, 1, 1] }, { name: 'Duck_Eye_Highlight_Right', classes: ['eye-highlight', 'right'], color: [253, 253, 253] } ] } ] })
Duck_Body_And_Head: 2532 triangles | Duck_Beak: 882 triangles | Duck_Wing_Left: 160 triangles | Duck_Wing_Right: 160 triangles | Duck_Tail_Left: 112 triangles | Duck_Tail_Right: 90 triangles | Duck_Eye_Left: 1478 triangles | Duck_Eye_Highlight_Left: 730 triangles | Duck_Eye_Right: 1489 triangles | Duck_Eye_Highlight_Right: 719 triangles
Ten parts: 3,936 triangles for the ones taken whole, and the eyes, 276 triangles that were subdivided into 16 each, 4,416, so 8,352 in all (4,212 before). The two eyes keep their own pieces of the texture, so they still look as before.
5 A model that moves: the fox
Start again with an empty scene and import Fox.glb. It is a different kind of mesh: one skinned mesh, fox, bound to a skeleton of 24 bones, with three animation clips (Survey, Walk, Run) that move the bones, not the mesh. Cutting such a mesh must not disturb any of that, and SEG (1.4.0 and later) keeps it: every part is a skinned mesh bound to the same skeleton with the original bind matrix, and the bone indices and weights of every vertex are copied unchanged. Ask for the report:

Fourteen islands, in seven left and right pairs. This is an object report, not a scene report, although the mesh is one welded surface (all fourteen islands touch in space, so there is one component and nothing for the scene grain to say): when the components come to one, SEG.describe reports islands. The sizes are in the mesh's own units, which are not the scene's (the importer scaled the file by 0.01293). Reading it:

The tail islands sit at z 0.15 and the ears and front legs at 0.87 and 0.69, so the fox faces +z with y up, and its left is +x: the islands with at x above 0.5 (0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12) are the left side and the others the right. SEG.source('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KhronosGroupArchives/glTF-Sample-Models/d7a3cc8e51d7c573771ae77a57f16b0662a905c6/2.0/Fox/glTF-Binary/Fox.glb', { licence: 'CC0 1.0 Universal (model, PixelMannen); CC BY 4.0 (rigging and animation, @tomkranis)', attribution: 'Low poly fox by PixelMannen (CC0); rigging and animation by @tomkranis on Sketchfab (CC BY 4.0); glTF conversion by @AsoboStudio and @scurest (Khronos glTF Sample Models: Fox)' }).then(s => { window.src = s })
