posts.title: A sparring match from a two-person motion capture
posts.text:
A sparring match from a two-person motion capture
All tutorials
The starting scene, sparring.json, seen through cam-wide at 12 s.
Two people sparred for 170 seconds in front of an optical motion-capture system. Here you turn that take into a 53-second match: register the pair, cut it as data, check every frame for collisions, move the camera shots onto the new timeline, and give both fighters somewhere to look.
Credits. The motion in this tutorial was recorded with an OptiTrack optical motion-capture system in the course “Martial Arts and Motion Capture” (GAME 294) at Arizona State University, run by Pavan Turaga and recorded by Assegid Kidane. The two performers' captured clips are used here as the source material for the editing techniques below; the cut, the cameras and the faces are authored in Strata.
Where this picks up. The scene (two rigged VRoid characters carrying the two captured clips, a bamboo hut, a floor, lighting, four cameras and a 37-shot sequence) is built in the dojo tutorial, Part 2 — start there if you want to build it. The finished, uncut scene is sparring.json in the tejaswigowda/test1 repo; open it and paste each block below into the Shell tab. The fighters are labelled #f1 and #f2 and carry the clips st1_1072026Skeleton and st2_1072026Skeleton, 170.17 s each. Every block is one undoable step.
1 Register the pair
The two clips were captured together, in one shared world frame: each fighter's root motion already says where they stand relative to the other at every moment. Move or retime one fighter alone and that relationship breaks and the bodies overlap. So the pair is registered as a single editable group, and every edit applies to both fighters at once.
const sparring = $M.group('sparring', ['#f1', '#f2']); sparring.collision(); // baseline: the full 170 s capture
The collision report measures the hip-to-hip distance on the floor over the timeline and flags anything under 0.6 m, a reasonable floor for non-contact sparring. For the full capture the closest the two ever get is 0.80 m: this is non-contact sparring — a strike that should read as connecting has to be sold by the cut, not by the geometry.
2 Find the exchanges
170 seconds is too long, and the middle of it is empty. Measuring where the two come close together, the exchanges are front-loaded — ten of them between 2.6 s and 43.2 s — then there is nothing from 43.2 s to 98.5 s, then they resume and thin out. Padding each cluster by −1.0 s before and +1.2 s after, and merging gaps under 0.4 s, gives eight spans:
# in out dur closest E01 1.60 9.00 7.40 s 0.94 m E02 14.60 22.10 7.50 s 0.96 m E03 30.80 44.40 13.60 s 0.80 m E04 97.50 103.40 5.90 s 1.11 m E05 104.80 110.80 6.00 s 0.93 m E06 113.70 117.60 3.90 s 1.08 m E07 134.70 140.60 5.90 s 1.10 m E08 158.40 161.10 2.70 s 1.17 m
That drops 44.4 – 97.5 s (53.1 s) and keeps 52.9 s, 31% of the source. Widen the handles if you want it longer, but don't pad back toward the lull. One fighter covers noticeably more floor than the other (91.5 m against 78.3 m): the more mobile fighter is characterisation you get for free, so favour it when you pick shots.
3 Cut it — as data
A cut here is not a re-bake. It is an edit list: eight spans stored on the timeline, a few hundred bytes. The captured clips are only ever read.
sparring.splice([ [1.6, 9.0], [14.6, 22.1], [30.8, 44.4], [97.5, 103.4], [104.8, 110.8], [113.7, 117.6], [134.7, 140.6], [158.4, 161.1], ].map(([from, to]) => ({ from, to })), { blend: 0.25 }); sparring.asCommand(); // the declarative form of this cut sparring.table(); // each span with its start and length on the new clock
The blend is mandatory. Over a 0.25 s window at every cut, each rotation is slerped from the outgoing pose to the incoming one, and the floor position is offset so the pair's centre continues from where it was — otherwise the bodies pop or teleport at every join. That offset is computed from the pair's centre and applied to both fighters, so how far apart they stand survives the cut.
Why you can't edit one fighter alone. $S('#f1').play('st1_1072026Skeleton', { from: 1, to: 5 }) is refused, because it would desynchronise the pair. Per-fighter timing (timeOffset, speedOf) needs an explicit sparring.breakRegistration(), which warns what you lose (they can clip through each other) and is undoable.
4 Check every frame
No renderer will tell you the fighters now overlap. The collision report runs over the edited timeline:
const report = sparring.collision(); report.min; // 0.741 report.ok; // true: no span under 0.6 m report.spans; // the closest approach inside each span
The cut's closest approach, 0.74 m, is a little closer than the capture's own 0.80 m, and it sits at the start of E07 (44.4 s on the new clock), inside the blend window. The blend interpolates both fighters' positions, so it can bring them nearer than either source span does; that is exactly the sort of thing this check exists to catch. If a span ever reports under 0.6 m, widen the blend or move the cut point.
5 Put the cameras on the new timeline
The four cameras' keys, and the Render tab's 37-shot sequence, were cut against the 170 s source. remapShots() moves the camera keys: an event that lies wholly inside one kept span is moved to the cut's clock; anything else is dropped and reported.
const r = sparring.remapShots(); r.kept; r.dropped; // 396 kept, 964 dropped (the keys that straddle a cut or fall in the lull) editor.timeline.toJSON().duration; // 52.9
The Camera Sequence in the Render tab is a separate list of which camera is live when. Move it onto the same clock: for each span, the shot that was live when the span began opens it, and any shot that began inside the span moves with it.
(async () => { const { edlTable } = await import('./intelligence/motionEdit.js'); const g = editor.timeline.group('sparring'); const spans = edlTable(g.edl).filter(r => !r.hold); const shots = scene.userData.renderShots.slice().sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at); const next = new Map(); for (const r of spans) { const open = shots.filter(s => s.at <= r.from).pop(); // the shot live as the span begins if (open) next.set(+r.outStart.toFixed(3), { ...open, at: +r.outStart.toFixed(3) }); for (const s of shots) if (s.at > r.from && s.at < r.to) { const at = +(r.outStart + (s.at - r.from) / r.speed).toFixed(3); next.set(at, { ...s, at }); } } scene.userData.renderShots = [...next.values()].sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at).map((s, i) => ({ ...s, id: 'shot-' + i })); })();
The Shell does not print what an async block returns; check scene.userData.renderShots.length afterwards (37 shots become 18, the last at 50.2 s). This block assigns the list directly, so it is not on the undo stack; to go back, reload the scene or re-run the shot list from the dojo tutorial. Open the Render tab to see the sequence on the 52.9 s timeline.
6 Give them somewhere to look
Two people watching each other for 53 seconds: most of the acting is where they look, and not looking dead. Both are timeline data. A gaze key whose target is a selector follows that fighter as they move; the eyes lead and the head lags, and past the eyes' range the head takes over, so there are no doll eyes.
const A = $S('#f1'), B = $S('#f2'); A.gaze(0, '#f2', { duration: 0 }); B.gaze(0, '#f1', { duration: 0 }); // a look away and back between exchanges (times on the cut's clock) for (const t of [6.4, 14.2, 28, 34.4, 40.2, 44.1]) A.gaze(t, 'away', { duration: 250, head: 0.2 }).gaze(t + 0.9, '#f2', { duration: 300 }); for (const t of [6.9, 14.7, 28.6, 34.9, 40.6, 44.6]) B.gaze(t, 'away', { duration: 250, head: 0.2 }).gaze(t + 0.9, '#f1', { duration: 300 });
Measured on this cut: wherever the other fighter is inside the eyes' range, the eyes sit within about 1° of their head, and sampling both faces costs about 0.6 ms per frame. Then add the idle layer:
A.face.idle({ seed: 11 }); // a seeded blink, a faint breath, a little gaze micro-noise B.face.idle({ seed: 12 });
The idle layer is seeded — the same scene renders the same blinks on every run — and it is an underlayer: it never becomes keys, A.face.idle(false) removes it, and the keys you authored are untouched. A held expression (hold: true) keeps blinks out of it. The same keys are in the Customize tab (Face performance) and the Animations tab's code panel; see Authoring a face for expression keys and the details.
7 Dress them, and let the faces act
Captured bodies carry no performance in their faces, and the two fighters arrive in unrelated clothes. Three passes fix that: costume, an expression arc that follows the exchanges, and light and camera to match. None of it touches a vertex, a skin weight or the skeleton, so the capture still drives both rigs exactly.
Costume. One fighter becomes a black gi, the other a white gi, both barefoot, so they read apart from any camera:
(async () => { const { CustomizeCommand } = await import('./commands/CustomizeCommand.js'); const dress = (id, top, bottom, name) => editor.execute(new CustomizeCommand(editor, editor.scene.getObjectByName(id), [ { op: 'recolor', target: 'part:shirt', color: top }, { op: 'recolor', target: 'part:bottom', color: bottom }, { op: 'hide', target: 'part:shoes' }, ], name)); dress('f1', '#262833', '#1c1d26', 'f1: black gi, barefoot'); dress('f2', '#ece7dc', '#e2dccd', 'f2: white gi, barefoot'); })();
An expression arc. Faces change over time, and every change is a key you can see and move in the Animations tab (and edit from Customize → Face performance). Three held looks carry the whole piece — focus at rest, exert for whoever is attacking, alert for whoever is defending — switched per exchange. Times are on the cut's clock, so each exchange starts where sparring.table() says it does:
const A = $S('#f1'), B = $S('#f2'); const base = { browInnerUp: 0, eyeWideLeft: 0, eyeWideRight: 0, mouthSmileLeft: 0, mouthSmileRight: 0, mouthFrownLeft: 0, mouthFrownRight: 0, jawOpen: 0 }; const LOOK = { focus: { ...base, browDownLeft: 0.2, browDownRight: 0.2, eyeSquintLeft: 0.12, eyeSquintRight: 0.12, mouthPressLeft: 0.18, mouthPressRight: 0.18 }, exert: { ...base, browDownLeft: 0.45, browDownRight: 0.45, eyeSquintLeft: 0.3, eyeSquintRight: 0.3, mouthPressLeft: 0.35, mouthPressRight: 0.35, mouthFrownLeft: 0.12, mouthFrownRight: 0.12, jawOpen: 0.04 }, alert: { ...base, browDownLeft: 0.05, browDownRight: 0.05, browInnerUp: 0.28, eyeWideLeft: 0.2, eyeWideRight: 0.2, mouthPressLeft: 0.15, mouthPressRight: 0.15 }, }; const look = (who, name, t, ms = 400) => who.face.keyAt(t, { shapes: { ...LOOK.focus, ...LOOK[name] }, duration: ms, easing: 'ease-out', hold: true }); A.face.keyAt(0, { shapes: LOOK.focus, duration: 0, hold: true }); B.face.keyAt(0, { shapes: LOOK.focus, duration: 0, hold: true }); // [start, length, who leads] for each span, on the cut's clock const rounds = [[0, 7.4, A], [7.4, 7.5, A], [14.9, 13.6, A], [28.5, 5.9, A], [34.4, 6.0, B], [40.4, 3.9, A], [44.3, 5.9, A], [50.2, 2.7, 'both']]; for (const [t, len, lead] of rounds) { const att = lead === 'both' ? [A, B] : [lead], def = lead === 'both' ? [] : [lead === A ? B : A]; att.forEach(f => look(f, 'exert', t + 0.2)); def.forEach(f => look(f, 'alert', t + 0.2)); [A, B].forEach(f => look(f, 'focus', t + len + 0.8, 600)); // settle between exchanges } // the closest approach (E03): the defender flinches, then recovers B.face.applyPreset('surprise', 20.5, { duration: 150 }); look(B, 'alert', 22.7, 500);
Presets expand to explicit per-shape keys, so a flinch like surprise is just more keys. The cut removes the long lull, so the quiet beat that follows it in the uncut capture is gone; to end on a bow, finish with a held smile once the last exchange lands: A.face.applyPreset('smile', 52.1, { duration: 600, hold: true }) on both fighters, then A.gaze(52.4, 'away', { duration: 400 }). The step 6 gaze keys and idle layer sit underneath all of this unchanged.
The committed scene. sparring.json in the repository carries this look on the uncut capture, so its expression keys are on the source clock (the eight spans start at 1.6, 14.6, 30.8, 97.5, 104.8, 113.7, 134.7 and 158.4 s). If you cut the scene as in step 3, use the cut-clock times above.
Light and camera. Use the same pass as the dojo: sky fill 0.85 → 0.6, sun key → 3.1, cool rim → 1.2, fog density → 0.02 (the commands are in Build the dojo scene, step 10), then bring the wide camera in. This keeps each wide shot's look direction and just moves the camera closer and lower:
(async () => { const { editCameraTrack } = await import('./intelligence/cameraMoveEdit.js'); const cam = editor.scene.getObjectByName('cam-wide'); editCameraTrack(editor, cam, 'Camera: tighten cam-wide', track => { for (const ev of track.events) { const p = ev.args.props; if (ev.op !== 'animate' || !p?.to?.position) continue; const L = p.lookAt, q = p.to.position; p.to.position = [L[0] + (q[0] - L[0]) * 0.9, 1.7, L[2] + (q[2] - L[2]) * 0.9]; // 10% closer, eye-level-ish p.lookAt = [L[0], 1.02, L[2]]; p.fov = 38; // was 42 } }); })();
Run it once (it is not idempotent), and then repeat the step 4 frame check — a tighter lens is exactly what pushes a fighter's hand or foot out of frame. On this capture, every wide-shot frame at 16:9 still holds both fighters' head, hips, hands and feet.
8 Render it and save
Press Play in the Animations tab: the timeline is 52.9 s, both fighters move, the cameras cut, and the eyes follow. Open the Render tab and render the camera sequence to video. Keep the tab in the foreground while it renders — browsers throttle hidden tabs, which makes frames stall. In the Git tab, set Scene file to a new name such as sparring-cut.json and press Commit Scene. The scene is saved compactly (one line, animation numbers quantized), and what is stored is the full capture plus the edit list, the camera keys and the face keys. sparring.json itself stays the uncut capture. Undo, or sparring.clear(), brings back the full 170.17 s capture exactly — the clips were never modified.
Honest limits. A cut is built from what was captured: it can drop, join and re-time, but it cannot invent a contact that was never there. The shot-remap blocks drop camera keys that straddle a cut, so look through the result before you render. The eyes' gaze on a moving target is exact where the geometry allows it and is clamped to a believable range where it does not.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Pavan Turaga (asset) Assegid Kidane (asset) Assets Sparring capture: clips st1_1072026Skeleton and st2_1072026Skeleton (170.17 s): Recorded with an OptiTrack system in "Martial Arts and Motion Capture" (GAME 294), Arizona State University; course run by Pavan Turaga, recorded by Assegid Kidane; the two performers are not named Licence: not stated. Tools None used.

posts.title: One dance, two characters
posts.text:
One dance, two characters
All tutorials
Two dancers on a blank white stage — a construct, if you like. Bruce starts a dance; The Boss picks it up three seconds later and copies it move for move, while a camera swings around so you see their faces for most of it. The characters are rigged and animated outside Strata with bodyrig-webCLI — it retargets one motion onto any skeleton and writes a single GLB with the animation baked in — then Strata stages and renders them. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
Two different sources, one pipeline. The two dancers come from completely different places: The Boss is a Mixamo .fbx (a mixamorig skeleton in centimetres, T-pose), and Bruce is a MetaHuman .glb (a ~1,200-bone rig in metres, A-pose, with 51 face blendshapes). bodyrig-webCLI maps one motion file onto both skeletons and writes a plain GLB for each, so Strata imports them natively — through the ordinary Import dialog, with no plug-in, converter or per-character setup — and they arrive with the same clip name and length, ready for the same $S() timeline grammar.
What you'll need. A free Mixamo account (an Adobe ID) for The Boss, a browser for bodyrig-webCLI (it runs entirely in the page — nothing is uploaded), and Bruce, a MetaHuman exported by creategamecharacters/metahuman-to-glb (see Make your own MetaHuman for what that project is). The pieces are free, but the characters keep their own terms: Mixamo's characters belong to Adobe and are not meant to be re-hosted, so this tutorial never asks you to commit the Boss file anywhere public.
1 Download The Boss from Mixamo
The Boss is a stock Mixamo character, so he comes with the standard mixamorig skeleton that bodyrig-webCLI already knows how to map.
Go to mixamo.com and sign in with your Adobe ID (free). Open the Characters tab and pick The Boss. Press Download. Choose format FBX Binary (.fbx) and pose T-pose, then download and save the file as boss.fbx.
Mixamo's menus change from time to time, so the labels above may read a little differently — what matters is the character as a rigged .fbx in a T-pose.
Want a different dance? You don't have to use Mixamo's motions. bodyrig-webCLI accepts BVH, FBX or GLB for the animation, and it ships a 33-second sample, mocap-33s.bvh, that this tutorial uses. If you'd rather pick one from Mixamo, open its Animations tab, choose a dance, and download it as FBX with skin set to Without Skin; the tool reads animation-only FBX files too.
2 Get Bruce
Bruce is already a GLB, hosted by the metahuman-to-glb demo. Save it from your browser or with curl (it is about 80 MB):
curl -L -o bruce.glb https://creategamecharacters.github.io/metahuman-to-glb/5.7/characters/bruce/bruce.glb
3 Bake the dance onto both with bodyrig-webCLI
Open tejaswigowda.com/bodyrig-webCLI (or clone the repo and run npm start for a local copy at http://127.0.0.1:8010). It is a static page: the badge in the header reads 100% local · zero egress, and you can confirm in DevTools' Network tab that your files never leave the machine.
Drop boss.fbx on the Character zone, and mocap-33s.bvh on Animation tracks. Both appear as chips (the motion reports its joint count and duration). The page bakes as soon as it has a character and a motion; the status bar ends with Done: boss_mocap-33s.glb and a live preview plays. To re-bake after changing an option, press Bake & export GLB. Press Download GLB to save boss_mocap-33s.glb. Swap the character: click the × on its chip, drop bruce.glb instead (leave the same motion loaded), and download bruce_mocap-33s.glb the same way.
bodyrig-webCLI after baking Bruce: character and motion chips on the left, the finished GLB playing in the preview on the right.
Because both characters were baked from the same motion file, they are two different sources mapped natively into Strata by one tool: the animation clip in each GLB has the same name, mocap-33s, and the same 33.1-second length — which is exactly what lets The Boss copy Bruce later with a plain time offset.
It's a CLI in a page. Every control is just a command in the box under Command: after dropping the files, bake --fps 30 is what the button runs. Useful flags are --foot-lock (pin planted feet with IK), --loop (close the cycle), --in-place and --trim 2:20 (seconds). Run help to see them all. For a MetaHuman, leave Align reference pose ticked — it is what makes the A-pose Bruce and the T-pose Boss follow the same motion.
Skip the dragging for Bruce. The tool also reads a deep link, so you can bake him straight from his URL: http://tejaswigowda.com/bodyrig-webCLI/?character=<bruce URL>&motion=<motion URL>&run=bake (URL-encode the two values). Add --hide Outfits to the command to leave the clothes out of the bake if you only want the bare body.
The GLBs are meshopt-compressed to keep them small (Bruce comes out near 39 MB, down from about 80 MB). Strata's loader already includes the meshopt decoder, so nothing extra is needed; tick off Meshopt compress only if you plan to open the file in a tool that lacks it.
4 Import both into Strata
Use File → Import (or drag both files onto the editor window). A progress banner tracks each file while it is read and parsed. When the Import glTF dialog appears, leave the compression options off — Strata skips mesh simplification on skinned and morph-target meshes anyway, and rigged characters don't benefit from it — and press OK.
Then check what arrived in the Shell:
scene.children.map(o => o.name); // ['bruce_mocap-33s.glb', 'boss_mocap-33s.glb'] scene.animations.map(a => a.name); // ['mocap-33s', 'mocap-33s']
Give them short names to address them by, and measure each character so you know whether the scale is sane. Strata normalizes each import (it centres and grounds the model, and rescales a centimetre-unit Mixamo rig by ×0.01), so both should come in close to 2 m. Each shell command runs in its own scope, so look the characters up again in every block that needs them:
const bruce = scene.children.find(o => o.name.startsWith('bruce')); const boss = scene.children.find(o => o.name.startsWith('boss')); relabel(bruce, 'bruce'); // Bruce becomes #bruce relabel(boss, 'boss'); // The Boss becomes #boss const height = o => new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(o).getSize(new THREE.Vector3()).y; [height(bruce).toFixed(2), height(boss).toFixed(2)] // about 2 m each
If one is off, scale his group so he stands about as tall as Bruce — one command, undoable:
const boss = scene.children.find(o => o.name.startsWith('boss')); const k = 1.8 / new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(boss).getSize(new THREE.Vector3()).y; editor.execute(new SetScaleCommand(editor, boss, boss.scale.clone().multiplyScalar(k)));
5 Stage the two dancers
Both characters were baked at the origin, so they would dance inside each other. Slide The Boss 2.8 m to the side:
const boss = scene.children.find(o => o.name.startsWith('boss')); editor.execute(new SetPositionCommand(editor, boss, new THREE.Vector3(2.8, 0, 0)));
6 Build a blank white stage
The stage is a featureless white void: a white background that the floor fades into, light fog to soften the horizon, a glossy white floor for a faint reflection, and two lights.
scene.background = new THREE.Color(0xffffff); scene.fog = new THREE.Fog(0xffffff, 14, 55); const floor = new Mesh(new PlaneGeometry(200, 200), new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff, roughness: 0.12, metalness: 0.1 })); floor.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; floor.receiveShadow = true; floor.name = 'Floor'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, floor)); const sky = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xffffff, 0xdddddd, 1.6); sky.name = 'Sky'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, sky)); const key = new DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 2.2); key.position.set(4, 8, 5); key.castShadow = true; key.name = 'Key'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, key));
The environment setting. If the void looks grey rather than white, check the Scene tab: Background and Environment can override what you set in code (see Build a night scene from scratch for the same trap).
7 Play the dance: Bruce leads, The Boss follows
Each imported clip is bound to its own character, so two clips can share a name without clashing — the selector decides whose clip plays. Put Bruce's on the Universal Timeline at 0 s and the Boss's at 3 s:
$S('#bruce').at(0).play('mocap-33s'); $S('#boss').at(3).play('mocap-33s');
Open the Animations tab and scrub: Bruce starts moving at once, The Boss begins three seconds in and repeats the same moves. The whole timeline is 36.1 seconds — the 33.1-second dance plus the Boss's 3-second head start.
Why bake the same motion twice? You could retarget live in the page, but a baked clip is plain keyframe data: it is versioned with the scene, selectable by $S, and rendered identically every time. Retargeting per character is the part that needs a tool; sequencing and staging is what Strata is for.
8 Add a camera that orbits the dancers
A static shot from the wrong side shows the back of both heads for most of the song. First, find which way the dance faces: at the playhead around 10 s, orbit the viewport until you see their faces. For the sample motion they face about 150° away from +Z, toward −Z and slightly +X. Build a camera clip that stays on that side and drifts ±35° around it with a slow push-in, keyed every half second:
const cam = new PerspectiveCamera(35, 16 / 9, 0.5, 60); // tight near/far = more depth precision cam.name = 'Orbit Camera'; editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, cam)); relabel(cam, 'orbit-camera'); // A camera helper that does the aiming for us. Object3D.lookAt points +Z at the // target; a camera looks down -Z, so use a camera, not a bare Object3D. const rig = new PerspectiveCamera(); const center = new THREE.Vector3(1.7, 1.0, 0.7); // between the two dancers const times = [], pos = [], quat = []; for (let t = 0; t <= 33; t += 0.5) { const az = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(150 + 35 * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * t / 33)); const r = 8.5 - Math.sin(Math.PI * t / 33); // push in, then ease out rig.position.set(center.x + r * Math.sin(az), 1.45, center.z + r * Math.cos(az)); rig.lookAt(center); times.push(t); pos.push(...rig.position.toArray()); quat.push(...rig.quaternion.toArray()); } addClip(scene, new THREE.AnimationClip('camera-orbit', 33, [ new THREE.VectorKeyframeTrack(cam.uuid + '.position', times, pos), new THREE.QuaternionKeyframeTrack(cam.uuid + '.quaternion', times, quat), ])); $S('#orbit-camera').at(0).play('camera-orbit');
Track names must be <object uuid>.<property>, which is why the clip is built from cam.uuid. If your dancers face another way, change the 150 (degrees from +Z) and check a few frames with holdTimelineAt:
const { holdTimelineAt } = await import('./editor/js/intelligence/timelineController.js'); holdTimelineAt(editor, 16); // jump the whole scene to t = 16 s editor.viewportCamera = cam; // look through the new camera editor.signals.viewportCameraChanged.dispatch();
Flickering clothes (z-fighting). A garment that hugs the body sits almost exactly on the skin under it, and for some frames of the dance the two surfaces tie in the depth buffer, so patches of skin show through the cloth. Two fixes, both already in this tutorial: keep the camera's near/far range tight (0.5–60 above, not 0.01–1000 — depth precision is spent mostly near the camera, and the ratio far/near is what matters), and push the layer underneath slightly back with a polygon offset. Bruce's outfit sits on his body mesh the same way, so if you see flicker on him, apply the same offset to his body mesh. The Boss's clothes are separate meshes (jacket, pants, shoes…), so list his meshes first, then offset whichever one is showing through: const boss = scene.children.find(o => o.name.startsWith('boss')); const names = []; boss.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) names.push(o.name); }); names; // pick the mesh that is poking through const mesh = boss.getObjectByName(names[0]); // replace names[0] with that name mesh.material = mesh.material.clone(); // never edit a material that has already rendered Object.assign(mesh.material, { polygonOffset: true, polygonOffsetFactor: 2, polygonOffsetUnits: 4 }); If a gap remains, raise the factor; if skin starts to poke through a layer that should be under it, you pushed the wrong one.
9 Render it
Open the Render tab. The Snapshot section saves the scene exactly as it is right now, with no grid or gizmos: hold the timeline at a moment you like (holdTimelineAt(editor, 16)), pick Orbit Camera and a size, and press Take Snapshot. For the video, scroll to Video Render. With no Camera Sequence shots, the render uses the viewport camera, so add one shot at 0 s pointing at Orbit Camera (+ Add Shot, then choose the camera). Pick 1280 × 720 at 30 fps and press Render & Export. The whole 36.1-second timeline renders; expect it to take about as long as the clip itself. Keep the tab in the foreground while it renders — browsers throttle hidden tabs, which makes frames stall.
To keep the scene, set your repository and token in the Git tab and use Commit Scene. The characters and their baked clips are stored as binary asset files next to a small scene JSON, so the commit is large but not unmanageable (a few dozen megabytes for this scene).
// Sanity-check what you're about to commit $S('#bruce').count(); // 1 editor.timeline.toJSON().tracks.map(t => t.target); // ['#bruce', '#boss', '#orbit-camera']
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets The Boss (Mixamo character, .fbx): Mixamo, Adobe Licence: Adobe Mixamo terms (free with an Adobe ID). Bruce (MetaHuman sample .glb): creategamecharacters, metahuman-to-glb; MetaHuman by Epic Games Licence: not stated for the character (the pipeline code is MIT); a MetaHuman is an Epic Games asset. mocap-33s.bvh (bodyrig-webCLI sample motion): bodyrig-webCLI sample motion (the page does not say who captured it) Licence: not stated (bodyrig-webCLI is GPL-3.0; the sample motion has no terms of its own). Tools bodyrig-webCLI (GPL-3.0) metahuman-to-glb (MIT) meshoptimizer (MIT) Mixamo (Adobe Mixamo terms (free with an Adobe ID))

posts.title: Restyle a VRM into an explorer with the JS Shell
posts.text:
Restyle a VRM into an explorer with the JS Shell
All tutorials
A .vrm is a glTF binary with a humanoid skeleton and a set of facial blendshapes — which means Strata imports it like any other rigged GLB. This tutorial takes the free female base model from hinzka/52blendshapes-for-VRoid-face and restyles it as a generic ruins-exploring expedition explorer using nothing but the JS Shell: auburn hair and a tan, a sage-green crop top and sand shorts cut out of the existing clothes, a belt, a satchel, a canteen, wristbands and a headband attached to the skeleton, lowered arms and a smirk. The target is an original archetype, not a particular character — the same steps restyle the base model into anything you can describe. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order.
The result of this tutorial — the VRoid base model after every block below, with the skeleton helpers hidden.
About the model. The repository's README says the VRM files may be used freely, personal or commercial, redistributed or sold, with no credit required. The female model is VRoid_V110_Female_v1.1.3.vrm (about 23 MB); the male one sits next to it. These steps use the female model's measurements — heights in metres, taken from its skeleton — so they won't line up on the male one without adjusting the numbers.
1 Download and import the VRM
Open the repository, download VRoid_V110_Female_v1.1.3.vrm (use the Download raw file button on its page, or clone the repo), then bring it into the editor either way:
Press the Import icon in the top bar and choose the .vrm file, or drag the file onto the editor window. A progress banner shows reading, then parsing, and then the Import glTF dialog appears. Leave the defaults and click OK. Don't turn on geometry compression for a rigged character: Strata skips mesh simplification for skinned meshes and ones with morph targets, so it would do nothing useful here.
Which way does she face? VRM 0.x models are authored facing −Z, the opposite of the editor's front view. Strata turns a 0.x VRM 180° around Y on import so the model faces the front camera; you'll see Rotation Y = 180° on the imported group in the Object panel. Everything below is written in world coordinates, so that turn doesn't change any of the numbers.
2 See what you imported
The shell runs every command in its own scope, so a const from one block is gone in the next. Anything you want to keep goes on window. Start with two handles: R, the imported model, and B, which finds one of the VRM humanoid bones by its short name (C_Hips, L_Hand, R_UpperLeg…). Then list the material names — they are how you'll address each part:
window.R = scene.children.find(o => o.name.endsWith('.vrm')); window.B = name => R.getObjectByName('J_Bip_' + name); const mats = new Set(); R.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) [].concat(o.material).forEach(m => mats.add(m.name)); }); [...mats]
Fourteen materials come back — …Face_00_SKIN, …Body_00_SKIN, …EyeIris_00_EYE, …FaceBrow_00_FACE, …HairBack_00_HAIR, …Hair_00_HAIR, and the three clothing pieces …Tops_01_CLOTH, …Bottoms_01_CLOTH and …Shoes_01_CLOTH. The face meshes carry the blendshapes:
const face = R.getObjectByName('Face').children.find(o => o.morphTargetDictionary); const shapes = Object.keys(face.morphTargetDictionary); shapes.length + ' shapes, ' + shapes.filter(n => /^[a-z]/.test(n)).length + ' of them ARKit (' + shapes.find(n => /^[a-z]/.test(n)) + '…)'
That prints 124 shapes, 52 of them ARKit (browInnerUp…): the VRM Fcl_… presets first, then the 52 ARKit shapes this model is known for (browInnerUp, jawOpen, mouthSmileLeft…), then a few underscore-prefixed helper shapes.
3 Recolor hair, skin and clothes
These materials are textured, so setting a color tints the texture (the color multiplies the map) rather than replacing it. That's what you want for skin and hair — the shading and the face detail survive. A tiny helper applies a color to every material whose name matches a pattern:
window.tint = (re, hex) => R.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) [].concat(o.material).forEach(m => { if (re.test(m.name)) m.color.set(hex); }); }); tint(/HAIR/, 0x6e3216); // auburn hair tint(/SKIN/, 0xeabf9c); // warm tan, face and body together tint(/Tops/, 0x5f7f5a); // sage green tint(/Shoes/, 0x4a3320); // brown boots tint(/EyeIris/, 0x6a4a2a); // brown eyes tint(/Brow|Eyelash|Eyeline/, 0x3a1d0f); 'tinted'
The viewport redraws on demand, so if nothing seems to change, move the mouse over it or orbit a little. The original hair is pale grey and the original shirt is white, so both pick up the new colors cleanly; the black trousers can't be tinted at all, which is why the next step replaces their texture.
4 Cut a crop top and shorts
The clothes are one mesh per garment, so a new silhouette is a matter of deleting the triangles you don't want. cutBelow(mesh, y) keeps only the triangles whose centre is above a world height, then pushes any vertices still below that height up onto it so the hem is flat. It uses applyBoneTransform to find where each vertex really is on the posed skeleton, and it works on a clone of the geometry so nothing else sharing the original is touched:
window.cutBelow = (mesh, y) => { mesh.updateMatrixWorld(true); const g = mesh.geometry.clone(), pos = g.attributes.position, idx = g.index.array; const wy = new Float32Array(pos.count), v = new THREE.Vector3(); for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) { v.fromBufferAttribute(pos, i); mesh.applyBoneTransform(i, v); // where the skinned vertex really is wy[i] = v.applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld).y; } const keep = []; for (let i = 0; i < idx.length; i += 3) if ((wy[idx[i]] + wy[idx[i + 1]] + wy[idx[i + 2]]) / 3 >= y) keep.push(idx[i], idx[i + 1], idx[i + 2]); for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) if (wy[i] < y) pos.setY(i, pos.getY(i) + y - wy[i]); // flatten the hem g.setIndex(keep); g.computeBoundingSphere(); mesh.geometry = g; }; R.traverse(o => { if (!o.isMesh) return; const m = [].concat(o.material)[0]; if (/Bottoms/.test(m.name)) { cutBelow(o, 0.7); m.map = null; m.alphaTest = 0; m.color.set(0xb9a273); } if (/Tops/.test(m.name)) cutBelow(o, 1.03); }); 'cut'
Heights are in metres from the floor: 0.7 is the upper thigh, 1.03 is under the ribs. The trousers get a flat brown color instead of the tint, because the original texture is dark and a dark texture times brown is still dark — and its transparency cut-out (alphaTest) was what made them capri length, so that goes too.
Two honest limitations. The hems come out a little ragged, because the triangles are big and a straight cut through them can't be perfectly clean; the belt in the next step hides the top edge of the shorts, but the bottom hem stays rough. And the base model has no torso under its clothes — the area is a black patch in the texture — so the next step adds a skin-colored band to stand in for the bare midriff.
5 Strap on the gear
The gear is plain three.js primitives parented to bones, so it follows the skeleton when the character moves. prop builds a mesh, places it using world coordinates, then calls bone.attach(mesh), which re-parents it while keeping that world placement. Every position below comes from the bone positions of this model — hips at y ≈ 0.91, hands at x ≈ ±0.54:
window.prop = (bone, geo, hex, pos, o = {}) => { const m = new THREE.Mesh(geo, new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: hex, roughness: o.rough ?? 0.7, metalness: o.metal ?? 0, side: THREE.DoubleSide })); m.name = o.name; m.position.set(...pos); if (o.rot) m.rotation.set(...o.rot); if (o.scale) m.scale.set(...o.scale); scene.add(m); // place it in world coordinates… scene.updateMatrixWorld(true); B(bone).attach(m); // …then parent it to the bone, keeping that placement return m; }; 'prop helper ready'
Now the gear itself: a skin-colored midriff band, a belt with a buckle, a satchel on the left hip and a canteen on the right, a leather wristband on each arm, and a red headband. The for loop runs once for each arm by flipping the sign of x:
const leather = 0x2a1b10, tan = 0x8b6a3e, steel = 0x8b8f94, skin = 0xeabf9c; prop('C_Spine', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.104, 0.108, 0.13, 28, 1, true), skin, [0, 0.99, 0.07], { scale: [1, 1, 0.8], name: 'midriff' }); prop('C_Hips', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.15, 0.15, 0.04, 28, 1, true), leather, [0, 0.935, 0.035], { scale: [1, 1, 0.78], name: 'belt' }); prop('C_Hips', new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.05, 0.035, 0.02), steel, [0, 0.935, 0.155], { metal: 0.8, rough: 0.35, name: 'buckle' }); prop('C_Hips', new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.06, 0.12, 0.14), tan, [0.18, 0.84, 0.03], { name: 'satchel' }); prop('C_Hips', new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.065, 0.03, 0.15), leather, [0.18, 0.9, 0.03], { name: 'satchel-flap' }); prop('C_Hips', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.04, 0.04, 0.11, 20), 0x4f6b4a, [-0.18, 0.84, 0.03], { rough: 0.5, name: 'canteen' }); for (const s of [1, -1]) prop((s > 0 ? 'L' : 'R') + '_LowerArm', new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.03, 0.03, 0.04, 16, 1, true), leather, [s * 0.5, 1.262, 0.013], { rot: [0, 0, Math.PI / 2], name: 'wristband' }); prop('C_Head', new THREE.TorusGeometry(0.1, 0.011, 8, 36), 0xa63d2a, [0, 1.47, 0], { rot: [Math.PI / 2, 0, 0], scale: [1, 1.15, 1], name: 'headband' }); 'gear on'
The model faces +Z in world space, so positive z is the front of the body (the buckle) and negative z is the back. L_ bones are on the character's left, which is world +X from the front — so the satchel is on her left hip and the canteen on her right.
Lit character, lit props. A VRM imports unlit (flat colour, ignoring lights) and the props above are ordinary PBR. To put everything under one light-responsive shading model, run toon(R) in the Shell: the character and the props become hard-banded toon with outlines, using the toon values stored in the VRM file. If the scene has no light, it adds a key and a sky light, since toon needs light to show. See the toon look guide for the options (shade colour, rim, outline width).
6 Lower the arms and pose a smirk
VRM models import in a T-pose. Rotating the two upper-arm bones about their local Z lowers the arms — the signs are opposite because the left and right bones mirror each other:
B('L_UpperArm').rotation.z = 1.2; B('R_UpperArm').rotation.z = -1.2; 'arms down'
For the face, a helper sets a blendshape on every mesh that has it (the face is split across nine meshes that share the same shape list), by name:
window.express = (shape, value) => R.traverse(o => { const i = o.morphTargetDictionary?.[shape]; if (i !== undefined) o.morphTargetInfluences[i] = value; }); express('mouthSmileLeft', 0.45); express('mouthSmileRight', 0.45); express('browInnerUp', 0.15); 'smirk'
Other shapes worth trying: jawOpen, eyeBlinkLeft / eyeBlinkRight, mouthPucker, browDownLeft, eyeLookUpLeft, or the VRM presets Fcl_ALL_Joy and Fcl_ALL_Surprised. They're ordinary morph target influences, so the Universal Timeline can keyframe them like any other number.
7 Frame the shot and take a snapshot
Move the viewport camera to a full-length view, and tell the orbit controls the same target so the next mouse drag pivots around her waist:
camera.position.set(0.5, 1.0, 2.2); camera.lookAt(0, 0.85, 0); editor.controls.center.set(0, 0.85, 0); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(camera); 'framed'
Click the skeleton icon in the top bar (Hide Skeleton Helpers) to turn off the green bone lines, then open the Render tab. The Snapshot section renders the scene once, offscreen, with no grid, gizmos or helpers: pick Current view, a size, PNG, and press Take Snapshot. Tick Transparent for a cut-out with no background.
Why this isn't a Customize-tab job. The Customize tab guarantees that a look change never touches the rig: no vertex, skin-weight or skeleton edits. The crop top and shorts here delete triangles and move vertices, and the arm pose rotates bones, so those steps are deliberately outside that guarantee — they are hand edits. The rest (tinting, bone-attached accessories, blendshape poses) is the kind of change the Customize tab does itself; see Make your own MetaHuman.
8 Save it
Everything above is ordinary scene state — geometry, materials, bone rotations, parented props, morph influences — so a normal commit captures it. Set your repository and token in the Git tab, then use Commit Scene. A quick sanity check before you commit:
[R.getObjectByName('belt') !== undefined, B('L_UpperArm').rotation.z, scene.getObjectByName('headband').parent.name]
That should print [true, 1.2, "J_Bip_C_Head"] — the belt exists, the arm is lowered, and the headband is parented to the head bone.
Credits and licences People Tejaswi Gowda (script) Assets VRoid_V110_Female_v1.1.3.vrm: hinzka, 52blendshapes-for-VRoid-face (credit is not required; given anyway) Licence: Custom terms in the repository README: free personal and commercial use, redistribution allowed, no credit required (no licence file). Tools None used.

posts.title: Build a wizard hat and sculpt a face into it
posts.text:
Build a wizard hat and sculpt a face into it
All tutorials
Two ideas in one scene. First, a floppy purple hat assembled from primitives — a lathe-turned brim, a three-section cone that bends, a band, a buckle and extruded stars. Then the part that is not a texture: a smiley face sculpted into the cone by pushing a dense mesh's surface outward along its normals, as one undoable step. Open the editor, open the Shell tab, and paste each block in order — or open the finished hat, hat.json (step 7).
The finished hat: lathe brim, bending cone, band and buckle, stars — and a relief smiley sculpted into the front.
Pasting long blocks into the Shell: if Enter seems to do nothing after a long paste, press Esc first (it closes the autocomplete dropdown that was swallowing the keypress), then Enter. On a non-empty scene, run clearScene() first.
1 Materials and the brim
Three materials: the purple everywhere, a darker purple for the band and gold for the buckle and stars. A fourth, jointMat, is the same purple with a polygon offset — step 2 explains why. The brim is a LatheGeometry: one 2D profile (radius, height) spun around the y axis. The profile runs out along the underside, up the curled rim, and back along the top, so the brim has thickness and an upturned edge from a single list of points:
const purple = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6a2bb8, roughness: 0.65, side: THREE.DoubleSide }); const bandMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2e1260, roughness: 0.5 }); const gold = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffd54a, roughness: 0.3, metalness: 0.7, emissive: 0x3a2a00 }); // Same purple, pushed back in depth so it never z-fights the cone walls it overlaps const jointMat = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x6a2bb8, roughness: 0.65, side: THREE.DoubleSide, polygonOffset: true, polygonOffsetFactor: 8, polygonOffsetUnits: 8 }); const hat = new Group(); hat.name = 'Wizard Hat'; // Brim: a lathe profile that dips, then curls up at the rim (out along the underside, back along the top) const brimProfile = [[0.85,0.02],[1.2,0.0],[1.7,-0.02],[2.05,0.04],[2.2,0.14],[2.2,0.18],[2.15,0.19],[2.0,0.1],[1.7,0.05],[1.2,0.06],[0.85,0.08]].map(p => new THREE.Vector2(p[0], p[1])); const brim = new Mesh(new LatheGeometry(brimProfile, 64), purple); brim.name = 'Brim'; hat.add(brim);
2 The cone: three sections that bend
A single cone cannot flop over, so build it in three tapering sections. Each section is a Group parented to the top of the previous one and rotated a little more (-0.25, then -0.5 radians); the cylinder inside is offset up by half its height so the group's origin is the hinge. Because every section inherits its parent's rotation, the bend accumulates into a curl. A sphere sits at each hinge, with the same radius as the section below, to fill the wedge that opens on the outside of the bend:
const H1 = 1.3, H2 = 1.2, H3 = 1.1; const seg1 = new Group(); seg1.name = 'Crown Section 1'; seg1.position.y = 0.07; hat.add(seg1); const m1 = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.72, 0.95, H1, 64), purple); m1.name = 'Crown 1'; m1.position.y = H1 / 2; seg1.add(m1); const seg2 = new Group(); seg2.name = 'Crown Section 2'; seg2.position.y = H1; seg2.rotation.z = -0.25; seg1.add(seg2); const j1 = new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.72, 64, 32), jointMat); j1.name = 'Joint 1'; seg2.add(j1); const m2 = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.42, 0.72, H2, 64), purple); m2.name = 'Crown 2'; m2.position.y = H2 / 2; seg2.add(m2); const seg3 = new Group(); seg3.name = 'Crown Section 3'; seg3.position.y = H2; seg3.rotation.z = -0.5; seg2.add(seg3); const j2 = new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.42, 64, 32), jointMat); j2.name = 'Joint 2'; seg3.add(j2); const m3 = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(0.05, 0.42, H3, 64), purple); m3.name = 'Crown 3'; m3.position.y = H3 / 2; seg3.add(m3); const tip = new Mesh(new SphereGeometry(0.07, 16, 12), purple); tip.name = 'Tip'; tip.position.y = H3; seg3.add(tip);
A bug worth checking for. The hinge spheres are almost, but not exactly, inside the cone walls, so with the default material they z-fight with them and a sawtooth edge appears at every bend (it gets worse the more finely the cone is tessellated). Shrinking the spheres does not cure it. Giving the joints their own material with polygonOffset pushes them slightly back in depth, so the cone walls always win the tie and the sphere only shows where the bend genuinely opens a gap. Matching the segment counts (64 on the cones and spheres) shrinks what is left.
3 Band, buckle and stars
The band is a cylinder whose two radii are read off the cone's own radius function r1(t) (radius at height t), so it hugs the slope instead of floating or sinking. The buckle is a box with a smaller dark box as its hole. The stars are a 10-point Shape (alternating outer and inner radius) run through ExtrudeGeometry; each is placed on the cone at an angle and then tipped by the cone's slope so it lies flat against it:
const r1 = t => 0.95 - 0.23 * (t / H1); // crown 1 radius at height t const band = new Mesh(new CylinderGeometry(r1(0.36) + 0.02, r1(0.14) + 0.02, 0.22, 40), bandMat); band.name = 'Hat Band'; band.position.y = 0.25; seg1.add(band); const buckle = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.3, 0.28, 0.06), gold); buckle.name = 'Buckle'; buckle.position.set(0, 0.25, r1(0.25) + 0.05); buckle.rotation.x = -0.1; seg1.add(buckle); const hole = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(0.16, 0.14, 0.07), bandMat); hole.name = 'Buckle Hole'; hole.position.set(0, 0.25, r1(0.25) + 0.055); hole.rotation.x = -0.1; seg1.add(hole); // Gold stars, tilted to hug the cone's slope const starShape = new Shape(); for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { const a = Math.PI / 2 + i * Math.PI / 5, r = i % 2 ? 0.07 : 0.17; i ? starShape.lineTo(Math.cos(a) * r, Math.sin(a) * r) : starShape.moveTo(Math.cos(a) * r, Math.sin(a) * r); } starShape.closePath(); const starGeo = new ExtrudeGeometry(starShape, { depth: 0.02, bevelEnabled: false }); const slope = Math.atan(0.23 / H1); [-0.9, 0.9, 2.4, 3.9].forEach((ang, i) => { const star = new Mesh(starGeo, gold); star.name = 'Star ' + (i + 1); const t = 0.85, r = r1(t) + 0.005; star.position.set(Math.sin(ang) * r, t, Math.cos(ang) * r); star.rotation.order = 'YXZ'; star.rotation.y = ang; star.rotation.x = -slope; seg1.add(star); }); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, hat)); tagClass(hat, 'hat');
4 Add it to the scene
One AddObjectCommand adds the whole hat, so it is one undo step. Tag the group with a class, add a cool ambient light, a white key light and a violet rim light from behind, set a dark background, and aim the camera:
editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, new AmbientLight(0xcfc4ff, 0.7))); const key = new DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 1.6); key.position.set(5, 8, 6); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, key)); const rim = new DirectionalLight(0x9a7bff, 0.8); rim.position.set(-6, 4, -5); editor.execute(new AddObjectCommand(editor, rim)); setBackground('#1b1530'); const cam = editor.camera; cam.position.set(3.2, 2.6, 5.6); cam.fov = 45; cam.lookAt(0.4, 1.6, 0); cam.updateProjectionMatrix(); editor.controls.center.set(0.4, 1.6, 0); editor.signals.cameraChanged.dispatch(cam); editor.signals.objectChanged.dispatch(cam);
5 Sculpt the face
The smiley is not painted on and not a separate decal object. It is the cone's own surface, pushed outward. Only the straight lower section (Crown 1) is sculpted, because the face lives on its front. Paste this whole block; the Shell does not allow top-level await, so everything runs inside an async function:
(async () => { const { SetGeometryCommand } = await import('/editor/js/commands/SetGeometryCommand.js'); const crown = editor.scene.getObjectByName('Crown 1'); // A dense replacement for the crown's straight section. thetaStart = PI moves the // seam to the back of the hat, away from the face (the front is +z). const H = 1.3, RT = 0.72, RB = 0.95, RAD = 320, HEI = 140; const g = new CylinderGeometry(RT, RB, H, RAD, HEI, true, Math.PI, Math.PI * 2); const rAt = t => RB - (RB - RT) * (t / H); // crown radius at height t // Soft dome falloff: 1 at the centre, 0 at distance 1 const bump = d => { const w = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, 1 - d)); return w * w * (3 - 2 * w); }; // The face, in surface coordinates: u = arc length around the hat, v = height above the face centre const TC = 0.8; const MR = 0.21, MY = 0.02, P0 = -2.55, P1 = -0.59; // smile = the lower arc of a circle const mouthDist = (u, v) => { const dy = v - MY, rho = Math.hypot(u, dy), ph = Math.atan2(dy, u); if (ph >= P0 && ph <= P1) return Math.abs(rho - MR); const e = p => Math.hypot(u - MR * Math.cos(p), dy - MR * Math.sin(p)); return Math.min(e(P0), e(P1)); // past the ends of the arc, measure to the nearest end }; const relief = (u, v) => { const base = 0.02 * bump((Math.hypot(u, v) - 0.3) / 0.06); // raised disc, flat top, soft edge const eyes = [-0.12, 0.12].reduce((s, ex) => s + bump(Math.hypot((u - ex) / 0.05, (v - 0.1) / 0.075)), 0) * 0.035; const mouth = bump(mouthDist(u, v) / 0.04) * 0.03; return base + eyes + mouth; }; // Push each vertex out along its own normal by the relief height const pos = g.attributes.position, nor = g.attributes.normal; for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) { const x = pos.getX(i), y = pos.getY(i), z = pos.getZ(i); const ang = Math.atan2(x, z); if (Math.abs(ang) > 0.9) continue; // only the front of the hat can be touched const t = y + H / 2; const h = relief(ang * rAt(t), t - TC); if (h > 0) pos.setXYZ(i, x + nor.getX(i) * h, y + nor.getY(i) * h, z + nor.getZ(i) * h); } g.computeVertexNormals(); // computeVertexNormals leaves a lighting seam where the first and last columns meet; average them for (let r = 0; r <= HEI; r++) { const a = r * (RAD + 1), b = a + RAD; const nx = nor.getX(a) + nor.getX(b), ny = nor.getY(a) + nor.getY(b), nz = nor.getZ(a) + nor.getZ(b); const len = Math.hypot(nx, ny, nz) || 1; nor.setXYZ(a, nx / len, ny / len, nz / len); nor.setXYZ(b, nx / len, ny / len, nz / len); } nor.needsUpdate = true; // A CylinderGeometry is saved by its parameters (radius, segments...), which would throw the // sculpted vertices away on Save. Copy them into a plain BufferGeometry so the file keeps them. const baked = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); baked.setAttribute('position', pos); baked.setAttribute('normal', nor); baked.setAttribute('uv', g.attributes.uv); baked.setIndex(g.index); editor.execute(new SetGeometryCommand(editor, crown, baked)); // one undo step editor.deselect(); return 'sculpted ' + pos.count + ' vertices'; })()
Close-up: two raised eyes and a smile on a slightly raised disc, all part of the cone's geometry.
Why each piece is there:
A dense mesh. The original cone has 64 sides and one row of height, so it has nowhere to put a ridge a few hundredths of a unit wide. The replacement has 320 sides and 140 rows (about 45,000 vertices); the smile's ridge spans several vertices instead of one, which is what keeps its edges smooth instead of stair-stepped. openEnded = true drops the caps, which are hidden inside the hat anyway. Surface coordinates, not world coordinates. The face is defined in u (arc length around the hat, angle × radius at that height) and v (height above the face centre). Because the cone is narrower higher up, using the radius at each vertex's own height keeps the face from stretching into an oval. Shapes from falloffs. bump(d) is a smooth dome: 1 at the centre, 0 at distance 1. An eye is bump of the distance from the eye's centre, scaled differently in u and v to make an oval. The smile is bump of the distance to an arc: the lower part of a circle, measuring to the nearest end once you are past the arc's ends. The raised disc is a bump with a flat top. Heights add up: disc 0.02, eyes +0.035, smile 0.03. Push along the normal. Each vertex moves along its own normal by the relief height, not straight out along +z, so the relief follows the cone's slope and stays the same height everywhere. The seam. A cylinder's first and last columns of vertices sit on top of each other, and computeVertexNormals leaves them with different normals, which shows as a lighting line. thetaStart = Math.PI moves that seam to the back of the hat (the face is at +z, angle 0), and the loop at the end averages the two columns' normals so it disappears there too. Bake it so Save keeps it. A CylinderGeometry is written to a saved project as its parameters (radii, segment counts), never its vertices, so a sculpted cylinder would reopen as a plain cone. Copying the finished attributes into an ordinary BufferGeometry makes the file store the vertices themselves. One undo step. SetGeometryCommand swaps the geometry through the editor's history. It is not a Shell global, so it is imported directly. undo() brings back the plain cone and redo() brings back the face.
6 Check it
Confirm the geometry really changed, and that the sculpt is reversible rather than baked into the scene:
const crown = () => editor.scene.getObjectByName('Crown 1').geometry.attributes.position.count; editor.scene.getObjectByName('Crown 1').geometry.type; // 'BufferGeometry' crown(); // 45261 undo(); crown(); // 388 (the original 64-sided cone is back) redo(); crown(); // 45261 $S('.hat').count(); // 1
Make the face your own. Everything lives in relief(u, v). Change TC to move the face up or down the cone, the eye centres ±0.12 and the 0.035 eye height to change the expression, or swap the smile's arc range P0 / P1 and radius MR for a frown or a surprised mouth. Re-running the block replaces the old geometry with a freshly sculpted one.
7 Open the finished hat
The finished scene is public in tejaswigowda/test1: hat.json opens straight in the editor with the brim, the bending cone, the sculpted face, the band, buckle and stars, the three lights and the dark background, all named and tagged as built above.
What is in the file. hat.json includes the sculpted face, because step 5 bakes the crown into plain vertex data before it is saved. Saved from the editor's Git panel, big geometry buffers go out as binary assets next to a small scene file (here about 22 KB of JSON plus a 2.5 MB crown buffer); File → Save writes everything inline, about 8.5 MB. Either way the face survives a save and reload, which a CylinderGeometry crown would not.
